articles.title: Cheap drones caused costly damage during the Iran war — the U.S. is fixing that
articles.text:
The US Army is handing out over $4.15 billion to any company able to stop low-cost drone attacks on home soil
As cheap attack drones proliferate, affordable counter-systems are needed
- US Army awarded $4.15 billion in counter-drone contracts to 10 companies
- Seven of the ten winners each received a $500 million base award
- The framework carries a maximum ceiling of $7 billion across all awards
The US Army has awarded contracts worth $4.15 billion to 10 companies developing technologies against cheap drones threatening military installations and critical infrastructure across the country.
The awards fall under Domestic Shield, a Department of Defense initiative intended to strengthen protection against unmanned aircraft without restricting procurement to individual suppliers.
Seven companies will receive $500 million each, while three others secured smaller awards, establishing a multi-vendor arrangement with a maximum value of $7 billion.
Ten suppliers share billions in counter-drone contracts
Allen Control Systems, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield, L3Harris WESCAM, Napatree Technology, RADA Technologies and SRC each received contracts with $500 million base values under the initiative.
Echodyne and PVP Advanced EO Systems secured awards worth $250 million apiece, while Smart Shooter received a contract valued at $150 million.
The contracts allow military services, federal agencies and allied partners to obtain commercially available counter-drone equipment through a common procurement framework rather than relying on separate purchasing arrangements.
Officials expect further awards below the established contract threshold before the end of October 2026, keeping additional suppliers eligible to participate as procurement continues.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The Army is working with Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Pentagon unit responsible for coordinating efforts against unmanned aerial threats, to administer the initiative.
The arrangement uses multiple suppliers to maintain competition and reduce dependence on technologies controlled by individual vendors.
Open architecture allows different counter-drone systems to work together
The contracted technologies include robotic weapon stations, optical rifle sights, compact radars, long-range tracking cameras, and command-and-control software.
These systems handle different tasks, including detecting aerial threats, tracking their movements and supporting responses, making coordination between equipment an important consideration.
To support that coordination, the Army is requiring open architecture standards that allow equipment from different suppliers to connect with existing defense networks.
“This multi-vendor marketplace enforces strict open architecture standards, breaking proprietary vendor lock, and ensuring new technologies can immediately integrate into our existing defense networks,” said Brent Ingraham, assistant secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology.
The need for these systems became more apparent during the 2026 US–Iran war, when Iranian drone attacks damaged American military facilities and equipment across the Middle East.
On March 3 2026, two Iranian drones struck the US Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, causing physical damage estimated at approximately $11.5 million.
Iranian drones also struck a fuel tank and damaged a US Army asset in Kuwait, while attacks against power stations and desalination plants continued after the ceasefire.
In Saudi Arabia, Iranian drones struck a CIA station in Riyadh, while attacks within a week left 29 American servicemen wounded.
Congressional Research Service estimated that 81 American aircraft and drones were destroyed or damaged during the conflict, with potential losses reaching $3.3 billion.
Iran carried out many of these attacks with swarms of cheap drones and bombs, necessitating affordable counter-drone systems that can intercept incoming threats without exhausting expensive military assets.
Via The Drone Front

articles.title: Maia 300 : Microsoft annonce le déploiement de sa nouvelle génération de puces IA
articles.text:
Microsoft franchit une nouvelle étape dans l'IA. Le géant américain vient en effet de présenter sa nouvelle génération de puces IA maison.
Les grands noms de l'intelligence artificielle ont tous besoin d'accumuler le plus possible de puces IA pour entraîner et faire fonctionner leurs modèles. Et s'ils cherchent à acquérir les meilleurs GPU de NVIDIA, ils développent aussi tous dans le même temps leurs puces maisons, que ce soit Anthropic, OpenAI (qui travaille même pour le coup directement avec Samsung) ou bien le géant de la tech Microsoft.
Maia 300, la troisième génération des puces IA produites par Microsoft
Microsoft a annoncé en ce début de semaine la nouvelle génration des puces IA créées directement en interne, baptisée Maia 300. Il s'agit de la troisième génération des puces made in Microsoft. Elle pourra traiter des données pour assurer des actions comme le codage ou l'exécution de tâches métier complexes.
La génération précédente est actuellement déjà en service dans les serveurs de Microsoft, que ce soit pour faire fonctionner les modèles développés par le géant américain ou les modèles d'OpenAI, disponibles sur le service de cloud computing de Microsoft Azure.
1 million de puces seront déployées dès l'an prochain
Ce qui est intéressant, c'est que cet accélérateur IA utiliser une autre architecture que les produits de NVIDIA. Là où un accélérateur IA de NVIDIA utilise des puces de calcul ultra-puissantes pour offrir la force brute maximale exigée par le marché, la Maia 300 mise sur une structure modulaire sur mesure (et sur la toute dernière génération de mémoire HBM4). Cette architecture personnalisée va permettre à Microsoft d'optimiser à l'extrême la vitesse de ses serveurs cloud, tout en réduisant drastiquement sa facture d'électricité.
Il faut aussi noter que la puce Maia 300 mêle aussi les procédés de gravure, puisque le coeur de calcul est produit avec le procédé de gravure en 2 nm de TSMC, alors que les puces d'entrées-sorties et les contrôleurs mémoires autour sont gravés en 3 nm (ce qui permet de rendre leur production moins couteuse).
« En substance, cela revient à offrir davantage de puissance de calcul pour chaque watt, chaque dollar et chaque octet de mémoire, grâce à une optimisation à l'échelle de l'ensemble du système » résume la présidente des Systèmes matériels et infrastructures Azure de Microsoft, Rani Borkar. Microsoft prévoit de rapidement déployer cette nouvelle génération, avec plus d'un million de puces Maia 300 en service dès l'année prochaine.

articles.title: Nouvelle mise à jour pour le répéteur Wi-Fi Freebox, qui répare un bug sur l'importante bande 5 GHz
articles.text:
Free a déployé ce lundi une mise à jour de son répéteur Wi-Fi pour Freebox. Le nouveau firmware corrige un bug rare touchant la bande 5 GHz et ajoute des correctifs de sécurité, le tout avec une installation quasi automatique.
Free a mis en ligne ce lundi 12 octobre une nouvelle mise à jour pour le répéteur Wi-Fi des Freebox, avec la version 2.9.3 de son firmware. Pour reprendre un terme cher à l'opérateur de Xavier Niel, elle ne révolutionne rien, mais corrige un accroc capable de faire perdre au répéteur l'usage de sa bande 5 GHz. Quant à l'installation, elle demande à peu près autant d'efforts que d'allumer la lumière, avec ou sans Alexa.
Free met à jour le répéteur Wi-Fi des Freebox pour ne plus perdre la bande 5 GHz
Le principal correctif de cette version 2.9.3 s’attaque à un bug plutôt rare, mais néanmoins gênant. Dans certains cas, la carte Wi-Fi 5 GHz du répéteur, c’est-à-dire le composant chargé d’émettre sur cette fréquence, refusait de démarrer. Or le Wi-Fi circule sur plusieurs bandes, un peu comme les voies d’une autoroute. Il y le 2,4 GHz porte loin mais reste plus lent et souvent encombré, quand le 5 GHz offre des débits bien supérieurs à courte distance. Quand le problème survenait, le répéteur se retrouvait donc privé de l'une de ses bandes de fréquence, et les appareils devaient faire sans.
Free ajoute à ce firmware des correctifs de sécurité, sans dire lesquels. C'est plutôt logique, car il est mieux d'éviter de détailler une faille tant que tout le parc n'est pas à jour. Le billet des développeurs ne précise pas non plus si les répéteurs Wi-Fi 7 et Wi-Fi 5, les deux commercialisés par Free, sont tous deux concernés.
Une mise à jour du répéteur qui se fait sans vous
Concernant l'installation de la mise à jour, l'abonné n'a pas grand-chose à faire. D'après Free, le correctif s'applique normalement de lui-même au redémarrage du Freebox Server, et les répéteurs suivent le mouvement. Si le vôtre se fait prier, il suffit de le redémarrer à son tour. Le débrancher puis le rebrancher fait parfaitement l'affaire.
Pour rappel, le répéteur Free prolonge le Wi-Fi de la box jusque dans les pièces les plus éloignées. Grâce à l'AP Steering et au Band Steering, il oriente chaque appareil vers le meilleur point d'accès et la bande la plus adaptée. Les abonnés Ultra, Ultra Essentiel, Pop et Pop S peuvent obtenir un modèle Wi-Fi 7 inclus sur demande, puis jusqu'à trois de plus à 20 euros l'unité.
Les abonnés Révolution Light peuvent obtenir jusqu'à quatre répéteurs Wi-Fi 5 au même tarif. Tous les répéteurs sont mis à disposition, ils ne sont pas vendus. La commande pour se faire directement depuis l'Espace Abonné ou l'app Free.

articles.title: I found the parry-focused swordplay of Valor Mortis incredibly satisfying, but this clash of Souls-like and first-person adventure isn't as sharp as it could be
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The snappy and satisfying parry-focused combat of Valor Mortis will surely delight fans of Sekiro and Lies of P who are looking for a ‘Souls-like’ experience from a new perspective. But while it builds on that core with some inventive set pieces and a gloomy atmosphere, the restrictions of the first-person view make some encounters clunky or irritating, and an obsession with trickery is grating.
Reasons to buy
- + Tight and satisfying combat
- + Inventive and varied set pieces
- + Gruesome world and creature designs
Reasons to avoid
- - Some clunkiness with the first-person view
- - Some dull and frustrating environments
- - Too reliant on traps and trickery
- - Not a huge variety of weapons and powers
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
There’s little else quite so satisfying in gaming as a really chunky parry sound effect. When you read your opponent precisely and time a deflection to perfection, hearing that impactful audio cue as a reward is about as good as it gets — especially if you can follow it up with a devastating finishing move. Valor Mortis nails this.
I never tired of hearing the reverberated twang of blades clashing in my time with the first-person ‘Souls-like’ from One More Level. And given how much time is spent duelling with the reanimated corpses of Napoleonic soldiers, body horror monstrosities, and a few unique creatures I won’t spoil, it’s really something the developers had to nail.
So, I’m pleased to say that they have, and it’s one reason why I stuck with Valor Mortis through several of its other less successful aspects.
Platform reviewed: PC
Available on: PS5, Xbox Series X|S, PC
Release date: October 13, 2026
The opening, however, is strong. You awaken on a battlefield, surrounded by corpses, the rousing voice of Vincent Cassel as Napoleon in your ear encouraging you to move forward. But this conflict has turned into something far worse than just blades and cannon fire. A plague of sorts has torn through the land, transforming humans into monsters and unlocking mystical powers for you to use in your quest to understand exactly what’s happened while you’ve slumbered.
It’s all a setup that fits the Dark Souls-inspired core of the game, with its dangerous, foreboding, war-torn world to explore. This time, lanterns serve as the safe spaces to save your progress, level up using the blood from dead enemies, tweak your build with several skill-tweaking gems, and restart from when you inevitably die.
Your power to fight back against the horrors builds slowly and doesn’t ever get massively expansive. First, a sabre. Then, a pistol. After that, well, it’s the ability to shoot fire from your hands and put enemies in stasis. You can switch between these and a handful more melee, ranged, and magical powers at will — and will often need to do so to tackle different enemy types most effectively.
Bonjour
For example, basic soldiers can be taken out with a few sword slashes. A more imposing axe-wielding officer is better handled by keeping your distance as you burn it with fire to set off the explosive keg on its back. There’s a malformed grenadier who protects its sack of explosives with an engorged hand, but when it moves to lob a grenade at you, a well-timed shot can cause a massive explosion.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As you proceed forward, each encounter requires you to assess whichever threats you’re facing and break down the best way to take them out or exploit a weakness with the tools at your disposal. Of course, you can always go wailing in with a sword, but it’s rarely the smartest move. You have limited stamina, and the aggressive enemies can obliterate you in just a few hits.
As is the trial-and-error nature of these types of games, it takes a few encounters with some new foes to get the better of them, but I wish Valor Mortis wasn’t so obsessed with the trickery of it all. Long delayed attacks that are preceded by multiple feints and five seconds of interpretive dance before a sudden blow pulverises you is kind of funny the first couple of times, but by the dozenth time I was getting irate.
The same goes for some aspects of the level design, which is regularly full of traps and “gotcha” moments. Enemies pop up out of bushes, others surprise you from behind doors, items are placed for you to be ambushed, or trigger rocks falling on you, or make you step on sections of floor that fall out from under you. I get that these moments are meant to keep you on your toes, but when they happen repeatedly in quick succession, they start to feel cheap rather than challenging.
There are a couple of boss fights that I could call out here that feel awesome to emerge from victorious because you perfectly parry all attacks to deliver a satisfying riposte or are wowed by a piece of clever inventiveness, but I wouldn’t want to spoil the specifics. Instead, I’ll keep it vague and just say that when a set piece cleverly mixes combat, puzzle, and platforming elements well, that’s when Valor Mortis hits its peak.
What I do like is that at least Valor Mortis mixes up linear gauntlets with open areas that give you more freedom in how you approach. There are opportunities to sneak up or around to get better vantage points and backstab enemies for an instant kill or significant damage. Thinning out larger groups is definitely something you’ll need to do, as even facing just two enemies at once puts you at a massive disadvantage in the game’s first-person view.
Variety is added further with some fantastic sections that combine the frenetic platforming of the team’s previous Ghostrunner series with the tight combat mechanics to create some entertaining and inventive set pieces. A section across broken-up ships that are suspended in time above the sea is a highlight, as you hop and swing between the splintered decks, take out snipers with your musket, and slash through any remaining soldiers prowling around.
Finding its footing
On the other hand, a diversion into a mine is perhaps one of the game’s most dreary and aggravating sections. Here, lots of tight, dark, and windy corridors are not the easiest to see or fight in. Then, while you’re also trying to dodge and parry different enemies, the game decides to throw freewheeling minecarts that can almost kill you in one hit down these same small alcoves at the same time. A fun idea, in theory, but there’s a point where a situation becomes too chaotic for you to assess it and react to it quickly enough, and so my approach changed to brute force and luck rather than skill.
But then I was quickly brought back again by another thrilling on-rails segment that makes full use of all abilities and weapons you’ve gathered until now, before culminating in a surprising out-of-this-world boss fight that puts the rewarding parrying mechanics front and centre.
When that works, it really works. And the flourishes One More Level adds with ranged weapons and magical abilities are welcome tactical options — even if you will have to rely on swordplay more than anything else. The fact I kept getting beat up but wanted to keep coming back to nail a parry combo shows where the strengths of Valor Mortis lie. It’ll likely scare many away, but if challenging Souls-likes are what you enjoy, here’s another with an intriguing premise and a neat twist to add to your list.
Should you play Valor Mortis?
Play it if…
You’re looking for your next Souls-like
As far as Souls-likes go, Valor Mortis is a good one, especially if you prefer the parry-focused combat seen in the likes of Lies of P and Sekiro.
You enjoyed Ghostrunner but wanted more involved combat
Valor Mortis is far from the speedy pace of the Ghostrunner series, but some of the developer’s inventive platformer and set piece design is in here, just with more emphasis on combat.
You’re a fan of horror
The world, environments, and monsters of Valor Mortis are tinged with horror, while some of the side stories you come across are equally unsettling or downright devastating.
Don’t play it if…
You get frustrated repeating encounters
You’d probably expect this based on the genre alone, but if quick deaths and repeating encounters until you master them are not what you enjoy, then Valor Mortis is best avoided.
You like a lot of weapons and build variety
A trio of swords, a trio of guns, and a few magical skills are all you really get in Valor Mortis. These all work fine and have different strengths and weaknesses, but it doesn’t make for a whole lot of variety in the long run.
Accessibility features
Valor Mortis offers very few accessibility features. In terms of dialogue, there is only an option to adjust the subtitle size between small, medium, and large. Mouse and keyboard, and controller options are available, with full key rebinding possible on the former and several control schemes available to choose from on the latter. You can also adjust the field of view, turn off or tone down camera shaking, as well as turn blood splatter and dismemberment on or off if you prefer a less gory experience.
How I reviewed Valor Mortis
I played over 10 hours of Valor Mortis on PC using an Xbox Wireless Controller and playing audio through my Bose QuietComfort Headphones. I’m using a fairly mid-range rig with a Ryzen 5 9600X, an AMD Radeon RX 9060XT, 48GB of RAM, and a Samsung 990 EVO Plus SSD. My monitor is the MSI MAG 27CQ6F.
With some tweaks to the settings, I was able to play the game on High at 1440p with frame generation on and maintain a comfortable 100+ fps at almost all times. It may not be a hugely demanding game, but it looks good and runs smoothly, which is ideal for reaction-based combat.
First reviewed October 2026.
James Pickard is a Deals Editor at TechRadar. After many years of scouring the net for the cheapest games and tech for his personal use, he decided to make it his job to share all the best bargains and coupon codes with you. James also has almost a decade of experience covering some of the biggest sales events of the year at Eurogamer and VG247, including Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Amazon Prime Day. When not deals hunting or stacking coupon codes to get the biggest savings, James can be found on the PS5, watching a classic film noir or cheering on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

articles.title: Plus besoin de retenir vos mots de passe : Proton Pass Plus coûte 2,49€ par mois
articles.text:
Classé premier de notre comparatif des gestionnaires de mots de passe, Proton Pass propose déjà une version gratuite généreuse. Sa formule Plus y ajoute un authentificateur intégré, des alias e-mail illimités et une surveillance des fuites : reste à savoir pour qui ces ajouts valent la dépense.
Proton Pass est le gestionnaire de mots de passe de Proton, la société suisse connue pour sa messagerie chiffrée, et notre test lui attribue la note de 9/10. Son abonnement Pass Plus est actuellement proposé à 2,49 € par mois sur un an au lieu de 4,99 €, soit 29,88 € facturés pour les 12 premiers mois. Au renouvellement, il passe à 35,88 € par an.
L’offre vise d’abord celles et ceux qui éparpillent encore leurs accès entre le navigateur, une application de double authentification et une adresse e-mail confiée à tous les sites. Si la version gratuite vous suffit déjà, la suite vous aidera à le vérifier.
Proton Pass Plus passe à 2,49 € par mois au lieu de 4,99 € sur le site de Proton, soit 29,88 € pour toute une année d’abonnement.
Pourquoi choisir Proton Pass Plus ?
- Les codes 2FA au même endroit : l’authentificateur intégré génère vos codes de double authentification et les remplit automatiquement, sans passer par une application séparée.
- Des alias sans plafond : la version gratuite s’arrête à 10 adresses masquées, Plus les rend illimitées et permet même d’écrire depuis un alias pour garder votre vraie adresse à l’abri.
- Un chiffrement qui va plus loin : l’adresse du site et l’identifiant sont chiffrés de bout en bout, pas seulement le mot de passe. Proton ne voit donc pas sur quels sites vous avez un compte.
Un coffre qui remplace plusieurs applications
Au quotidien, Pass Plus remplit identifiants et codes de double authentification dans la foulée, depuis l’extension, l’application mobile ou les applications natives pour Windows, macOS et Linux. À l’inscription sur un site, un alias remplace votre adresse réelle et renvoie les messages vers la boîte de votre choix. Le service surveille enfin les fuites de données pour vos adresses Proton, vos alias et jusqu’à dix adresses personnelles, et signale les mots de passe faibles ou réutilisés.
Ces ajouts parlent surtout aux foyers et aux petites équipes : le partage s’étend à dix personnes, contre deux en gratuit, et des liens sécurisés transmettent un accès ponctuel sans le copier dans un message. L’accès d’urgence permet aussi à un proche de confiance de récupérer vos données après un délai d’attente. En revanche, notre test de Proton Pass relève une extension perfectible : les inscriptions en plusieurs étapes échappent souvent à la détection, et certaines pages de connexion bloquent le remplissage automatique. Si dix alias vous suffisent et que vous n’avez pas besoin de codes 2FA intégrés, la version gratuite, sans limite d’identifiants ni d’appareils, fera l’affaire.
Face à Bitwarden, 1Password ou NordPass, où se situe Proton Pass ?
Proton Pass occupe la première place de notre comparatif des meilleurs gestionnaires de mots de passe, devant 1Password, NordPass et Bitwarden. Bitwarden reste une alternative sérieuse pour qui veut une version gratuite open source sans limite d’appareils, quand 1Password ne propose qu’un essai de 14 jours. Pass Plus se distingue surtout par le chiffrement des métadonnées et ses alias intégrés, même si NordPass propose lui aussi un masquage d’adresse. À plusieurs, Pass Family, à 4,99 € par mois sur un an pour six personnes, sera plus logique.
✅ Les points forts
- Authentificateur 2FA intégré, avec remplissage automatique des codes
- Alias e-mail illimités, utilisables pour envoyer des messages
- URL et identifiants chiffrés de bout en bout, en plus des mots de passe
- Applications natives pour Windows, macOS et Linux, en plus du mobile
❌ Les limites
- Extension perfectible sur les inscriptions en plusieurs étapes et certaines pages de connexion
- Un seul audit indépendant publié, mené par Cure53 en 2023, qui ne couvre pas les applications de bureau
- Renouvellement à 35,88 € par an après la première année
Proton assortit Pass Plus à 29,88 € la première année d’une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours, de quoi vérifier qu’il colle à vos usages.
À 2,49 € par mois la première année, Proton Pass Plus se justifie dès que vous voulez regrouper mots de passe, codes de double authentification et adresses masquées dans un seul outil. C’est son vrai argument face à la version gratuite, qui couvre déjà le stockage et la synchronisation. Le chiffrement des adresses de sites et des identifiants parlera aussi aux personnes attentives à leur vie privée. Gardez en tête que le tarif remonte à 35,88 € par an au renouvellement.
Celles et ceux qui partagent des accès avec leurs proches ou multiplient les inscriptions en ligne en tireront le plus. Si vous attendez un remplissage automatique sans accroc sur tous les sites, l’extension demandera encore de la patience. Pour une poignée de comptes, la version gratuite reste un bon point de départ, à faire évoluer vers Plus le jour où les alias viendront à manquer.

articles.title: The Apple Upgrade program is great for consumers and Apple, but bad for carriers like Verizon and AT&T — here's why
articles.text:
19 years ago, the iPhone broke the cell carrier business and built what we have today — and Apple's new Upgrade program could break it all over again
Opinion: The Apple Upgrade program is a net positive for consumers, but there are knock-on effects that could yet have a lasting impact
Where were you when the first iPhone went on sale back in 2007? I remember clearly that I was working for Phones4U — a third-party phone reseller in the UK — and the iPhone launch completely decimated the business, as suddenly Phones4U wasn't a reseller of the most popular phone on the market.
The same existential threat applied to all carriers except AT&T and O2, which had exclusive launch rights to the iPhone in the US and UK, respectively.
Fast-forward 19 years, and Apple has repeatedly proven that the iPhone's popularity gives it considerable power over its carrier partners — customers are no longer loyal to the carrier providing the mobile service, but to the brand behind their favorite phone.
Apple's newest commercial venture, the Apple Upgrade program — which was announced earlier this year and is, at the time of writing, still only available in the US — is the latest dagger to the heart of major MNOs (Mobile Network Operators).
But despite being a fantastic deal for customers and Apple itself (and make no mistake: I believe it's a net positive move), the Apple Upgrade program could yet prove a double-edged sword for the mobile industry as a whole. Let me explain.
Carriers used to have ALL the power...
To understand what the Apple Upgrade program is, you have to first understand how the industry worked before the original iPhone. To say that Apple has irrevocably changed the carrier business model on numerous occasions may seem like hyperbole, but it’s hard to overstate the company's lasting effect.
Before the original iPhone, carriers were integral to a phone's success. Carriers controlled which phones were sold in stores, which phones received the bigger marketing pushes, and which were “certified” to work with that carrier.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
This meant that all phone makers had to focus more on acquiescing to carrier requests — including shipping customized devices with several preloaded apps and even carrier-specific branding — than meeting their customers' needs.
In many ways, carriers were the customer rather than the end-user itself, and they proved even more integral, as each carrier also controlled when software updates were released to its phones. I remember clearly how customers would blame the phone maker for software-related shortcomings rather than the carrier, even if the software update was delayed by the carrier’s own internal testing.
The power of carriers was inevitably going to be replaced by a different model, but the iPhone had a marked effect on the power wielded by carriers in more ways than one.
... until Apple launched the original iPhone
If you’ve seen the BlackBerry movie, you’ll remember the line used to describe the original iPhone before it went on sale: it had the "highest interest of any consumer electronic item in history". To go further, its original $499 / £269 price also made it the most expensive phone in history at the time.
But contrary to industry standards at the time, the exceptional consumer interest in the original iPhone meant carriers were clamoring to stock it, rather than Apple having to entice them to sell it. This complete reversal of established norms also meant Apple was able to stamp out many of the key controls carriers had, and the effect was stark.
Let’s consider each of the previous requests that carriers would make of a phone maker. Branding on the phone itself or in the software? Gone for the iPhone. Preloaded carrier apps and other bloatware? Gone for the iPhone. A software update schedule controlled by carriers? Apple releases updates to all phones at the same time globally. Customized models? Carriers should be grateful they get to stock the iPhone at all.
However, Apple's unique position went even further. Phone makers used to have to discount phones and offer incentives, but for many years, Apple did not. Granted, we are now in an era in which Apple competes through trade-in promotions and works closely with its carrier partners, but it was the last major phone maker to embrace promotional pricing of any kind.
It's not just Apple that has benefited from these changes; as Apple established new ground rules, companies like Samsung, Google, and LG have all benefited from a different playbook than in the pre-smartphone era.
Now, with the Apple Upgrade program, Apple again holds outsized control over the customer journey. For many, this is a great program, but for other stakeholders, it’s decidedly not. Here’s why.
The Apple Upgrade program is a great deal for consumers
The Apple Upgrade Program is a leasing program provided by Apple, with financing by Klarna. It lets you lease a new iPhone, Mac, iPad, or Apple Watch and pay for it monthly over a fixed lease period (between 12 months and 36 months). At the end of the lease, you can opt to return the item to Apple at no charge or buy it out for the remaining value; the latter is a particularly attractive offer for customers.
Most lease programs have you spending more money over the course of the lease compared with buying the item outright. This arbitrage is how the financing lender makes their money, but with the Apple Upgrade program, you’ll never pay more in total than the outright purchase value.
This is crucial: Apple is effectively offering 0% financing across its range of products, and while it likely pays Klarna directly for providing these services, it does not pass any additional costs on to the customer. In essence, you can still buy any Apple item you plan to, but you now have a more flexible way to pay for it, with no credit card or specific credit limit needed.
... and also great for Apple
The current state of RAMageddon — aka the soaring cost of all technology due to the shortage of RAM modules — meant it was inevitable that Apple would have to increase its product prices, which it did by a considerable margin in both June and September this year.
Despite Apple customers traditionally being less price-sensitive than Android customers, rising prices during a global cost-of-living crisis would inevitably have impacted its financial statements and, therefore, its share price.
The Apple Upgrade program changes this reality in a big way: in the US at least, it’s now far easier for customers to buy Apple products (and more of them) than they used to be able to, and Apple itself gains far more valuable numbers to present to its shareholders: the number of customers on subscriptions; the dollar value of those sold; and the number of customers.
More than that, the Upgrade Program offers Apple predictable revenue numbers for quarters and years into the future, and allows it to launch more products across the year without worrying as much about established launch cycles and windows.
It also makes all of its new products far more accessible to the masses, which is particularly prescient given the now-confirmed $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499 launch price of the iPhone Duo, which begins shipping next week.
However, the Apple Upgrade program is bad for carriers...
For all its positives, there are two areas where the Apple Upgrade program could have a negative effect — and both stem from its potential impact on carriers.
Like the now-discontinued iPhone Upgrade program before it, an iPhone purchased via the Apple Upgrade program is seemingly unlocked for use on any network. It still requires activation with one of the Big Three carriers — Verizon, T-Mobile US, or AT&T — at the point of sale, but once you complete said activation, you can switch to a different carrier of your choosing.
This undoubtedly reduces the need to be locked into a long-term, multi-year contract with your carrier and, crucially, removes a key source of revenue from locked devices: roaming fees. Together, they will impact carriers’ revenue, inevitably leading to several knock-on effects for the consumer.
First, customers will inevitably end up paying more for their service plans, whether through higher plan costs, higher add-on costs, or even increased out-of-bundle charges.
Second, the above will lead to an even more booming MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) market, but as we’ve seen with Mint Mobile, these MVNOs will also inevitably be acquired by the aforementioned big carriers they rely on.
The biggest impact will be felt in network technology and retail footprint. Verizon, T-Mobile US, and AT&T are publicly traded and have a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders. They might pay even more for future spectrum holdings, but the adoption and rollout of future technologies could be much slower if the Apple Upgrade program takes off in the way Apple clearly hopes. This isn’t just hyperbole; we’ve already seen this happen with the 5G rollout and the LTE rollout before it.
The impact will be even more acute for those who like to frequent carrier retail stores. T-Mobile has already made some services fully digital, and, like other industries, phone retail seems to be undergoing a managed decline. Further pressure on carriers’ revenue sources will simply accelerate this shift, leaving vulnerable customers most likely to feel the effects.
So, yes, the Apple Upgrade program is a fantastic deal for most people involved, but I am concerned about the impact it will have on carrier operations, and specifically how these operations might impact consumers in the long term.
Having said all that, my next Apple purchase will almost certainly be through the Apple Upgrade program — it’s a deal that’s too good not to take advantage of, especially if you’re buying one of Apple's higher-spec models.

articles.title: Agences de communication et studios créatifs : des cibles sous-estimées qui détiennent des données clients sensibles
articles.text:
Vous vous demandez peut-être ce qui, dans les dossiers de votre agence de publicité ou de votre studio créatif, peut bien intéresser des cybercriminels. Et c’est bien normal, car votre cœur de métier, c'est la création, pas la cybersécurité.
La réponse est simple. Une agence travaille presque toujours pour plusieurs clients à la fois, et pour chaque nouveau contrat, vous créez une base de données supplémentaire qui vient s’ajouter à vos serveurs.
Pour un pirate informatique, cette mine d’informations stockée dans une petite structure comme votre TPE ou votre PME vaut souvent plus qu’une grande entreprise.
Parce qu’en perçant une seule fois vos défenses, il accède aux clients de plusieurs organisations à la fois. Une grande entreprise cliente consacre souvent plus de moyens à sa sécurité informatique qu'une agence de taille modeste. Les cybercriminels le savent et attaquent d’abord le prestataire, plus vulnérable, plutôt que l’entreprise qu’il sert, c’est-à-dire vous.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Vos données ne sont jamais seulement les vôtres
Vos briefs confidentiels, les identifiants des comptes publicitaires de vos clients et leurs bases d’abonnés à votre newsletter sont souvent hébergés sur les mêmes serveurs, quel que soit le client concerné. Si vous dirigez un studio créatif, vous conservez aussi des maquettes de campagnes encore secrètes et des calendriers de lancement que les marques n’ont pas encore rendus publics. Un cybercriminel qui arrive à passer vos dispositifs de cybersécurité accède, d'un coup, à l'ensemble de vos clients.
C'’est ainsi qu’en janvier, des attaquants ont compromis un sous-traitant chargé du support client de ManoMano. Ils ont récupéré des noms, des adresses e-mail, des numéros de téléphone et l’historique de conversations de plusieurs clients de l’entreprise. Mais ce n’est pas ManoMano qui était la cible de l’intrusion. La CNIL, l’ANSSI et la plateforme cyber d’Île-de-France en ont été informées. Les données de vos clients transitent par vos outils et sont donc en danger au même risque que les vôtres.
Au titre du règlement européen sur la protection des données, vous avez souvent la qualité de sous-traitant de vos clients dès que votre agence traite leurs données personnelles. Vous devez donc respecter des obligations de sécurité précises, prévues par l’article 28 du texte, et vous répondez de vos manquements aux côtés de la marque que vous servez. Et attention, ça ne plaisante pas. En mai 2025, la CNIL a sanctionné Solocal Marketing Services à hauteur de 900 000 euros pour des manquements liés au consentement dans ses campagnes de prospection commerciale. La sanction portait sur la façon dont l’entreprise traitait les données de prospects avant de les exploiter commercialement, sans lien avec un piratage. Le secteur du marketing et de la communication est donc déjà sous surveillance étroite du régulateur français.
Les pirates informatiques exploitent d’abord les maillons humains et techniques
Le courrier électronique est l’outil le plus simple à pirater. Votre agence échange chaque jour avec des dizaines de journalistes, d’influenceurs et de fournisseurs extérieurs. Dans ce flux, vous ne pouvez pas forcément repérer un message frauduleux. Un attaquant peut imiter la facture d'un de vos prestataires habituels ou la demande urgente d'un client. Il suffit de cliquer une seule fois sur une pièce jointe piégée pour installer un accès durable dans vos systèmes. Vous n’avez pas le temps, agissez dans l’urgence ou par habitude et les cybercriminels profitent aussi de cela.
En plus de la messagerie, d’autres outils de votre système sont vulnérables.
Pour vos campagnes publicitaires, si votre compte Meta Business ou Google Ads est mal protégé, vous donnez directement accès aux budgets publicitaires de vos clients. En retrouvant un mot de passe réutilisé sur plusieurs plateformes, vous permettez aussi d’ouvrir bien plus qu’un seul compte à n’importe quel intrus.
Votre agence travaille aussi, la plupart du temps, avec des graphistes, des monteurs ou des rédacteurs freelances connectés depuis des ordinateurs personnels. Si leur matériel personnel n’est pas sécurisé, un attaquant peut ensuite atteindre vos outils partagés.
Votre agence est, la plupart du temps, une TPE ou une PME. Le baromètre 2025 de Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr indique que 16 % des TPE-PME interrogées ont déjà subi une cyberattaque au cours des douze derniers mois, et 22 % ne disposent d’aucune sauvegarde de leurs données. Trois répondants sur quatre consacrent moins de 2 000 euros par an à leur sécurité informatique. Et vous ?
Protégez-vous sans ralentir votre activité ni nuire à votre créativité
Commencez par séparer les accès. Réservez les droits d’administration des comptes publicitaires et des CRM à un nombre restreint de personnes, et activez la double authentification sur chaque outil qui le permet. Avec cette précaution, vous repoussez la plupart des tentatives de piratage de compte, même quand un mot de passe a fuité ailleurs.
Adoptez ensuite un gestionnaire de mots de passe pour toute l’équipe, plutôt que des mots de passe partagés dans un fichier ou répétés d’un outil à l’autre. Vous limitez les dégâts si un compte est compromis.
Mettez également à jour vos logiciels de création et vos extensions de navigateur dès qu’un correctif est disponible. N’oubliez pas que du point de vue d'un cybercriminel, une faille connue et non corrigée n’est pas un oubli, c’est une faille à exploiter.
Sauvegardez vos fichiers de travail et vos bases de contacts en dehors de votre poste principal, sur un service de stockage en ligne ou sur un disque externe déconnecté après chaque copie. Vous évitez qu'un rançongiciel ne détruise en une nuit des mois de travail créatif.
Vérifiez enfin les pratiques de sécurité de vos prestataires numériques, notamment les plateformes d’envoi d’e-mails et les outils de stockage en ligne, avant de leur confier des données clients. En tant que sous-traitant de vos clients au sens du règlement européen sur la protection des données, vous devez formaliser ces garanties dans vos contrats.
Formez vos équipes, en particulier les personnes qui suivent les budgets publicitaires au quotidien, à reconnaître un lien suspect ou une demande de virement inhabituelle. Une équipe formée repère souvent ce qu'un logiciel de sécurité laisse passer.
Une agence qui découvre une fuite de données et ne la signale pas à la CNIL dans les 72 heures risque une amende administrative pouvant s’élever à 10 millions d’euros ou 2 % de son chiffre d’affaires mondial, sans parler des pertes liées au piratage.

articles.title: Has OpenAI started the 'mathpocalypse'? Experts say AI's solving of iconic math problems may cause huge issues in the long run
articles.text:
Has OpenAI started the 'mathpocalypse'? Experts say AI's solving of iconic math problems may cause huge issues in the long run
AI is solving advanced math problems at an alarming rate
- OpenAI has solved or partially solved 372 outstanding mathematical challenges
- Some of the solutions, while clear, cannot be understood by some humans, and were produced with an internal, unreleased AI model
- Renowned mathematician Terence Tao has called for colleagues working with OpenAI to abandon their projects
OpenAI has stunned the world of advanced maths by releasing solutions and partial solutions to 372 outstanding problems that have puzzled the world’s greatest minds for decades.
Just two years ago, AI was finding it tricky to handle GCSE-level mathematical challenges. Today, it is solving problems that have taken humans years to even establish the existence of. The solutions provided, meanwhile, are considered almost as complex as the problems, and the scale – published in 722 papers – make it difficult for human mathematicians to understand and verified.
The impact of the release has prompted one of the world’s greatest mathematicians, Terence Tao, to call for a return to a traditional vision of science.
Demonstration of power
OpenAI’s publication of its work on these advanced mathematical problems is the latest demonstration of how far the technology has come. Just a few weeks ago, the company published its proposal for the Navier-Stokes equation (concerning the behaviour of viscous fluids), generated by its unreleased specialized math model.
Tao is leading the opposition, as one of the field’s leading voices, and a man considered to be the greatest living mind in mathematics.
Following OpenAI’s contribution, he shared a post from the Association for Human Mathematics, which concludes:
“Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power. We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAI and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
However, as powerful as that conclusion is, their response to OpenAI’s intervention as a whole highlights that the company may have overstepped.
Questions of legitimacy
The Association for Human Mathematics states that “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” continuing that “The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, from whom OpenAI has claimed to derive its legitimacy, opened their initial advisory statement by saying that frontier AI corporations should not test advanced mathematical problems on internal models.”
By ignoring the position of the advisory group, they state that OpenAI has essentially gone beyond the pale, and “indicated total disregard for the norms of scientific research — norms that guarantee that mathematics remains trustworthy, ethically researched, and in the public interest.” Furthermore, they encourage mathematicians to treat the publication with “due skepticism.”
OpenAI has responded by stating "we want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics." However, its actions are being interpreted as reckless, and this showboating may well prove to be damaging for OpenAI and the wider AI industry.

articles.title: I watched all eight episodes of 'VisionQuest' on Disney+ — and the new Marvel TV show is a mind-bending sci-fi triumph powered by Paul Bettany's Vision and James Spader's Ultron
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Anchored by electrifying performances from Paul Bettany and James Spader, VisionQuest is a subversive, genre-bending slice of superhero sci-fi. Equal parts tragic, funny, and deeply human, it brings the MCU's Wanda/Vision trilogy to a triumphant close while setting up an exciting future for some of its eclectic cast.
Reasons to buy
- + A deeply satisfying trilogy capper
- + Bettany and Spader’s electric dynamic
- + Emotionally rich themes
- + Multi-genre storytelling at its finest
Reasons to avoid
- - Minor mid-season pacing stumbles
- - Some character arcs lack depth
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Light spoilers follow for VisionQuest.
No Marvel movie trilogy is perfect. That might sound like a loaded statement, but ask any Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) fan and they'll concede that even the franchise's gold standards — the original Captain America films, or Guardians of the Galaxy movie series, to name just two — have flaws.
So, it falls to Marvel's TV show department to show its big-screen counterpart how to deliver a truly complete arc. And, with two acclaimed entries — WandaVision and Agatha All Along — under its belt, the Wanda/Vision TV trilogy only needed to stick the landing with a strong, final act to stake its claim as the MCU's best three-part story.
Thankfully, VisionQuest does exactly that, delivering a scintillating slice of superhero science fiction, and a surprisingly deep and emotionally resonant conclusion to the Wanda/Vision Saga.
Paranoid android
Set some time after WandaVision's finale, VisionQuest reunites us with White Vision (Paul Bettany), the reanimated, blank-slate synthezoid rebuilt by S.W.O.R.D after Thanos destroyed the original. Now laying low in Edinburgh as a bartender named Sherwood, he's grappling with a severe identity crisis, caught between his vacuous programming and the restored memories of his past life.
Searching for purpose, Vision has turned inward and now consults the AI programs embedded in his programming, including Ultron (James Spader), whose leftover code lingers in Vision's system.
Unfortunately, his peaceful existence is about to be interrupted.
Hunted by Paladin (Todd Stashwick), a mercenary hired by a mysterious client who wants his highly-advanced tech, Vision's quiet life is further upended when he meets Thomas Shepard (Ruaridh Mollica), a thief claiming to be one of Vision and Wanda's twin sons. Forced to go on the run, Vision must evade capture, uncover the truth about Thomas, and resist Ultron's insidious influence.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
After 12 years portraying Vision, Bettany has more than earned his shot at leading a solo project that not only lets him shine, but add profound substance to the synthezoid.
Armed with his obvious talent, and clever scripts from showrunner Terry Matalas and his writing team, Bettany thrives on the earnest, amusing, mind-bending, and occasionally sinister material he has to work with.
Crucially, as this Marvel Phase 6 show reminds us, this isn't quite the Vision we knew, but a repurposed and weaponized Re-Vision (if you will) of the original — and Bettany plays the uncanny shift brilliantly.
Indeed, he delivers a striking performance as a morally gray Vision, whose emotional turmoil gives rise to a colder, darker version of the character that strays dangerously into Ultron 2.0 territory more than once. Yet there's a strange delight in seeing this side of Vision fully unleashed on his foes, delivering some unexpectedly bloody, brutal beatdowns along the way.
Only highlighting his ruthless streak would be a disservice to the depth Bettany brings, though.
Given the performances of VisionQuest's terrific supporting ensemble, of which the spellbinding Spader is the clear highlight (more on him shortly), I initially worried that Bettany would be upstaged in his own show. Those fears were completely shattered by his mesmeric, commanding display in the penultimate episode — a chapter that, major spoilers notwithstanding, makes Bettany's infamous dual-acting scene in WandaVision's finale feel like small fry.
Father and son
While VisionQuest is naturally positioned as a Vision-first story, it wouldn't have worked as well without the scene-stealing Spader.
Reprising his role 12 years on from his only MCU appearance, in Avengers: Age of Ultron, Spader is an utter delight from the outset. Ultron's abrupt death was a sore point for fans wanting more of Spader's sassy, loquacious, and menacing android in the MCU, and VisionQuest gives him the chance to chew the scenery again, with a multifaceted performance that keeps you guessing about his true motives at every turn.
As the proverbial family misfit of Vision's surrogate AI clan, and the button-pushing devil on Vision's shoulder, Ultron's modus operandi remains grounded in manipulation. Yet, despite his destructive father-figure tendencies, there's far more to this version of Ultron than meets the eye — a depth that truly reveals itself whenever Spader and Bettany share the screen.
Their brief, piercingly philosophical exchange in Age of Ultron already teased their sharp dynamic, but an eight-part series gives Bettany and Spader room to fully unpack the complexities of Vision and Ultron's paternal bond.
Indeed, there's a genuine earnestness to their paradoxically human conversations, which carry the weight of a two-hander Shakespearean tragedy. And, while their odd-couple partnership offers plenty of welcome levity, it's the soulful, quiet segments that ultimately left the biggest impression on me.
The bond between Bettany's Vision and Mollica's charismatic yet anguished Shepard receives a similarly compelling, if slightly less expansive, exploration.
Driven by striking parallels in their search for identity, their dynamic is equal parts melodrama, humor, charm, and raw sentiment. Bettany and Mollica capture the ill-equipped dad and parentally unanchored son with real nuance, fitting seamlessly into VisionQuest's overarching study of intergenerational paternal trauma. Watching them navigate this fledgling family connection, and the trust that slowly takes root, is easily another of the Disney+ show's biggest strengths.
This modern glitch
VisionQuest's long-form storytelling format affords it the time and space to explore Vision's AI family, even if it's fairly selective in terms of who actually gets the spotlight.
The bubbly E.D.I.T.H (Emily Hampshire) is an easy standout among Vision's digital siblings, though lacks the complete character arc given to the overly cautious F.R.I.D.A.Y (Orla Brady). The rest of of the AI ensemble serves as comic relief — a role capably filled by Henry Lewis' D.U.M-E and Jonathan Sayer's U occupy — while James D'Arcy's J.A.R.V.I.S, is criminally underused, for reasons I can't reveal here in order to avoid spoilers.
Fortunately, Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) doesn't suffer the same fate. Teased as one of four villains in VisionQuest's official trailer, this morally complex android plays a far more important role than I had initially anticipated.
I had concerns that separating Bettany and Spader's electrifying dynamic at VisionQuest's midpoint might impact its narrative impetus. However, Spader and Miller's captivating chemistry as misfits with a united goal quickly allayed those fears. Drawn together by a shared emotional void, their tragic, dysfunctional romance provides a bittersweet alternative to Bettany and Spader's dynamic that admirably fills the void.
Narratively, VisionQuest doesn't always hit the sweet spot.
Todd Stashwick's cold and calculating Paladin makes for an intriguing threat early on, but he's disappointingly sidelined as the plot advances, which frustratingly leaves his backstory somewhat unexplored. Elsewhere, the show's first major plot twist lacks the heart-shattering impact it strives for, while a few tense midseason beats are undermined by jarring editing choices.
By contrast, VisionQuest's tonal shifts rarely drag its story down. A multi-genre narrative in every sense, it effortlessly flits between light-hearted, clever, and innuendo-based humor, and dark, visceral moments (believe me, it's more violent that you'd expect) without letting its sci-fi elements overwhelm the human core.
And then there's the perpetual elephant in the room: the long shadow cast by Tony Stark. Marvel's habit of tethering stories to Robert Downey Jr's iconic character can often feel like a tired trope, yet here it works. VisionQuest isn't shy or subtle about its overarching exploration of the 'sins of the father', retracing the AI family tree through Stark, and — again I'm avoiding major spoilers here — even further back into the MCU’s past. Given how deeply that lineage intersects with Vision, Ultron, and the rest of this eclectic cast, Stark's looming presence feels entirely organic to the story being told.
My verdict
VisionQuest is a terrifically assembled, genre-bending conclusion to the Wanda/Vision TV trilogy. Equally enjoyable as a standalone tale as it is as part of a larger saga, it delivers an emotionally rich examination about what it means to be human — all wrapped up in a mind-melting, expectation-subverting package that's full of gusto, poise, and visual flair.
As its end credits rolled for the final time, I couldn't help but be reminded of Vision's famous quote from Age of Ultron: "A thing isn't beautiful because it lasts." As an eight-part miniseries, there's an obvious finality to VisionQuest, but that doesn't mean we can't appreciate it for the triumph it is, both now and for years to come — and that's the exact kind of beauty I can get behind.
VisionQuest makes its worldwide debut on Disney+ with a two-episode premiere on Wednesday, October 14.

articles.title: Amazon partage avec les entreprises les outils inspirés de son million de robots, la France en bonne place
articles.text:
Amazon Web Services a lancé sa Physical AI Toolchain, une boîte à outils open source pour concevoir des robots dotés d'IA physique. Une étude sur la discipline classe la France parmi les marchés « en accélération », mais pointe des clients encore frileux.
Depuis le 8 octobre, Amazon Web Services met à disposition des entreprises sa Physical AI Toolchain, une boîte à outils d'IA physique nourrie de l'expérience d'Amazon et de sa flotte de plus d'un million de robots. La promesse belle, puisque la solution open source a été conçue, avec NVIDIA d'ailleurs, pour aider les entreprises à lancer leurs propres machines intelligentes, capables de percevoir, de raisonner et d'agir, en quelques semaines plutôt qu'en plusieurs années. Mais l'étude publiée dans la foulée par l'entreprise dessine un tableau plus nuancé, où le frein n'est pas forcément la technologie et où la France se distingue, dans un sens comme dans l'autre.
IA physique : AWS ouvre la boîte à outils de ses robots
L’IA physique, c’est l’intelligence artificielle qui sort de l’écran pour piloter des robots, des drones ou des machines industrielles. Grâce à leurs caméras et à leurs capteurs, ces machines perçoivent ce qui les entoure et adaptent leurs gestes. Pour aider les industriels à en concevoir, des usines aux entrepôts, AWS découpe le travail en étapes. On commence par générer des données d’entraînement par ordinateur, dites synthétiques, pour limiter les coûteuses collectes dans le monde réel. Le modèle d’IA, véritable cerveau de la machine, s’entraîne ensuite et fait ses gammes dans une simulation, avant de rejoindre le vrai matériel. Une fois installé dans le robot, il décide sur place, sans dépendre d’une connexion permanente au cloud.
Les données recueillies par les machines sur le terrain repartent dans le cloud pour réentraîner les modèles, et toute la flotte profite ensuite de ce que chaque robot a appris. AWS promet que plus une entreprise déploie de machines, plus elles deviennent performantes, et la centième profitera de tout ce que les 99 précédentes auront appris. Une entreprise peut toutefois se contenter des briques qui l'intéressent, comme la simulation ou l'entraînement, les brancher à ses propres outils, puis mettre à jour à distance, sans intervention sur place, des milliers d'appareils. Uwem Ukpong, le vice-président d'AWS Industries, explique que l'objectif du mastodonte est ici de libérer les ingénieurs, jusque-là trop accaparés par la tuyauterie informatique au détriment de l'innovation.
Côté technique, AWS et NVIDIA se partagent le travail. Amazon apporte la puissance de son cloud avec SageMaker, sa plateforme d'entraînement des modèles d'IA, ses serveurs de calcul EC2, équipés de puces graphiques pour faire tourner les simulations, IoT Greengrass, qui expédie les modèles vers les machines sur le terrain, et Bedrock AgentCore, chargé de coordonner l'ensemble.
NVIDIA fournit, de son côté, les briques propres à la robotique. Il y a Isaac Sim, un simulateur qui reproduit le monde réel, Isaac Lab, où les robots apprennent par essais et erreurs, GR00T, conçu pour entraîner les humanoïdes, et Cosmos, qui génère des mondes virtuels pour multiplier les scénarios d'entraînement. Le code de la boîte à outils est ouvert, mais l'ensemble s'appuie sur des services AWS payants. L'étude publiée en parallèle par Amazon tombe à pic, puisque 72 % des start-up de l'IA physique jugent le cloud indispensable, et 62 % n'auraient pas pu démarrer sans lui.
La France en bonne place dans la course à l’IA physique
L'étude en question, réalisée par le cabinet Strand Partners et présentée par AWS, a interrogé 4 420 start-up dans 20 pays. Une sur sept conçoit déjà de l'IA physique. Oubliez pourtant les androïdes de science-fiction, puisque seules 12 % de ces conceptrices travaillent sur des robots humanoïdes ou entièrement autonomes. Leur terrain de jeu favori reste la vision par ordinateur (55 %) et les capteurs embarqués (50 %), autrement dit les yeux et les nerfs des machines. Selon elles, l'industrie et l'automobile (55 %) seront bousculées en premier, juste devant la logistique et le commerce (52 %).
La France fait bonne figure. 17 % de ses jeunes pousses développent de l'IA physique, contre 15 % en moyenne dans les vingt pays étudiés. Le rapport range l'Hexagone parmi les marchés « en accélération », ceux qui talonnent les pays les plus avancés, et la France en prend la tête, à égalité avec Singapour. Devant elle, un peloton de six pays, dont les États-Unis, le Japon et le Royaume-Uni, est emmené par l'Allemagne (24 %). Sur l'emploi, en revanche, l'optimisme se fait plus mesuré. Dans l'ensemble des pays, 58 % des start-up pensent que l'IA physique créera plus d'emplois qu'elle n'en supprimera. En France, elles ne sont que 50 %, et 19 % redoutent l'inverse, la part la plus élevée des vingt pays.
Le principal frein à l'essor de l'IA physique ne vient pas de la technologie, mais des clients. Car seul un quart des start-up du secteur estime que son marché est prêt à déployer l'IA physique. Elles ne sont que 14 % à penser que la plupart des entreprises de leur pays pourraient sauter le pas dès aujourd'hui, beaucoup n'ayant tout simplement jamais vu ces machines fonctionner. Résultat, 70 % disent que des clients trop lents à se décider freinent leur croissance. On peut y ajouter d'autres obstacles, comme avec les 66 % qui ont du mal à trouver des financements, car le matériel coûte cher et demande de longs développements, et 48 % voient les droits de douane ou les barrières commerciales compliquer l'accès à leurs composants. Le temps presse pourtant, puisque 76 % s'attendent à ce que l'IA physique devienne courante dans leur secteur d'ici cinq ans.

articles.title: Trying to change your browser? It might be harder than you think, based on one simple thing
articles.text:
Trying to change your browser? It might be harder than you think, based on one simple thing
Mozilla says Microsoft is abusing its dominant position wherever it can
- Mozilla accused Microsoft of using Windows, Edge, Bing, and Copilot to steer users toward Edge
- Firefox maker claims stricter EU regulations force fairer browser choice than elsewhere
- Browser competition increasingly overlaps with the fight for AI distribution and user reach
Mozilla has accused Microsoft of abusing its dominant position wherever it can to push people towards Edge, and away from other browsers.
The company framed the story as if it wants “better for the people”, while Microsoft only does it when it’s forced to, but is that really the case?
In a newly released blog, Mozilla noted it has now been 100 days since it published Over The Edge 2.0, a report from “leading experts on deceptive design Dr. Harry Brignull and Cennydd Bowles on how Windows, Edge, Bing, and Copilot are designed to steer people away from the browser they choose.”
Better for the people
In the report, Mozilla said that in the European Economic Area (EEA), where the Digital Market Acts (DMA) is being enforced, Microsoft is forced to “play fair”.
Anywhere else around the world, including the US, UK, India, and other parts of the planet, it still uses its “shady tactics”. These include the Windows 10 message “You’re almost done setting up your PC” which allegedly uses “tricky wording” to pull people off the default they picked, Windows Search and Widgets opening links in Edge instead of the default browser, and Windows keeping Edge as the default for common browser file types like PDF and SVG, even after another browser were set up as the default.
Mozilla claims that even within the EU, Microsoft is doing all it can to steer people towards Edge. That includes pre-pinning the browser to the taskbar which, according to the company, “seems to directly violate the ‘principled approach to app pinning and app defaults’, Copilot opening web links in a side-panel instead of in the browser, and Windows Backup “silently” trying to set Edge as the default when it restores a PC and “fails to properly bring the user’s own browser along. “
“Most of the 2024 patterns are still there. The 2026 patterns are worse. Microsoft is using new surfaces like Copilot and the migration to Windows 11 to further undermine user choice,” Mozilla claims.

“We also shared the report with Microsoft and talked to them about the issues raised in the report. We knew that an immediate change was unlikely, but we hoped that, when faced with independent evidence of harmful design practices impacting Windows users, they would also want better for people,” Mozilla said.
“Instead, it became clear that Microsoft will respect user choice only when it is forced to. Microsoft’s standard for respecting people’s choices is legal compliance. Not what’s best for its users. Not its own published principles. Not what’s technically feasible. Not even what it already does for users in Europe.”
A story on AI
Mozilla said it shared the report with Microsoft but did not say if the company replied in any way. We’ve reached out to Microsoft with a request for comment and will update this article when we hear from them.
In the meantime, we believe it is also important to mention what Mozilla said in the blog’s introduction:
“As AI reshapes our online experiences, the stakes couldn’t be higher. Browsers are a key distribution layer for AI tools and services, while still determining many of the privacy and security functionality people rely on every day. Steering people toward one browser can therefore shape which AI services reach users and the protections that come with it.”
So the question becomes - is this really about wanting better for people, or wanting people to use one AI model instead of another AI model? If demanding equal browser opportunity is fair game, then demanding equal AI opportunity is also fair game, so why not just say so? Why hide behind alleged altruistic causes and principles?
In the blog, Mozilla says it has a “simple” ask - to expand the “fairer designs” currently being enforced in the EEA everywhere on the planet, and to “stop the remaining harmful design practices that persist in the EEA.”
The company concluded the blog by saying there will be no more mister Nice Guy. It says it “stepped up” public pressure on the company and has reached out to regulators and policy makers.
“We hope that regulators in the US, the UK, India, and Brazil are paying attention.”
