Petit format, très grosse facture
La transformation ne s’arrêterait pas à l’écran. Les bordures seraient affinées, la caméra selfie déplacée pour les appels vidéo en mode paysage et le châssis pourrait devenir résistant à l’eau. Apple travaillerait aussi sur des haut-parleurs utilisant les vibrations, une première sur iPad.
À l’intérieur, la puce A20 Pro des iPhone 18 Pro remplacerait l’A17 Pro, avec la puce réseau N1 et, sur les versions cellulaires, possiblement le modem C2. Le stockage de base pourrait également passer de 128 à 256 Go. De quoi mieux justifier la hausse… car elle s’annonce brutale.
Selon Mark Gurman, Apple viserait environ 799 $ aux États-Unis, contre 599 $ aujourd’hui. En France, où l’iPad mini 7 se négocie désormais à 630 € après une hausse cet été, une conversion comparable placerait son successeur autour de 900 à 920 €. Ce serait davantage que l’iPad Air 11 pouces, affiché à partir de 820 €. La hausse du prix de la mémoire et du stockage viendrait encore alourdir la note. Apple n’a par ailleurs pas indiqué si l’actuel mini resterait au catalogue.
L’iPad classique se fait désirer
Ceux qui comptaient se rabattre rapidement sur l’iPad d'entrée de gamme risquent d’attendre. Son successeur, connu sous les références J581 et J582, ne serait lancé qu’au début de 2027. Il conserverait un prix américain proche de 449 $, mais gagnerait une puce A19 et 8 Go de RAM, assez pour prendre en charge Apple Intelligence.
Ce modèle pourrait aussi recevoir le modem C1X avec 5G sub-6 GHz, ainsi que le wifi 7, le Bluetooth 6 et Thread grâce à la puce N1. Les prochains iPad Air et iPad Pro seraient eux aussi repoussés à 2027, avec notamment l’Oled attendu sur l’Air et un meilleur refroidissement envisagé sur le Pro.
Avant cela, Apple doit tenir un événement consacré à la maison connectée le 13 octobre. Le rendez-vous de fin de mois, avec l’iPad mini, devrait ensuite fermer le bal des lancements Apple pour 2026.

articles.title: Pour faire passer la pilule de la hausse de prix, Gemini pourrait s'offrir un relooking sur smartphone Android
articles.text:
Est-ce une manière pour Google d’adoucir le passage à une nouvelle formule d’abonnement beaucoup moins avantageuse pour son chatbot Gemini ? Google s’apprête, semble-t-il, à retravailler l’interface de Gemini Live, le mode de conversation fluide.
Le changement devrait intervenir en premier lieu sur l’application Android. La nouveauté à venir a été repérée par des sérieux du game comme disent les jeunes (personne ne dit ça), à savoir le site Android Authority en partenariat avec le dénicheur AssembleDebug.
Nouvelle interface plus sobre
En jouant avec la dernière version de l’application (v17.65.17), le développeur est parvenu à activer une interface encore jamais vue. Comme vous pouvez le voir, celle-ci est encore assez sobre, voire un peu déplumée, signe sans doute d’un travail en cours non achevé.
Sur les captures ci-dessus, vous pouvez voir à gauche l’interface actuelle et à droite celle repérée par nos confrères. Le watermark Android Authority n’est évidemment pas dans l’interface de base. Google a, semble-t-il, laissé tomber la pilule en bas de l’écran, un brin inutile, il faut dire, pour ramener les ondes sinusoïdales censées représenter votre voix et celle de Gemini directement dans la fenêtre. Il y a aussi moins de boutons : un simple bouton rouge pour mettre fin à la conversation, un autre pour ouvrir ou fermer le micro et un dernier pour passer en mode texte.
On remarque au passage que cette version de l’interface n’intègre ni le partage d’écran ni le partage de caméra, deux fonctionnalités pourtant phare pour l’IA multimodale de Google. Difficile à ce stade de savoir si la firme de Mountain View les a retirées pour les ranger dans les paramètres de l’application ou bien si les boutons reparaîtront sous une forme ou une autre dans la version finale de l’interface.
Une autre petite nouveauté a été repérée dans l’interface actuelle de Gemini Live : en haut à droite, un bouton permettant de désactiver le mode haut-parleur. De quoi s’éviter de devoir ajuster le volume pour ne pas partager la réponse à toutes les personnes qui vous entourent, et converser avec Gemini comme si vous étiez au téléphone. Une vision tout aussi dystopique que pratique.

articles.title: The Zocket Story: Building Brand Brain, the context and orchestration layer for AI-native enterprise marketing
articles.text:
Zocket
View Brand Publisher
The Zocket Story: Building Brand Brain, the context and orchestration layer for AI-native enterprise marketing
How Zocket evolved from simplifying digital advertising to rethinking how enterprise consumer brands run marketing in an AI-native era.
When Zocket was founded in India in 2021, the company began with a focused ambition: make digital marketing significantly easier for businesses.
What followed was a much larger journey.
As Zocket moved deeper into marketing, worked with increasingly complex organizations, and watched artificial intelligence reshape the industry, the problem it set out to solve evolved. What began as an effort to simplify digital advertising became a much bigger question: How should modern enterprises run marketing in the AI era?
Answering that question meant looking beyond individual tools and isolated AI use cases. It meant rethinking how brand knowledge, consumer intelligence, creative, media, and governance could operate as one connected system, with AI carrying the context of the brand across decisions and orchestrating action across marketing workflows.
In 2026, Zocket evolved from a self-serve advertising platform to an enterprise AI company working with consumer brands to build the context and orchestration layer for AI-native marketing.
Today, Zocket works with 100+ enterprise brands across 25+ countries. At the center of this proposition is Brand Brain, a shared intelligence layer designed to understand brand, consumer, and business context, and make that intelligence available across marketing workflows.
From digital advertising to enterprise marketing AI
Zocket was founded by Karthik Venkateswaran, Nandha Kumar Ravi, Sundar Natesan, and Mukund Srivathsan, a founding team that had already spent years building together.
Before Zocket, the four built GoBumpr, a technology platform connecting vehicle owners with automobile service providers, which they scaled across multiple Indian cities before exiting the business in 2021.
That experience gave the team a firsthand understanding of building a consumer business in an increasingly digital economy. Customer acquisition was becoming more important, but reaching and engaging consumers was also becoming increasingly complex.
Zocket initially focused on simplifying that complexity. Its platform brought together more than 150 variables to inform decisions around creative, copy, targeting, and channels. The company subsequently raised a $3 million seed round led by Kalaari Capital, with participation from Kettleborough VC.
But as Zocket began working more deeply within marketing, the team realized that the larger problem was not any single marketing activity. It was the fragmentation surrounding it.
Zocket Founders
Why AI needs more than a prompt
Generative AI has dramatically reduced the time required to create content, analyze information, and produce marketing recommendations.
But enterprise marketing requires something models do not inherently possess: the context of the brand.
A brand is not simply a logo, prompt, or guideline document. It is the accumulation of campaigns, consumer interactions, product knowledge, creative history, performance data, market intelligence, regulatory requirements, and organizational decisions.
For AI to become useful at enterprise scale, it needs to understand that context. It needs to know how a brand communicates, what consumers are saying, which claims are approved, what has worked previously, what cannot be said, and where human intervention is required.
And context alone is not enough.
That intelligence must be orchestrated across marketing workflows, allowing consumer signals to inform creative, creative to connect with paid media, performance to influence subsequent decisions, and governance to remain consistent throughout.
This became the foundation for Brand Brain.
Brand Brain: From fragmented data to shared intelligence
Brand Brain is Zocket's shared intelligence layer designed to give AI persistent context about a brand's identity, consumers, guidelines, campaigns, performance, and governance rules.
Rather than treating consumer intelligence, brand guidelines, creative history, customer conversations, and campaign performance as disconnected inputs, Brand Brain brings relevant signals together and interprets them within the context of the enterprise.
The objective is not simply to aggregate more data. Enterprises already have enormous amounts of it.
The challenge is determining what information matters, how different signals relate, and how that context should influence the next action.
A change in consumer sentiment can influence messaging. Campaign performance can inform the next creative decision. Brand guidelines establish boundaries for what AI can generate. Market signals can influence how and where campaigns are activated.
This creates a continuous intelligence loop:
Signals → Context → Intelligence → Execution → Outcomes → Learning
Zocket extends this intelligence across six specialized marketing modules: Tasks, AI Designer, Brand Moderator, Consumer Insights, AI Paid Media, and Reporting.
Brand Brain sits across these modules as the shared context layer, allowing each capability to operate from a common understanding of the brand rather than starting from an isolated prompt. Zocket's Home experience acts as the prompt router, directing intent into the relevant workflows while Brand Brain maintains the underlying context.
As Karthik Venkateswaran, Co-founder and CEO, Zocket, explains: “Enterprise marketing does not need another AI tool operating in isolation. It needs AI that understands the context of the brand and can orchestrate that intelligence across marketing.
“That is what we are building with Brand Brain: a shared context and orchestration layer for how enterprise consumer brands run marketing in an AI-native era.”
Building AI for enterprise scale
For enterprise brands, intelligence and automation also need governance.
Large organizations operate across products, sub-brands, markets, and regulatory environments. Communication approved for one product may not be appropriate for another, while certain marketing decisions may require legal, compliance or brand approval.
Zocket's enterprise approach combines intelligence and orchestration with controls around permissions, approvals, brand rules, and traceability.
Teams can determine where AI can act, where human approval is required and where actions need to be escalated, creating a human-in-the-loop approach to consequential marketing decisions.
Mukund Srivathsan, Co-founder and CTO, Zocket, says the model is not the moat and the real challenge is building the context around it. “Brand Brain brings together brand knowledge, consumer signals, performance history and governance, and makes that intelligence available to every AI workflow. That is what allows AI to move from generating isolated outputs to making more informed, connected marketing decisions at enterprise scale,” he says.
The value of enterprise AI is therefore not determined only by what it can generate. It is determined by whether an organization can govern it, control it, and reliably apply it across marketing workflows.
From enterprise adoption to industry recognition
The shift is increasingly reflected in Zocket's enterprise footprint.
Today, the company works with 200+ enterprise brands across 25+ countries, including consumer brands such as Bata and Dabur, applying AI across areas including consumer intelligence, creative, paid media, and brand governance.
In 2026, Zocket's approach was recognized through the Accenture Tech Next Challenge 2026, where it was named a winner for its work around AI-native marketing and autonomous growth.
Zocket also won Best Use of AI in Media & Entertainment at the ET Enterprise AI Awards 2026, reflecting its growing focus on bringing context-aware AI into real enterprise marketing workflows.
For Zocket, these milestones represent a very different company from the one that began by simplifying digital advertisements five years ago. But the underlying principle remains the same: technology should remove complexity from marketing rather than create more of it.
The next chapter
The next phase of enterprise AI will not be defined simply by how much content brands can generate or how many tasks they automate.
It will be defined by how effectively organizations connect context, intelligence, and action while maintaining the governance and control their brands require.
Consumer intelligence should inform creativity. Creative should connect with paid media. Performance should contribute to what happens next. Brand and compliance rules should remain present throughout the process.
That is the future Zocket is building toward.
What began as a question about making digital marketing easier has evolved into a much more ambitious one:
How should enterprise consumer brands run marketing in an AI-native era?
For Zocket, the answer lies in giving AI the context of the brand and orchestrating that intelligence across marketing.
To learn more, visit www.zocket.com

articles.title: WhatsApp quiere que podamos programar mensajes. La función parece sencilla, pero cambia una regla básica de la app
articles.text:
No siempre escribimos un mensaje porque queramos hablar con alguien en ese preciso momento. A veces recordamos algo de madrugada, pensamos en felicitar a alguien por su cumpleaños o preparamos una respuesta que preferiríamos enviar unas horas después. Sin embargo, en una conversación corriente de WhatsApp, pulsar el botón de envío significa pedirle a la aplicación que envíe el mensaje en ese instante. Nos hemos acostumbrado tanto a esa relación entre escribir y enviar que parece una característica inevitable de la mensajería, aunque no tiene por qué serlo.
Eso es precisamente lo que WhatsApp está empezando a poner a prueba. Según ha documentado WABetaInfo este 12 de octubre, algunos participantes del programa beta de Android ya tienen acceso a una función para dejar preparados mensajes y establecer cuándo deben enviarse, una posibilidad que hasta ahora no estaba integrada en las conversaciones habituales de la aplicación. La novedad aparece en la versión 2.26.40.7, después de varios meses de desarrollo, mientras la compañía también trabaja en llevarla al iPhone. Por ahora, no hay una fecha anunciada para su disponibilidad general.
Escribir ahora, enviar después
El funcionamiento que se está probando no exige salir de la conversación ni realizar demasiados pasos. Después de escribir el mensaje, basta con mantener pulsado el botón de envío para que aparezca una ventana en la que escoger la fecha y la hora. Los especialistas detallan que la beta permite programarlo con una antelación de entre diez minutos y dos semanas. Una vez configurado, el mensaje queda pendiente y puede consultarse o eliminarse desde un apartado específico de la información del chat. Llegado el momento, WhatsApp lo envía automáticamente, incluso si el dispositivo del remitente está desconectado.
Pero hay una consecuencia que va más allá de poder elegir una hora. Hasta ahora, podíamos interpretar la hora de envío de un mensaje como una referencia del momento en que alguien decidió enviárnoslo, aunque su entrega pudiera retrasarse por problemas de conexión. Con esta función, podríamos recibir a las diez de la mañana algo que otra persona dejó preparado la noche anterior. En febrero, cuando todavía estaba en desarrollo, WABetaInfo señaló que el destinatario no podría saber que el mensaje había sido programado. Por ahora, no está confirmado que ese comportamiento se mantenga en la versión definitiva.
La programación tampoco se limita a los mensajes de texto. Las pruebas incluyen enlaces, fotografías y vídeos, tanto en conversaciones individuales como en grupos. Hay, sin embargo, algunas condiciones: por ahora, las imágenes y los vídeos solo pueden programarse de uno en uno. En los grupos, WABetaInfo señala que quienes se incorporen después de que se haya programado un mensaje no lo recibirán. La programación también es compatible con el cifrado de extremo a extremo, según la información publicada por el medio especializado.
La idea, en realidad, lleva años funcionando en otras aplicaciones. Telegram incorporó los mensajes programados en 2019 e Instagram, otra plataforma de Meta, también permite elegir cuándo enviar mensajes directos desde 2025. WhatsApp ya permite programar determinadas comunicaciones comerciales mediante herramientas para empresas, pero lo que ahora está probando es diferente: llevar esta posibilidad directamente a las conversaciones habituales de sus usuarios. Aunque todavía queda por conocer cuándo se incorporará a la versión general, las pruebas apuntan a un cambio interesante. No se trata solo de decidir qué queremos decir, sino también de elegir cuándo queremos enviarlo.

articles.title: Petit mais costaud : ce mini PC avec un Ryzen 5, 16 Go de RAM et 1 To de stockage est bradé à -31%
articles.text:
Le GMKtec présenté ici est un mini PC conçu pour la bureautique avec un stockage particulièrement généreux d'1 To, avec 16 Go de RAM pour la fluidité et un prix de 322,99 euros au lieu de 469,96 euros sur Amazon.
Un mini PC comme le GMKtec présenté ici est pour vous si vous cherchez un ordinateur de bureau mais que vous n'avez ni l'espace ni le budget pour une tour encombrante et parfois bruyante. Ce modèle ne se contente pas d'une puce d'entrée de gamme habituelle mais fait le pari d'une puce AMD Ryzen qui permet de muscler ses performances graphiques, en l'absence d'une carte dédiée. C'est un bon compromis pour les télétravailleurs, les amateurs de rétrogaming et celles et ceux qui veulent un PC de salon discret sans se ruiner. Une machine que vous retrouvez en promo pour quelques jours avec 31% de réduction sur Amazon.
Voici le GMKtec Nucbox G10 à 322,99 € au lieu de 469,96 € sur Amazon
Pourquoi choisir le GMKtec Nucbox G10 ?
- Le processeur AMD change la donne : oubliez les puces N100 ou N95 qui s'essoufflent vite, le Ryzen 5 3500U offre une vraie puissance, appréciable pour le multitâche.
- Sa puce graphique est top pour le rétro-gaming : la Radeon Vega 8 fait tourner sans broncher vos émulateurs préférés et même quelques jeux 3D compétitifs comme Rocket League.
- Une bonne évolutivité malgré la flambée des prix, puisque la RAM n'est pas soudée et que le boîtier dissimule un second emplacement M.2.
Un format de poche pour un setup minimaliste et efficace
Une fois posé sur votre bureau, le GMKtec G10 se fait vite oublier, surtout que vous pouvez le fixer derrière un écran avec un support VESA compatible. Il est plutôt bien doté avec deux ports USB 3.2 5 Gbps, un port USB-C PowerDelivery et un second DP, DATA et PD, un port USB 2.0, un HDMI 2.1 4K@60 Hz et un DP 1.4 4K@60 Hz, ainsi qu'un port Ethernet 2.5G. Par contre, les puristes du travail sans-fil vont devoir se contenter du WiFi 5 et du Bluetooth 5.0, des normes qui, certes, fonctionnent, mais qui commencent à se montrer vieillissantes à l'heure où le le WiFi 6 s'est démocratisé un peu partout.
Plus musclé que la concurrence avec un petit réglage
Ce mini PC fait face à la concurrence équipée d'une puce Intel, mais ce modèle Nucbox G10 se démarque par sa puissance brute avec 16 Go de RAM en double canal et un très confortable SSD de 1 To. Sa principale limite réside dans son BIOS bridé par défaut autour de 20 W pour des raisons de consommation. Donc pour exploiter pleinement ses 45 W, il va falloir mettre les mains dans le cambouis logiciel lors des premiers démarrages.
✅ Les points forts
- La puissance du Ryzen 5, supérieure aux puces Intel N100/N95
- La puce graphique Vega 8 idéale pour le jeu léger et le rétrogaming
- La RAM n'est pas soudée et on peut ajouter un deuxième SSD
- La bonne connectivité
- Windows 11 est préinstallé
❌ Les limites
- La puce WiFi 6 et le Bluetooth 5.0 d'une autre génération
- Les performances bridées par défaut, nécessitant de faire un tour par le BIOS
- L'architecture de son processeur date originellement de 2019
Jusqu'au 23 octobre 2026, le GMKtec Nucbox G10 passe de 469,96 € au lieu de 322,99 €
Le GMKtec Nucbox G10 est une bonne surprise, avec un rapport qualité/prix intéressant face à la concurrence d'entrée de gamme. Son stockage généreux, pour ce prix, et ses capacités graphiques au-dessus de la moyenne fait qu'il convient bien aux étudiants, aux travailleurs à domicile et aux joueurs occasionnels qui cherchent un PC secondaire performant.
Par contre, si vous êtes un gamer assidu qui veut faire tourner des jeux récents ou du montage 4K, ça va être compliqué. L'architecture datant de 2019 montre logiquement ses limites sur les tâches extrêmes. Aussi, il ne faut pas avoir peur de fouiller dans les paramètres du BIOS pour activer le mode "Performance" pour avoir un vrai gain en fluidité.

articles.title: Technics EAH-A1000 review: over-ear headphones with class, detail and comfort that err just slightly on the side of caution
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Technics has come so very close to perfect for the money, here. The EAH-A1000 are quite beautiful to look at and, unlike many winsome sets of headphones, you'll still think they're beautiful several hours after putting them over your ears. There's a delightful sense of pride in ownership too, and carrying them around is a breeze thanks to their easy-folding and solid-but-lightweight hard-shell case. My only minor gripes concern a sound that, while agile and insightful, occasionally plays things a tiny bit safe (for fear perhaps of offending), and physical controls on the right ear cup that occasionally fail to register my presses. Small issues in a formidable pair of headphones I think you'll agree — and I still predict a huge hit.
Reasons to buy
- + Layered, expansive audio quality
- + Still the only company regularly offering triple-device connectivity
- + Competent spatial audio and ANC
- + Supreme comfort
Reasons to avoid
- - Occasionally a little polite-sounding
- - Physical buttons sometimes fail to register presses (including playback and power)
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Technics EAH-A1000: Two-minute review
If you were expecting a minor update over Technics' previous over-ears in the EAH-A1000, you're in for a surprise. Because in the four-years-and-loose-change since its last over-ear offering, Technics' various audio departments have been very, very busy — and I'm referring to the design team as well as the sonic engineering squad.
Here's a novel idea to kick things off: these headphones have Technics' own proprietary, top-secret metallic juice concoction oiling the drivers. Those familiar with the company's hugely successful earbuds (and if you read this publication regularly, you will be) will remember the firm's Magnetic Fluid Driver technology.
Technics pioneered it to aid the pistonic motion of those tiny drivers. As they busily move back and forth to create physical sound waves from electrical signals, said fluid helps the units stay extra-true in their work and free from variance. But it's no small feat to scale up from 10mm mechanisms within concha-fit earpieces to 40mm drivers that cover the whole ear, and that is what has been achieved, all without adding any weight to the headset.
So are the new, far more attractive EAH-A1000 (all vegan leather, svelte arms, and brushed metallic top plates) ready to assume a spot in our best noise-cancelling headphones guide then? Yes, depending on your listening tastes. There's detail, width, a lovely circumaural presentation and musical timing in droves. However, depending on the kind of music you regularly listen to, or the sonic tuning you prefer, they'll either be just what you need or fall just slightly short in terms of oomph, bass clout and zeal. And as much as I adore them, I have to confirm that my heart and ears belong in the latter group.
If triple-device connectivity seems like something you'd really like from your headphones, these are an excellent buy — and believe me when I tell you it's hard to return to a state of only being connected to two source devices at once (rather than seamless sonic switching between your tablet, phone and laptop at will) when you've become used to three.
And in terms of features elsewhere, the Technics score highly for ANC, which is robust and effective but never sweetens or hollows out your music unnecessarily. I do find the Ambient profiles (there are two; 'Transparent' for sounds around you, or 'Attention' which aims to hone in on voices and announcements specifically) a little light touch, though. If you value Sony's Quick Attention feature to actively pipe in sounds when you cover an ear cup, you'll be disappointed here. Technics' profiles do dampen your audio and the result is natural, but it feels a touch too passive, no matter how much I dial up the transparency on the graph in the app.
I really enjoyed this same, slightly lighter touch feel within the spatial audio profiles, though. Your options are static or head-tracked and they are of course device- and streaming-service agnostic (Technics does not currently make mobile phones or offer a music streaming service, so it cannot tie you into an ecosystem in the way that Apple can). For me, these offer a more enveloping, engaging soundstage at the times when you may want that — in classical tracks, say.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Call quality is also very good, although Sidetone fans (and I'm one of those) might be dismayed to learn that Technics' excellent voice amplification tech for its earbuds, whereby your own voice doesn't sound so muffled as you speak, has never made it to its over-ears.
I'll get granular on my very minor issues with the on-ear controls in due course, but for this money — which is significantly less than AirPods Max 2 (but with a much better battery life) and the same asking fee as the also-new Sonos Ace Ultra — the sonic detail is excellent value for money. They're not the most punchy and zealous cans I've ever heard, but they are diligent, accurate and beautifully musical. And mark my words, some people will adore them for critical listening.
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Price & release date
- Released on September 29, 2026
- Priced $449 / £399 / AU$699
Technics has priced these headphones at $449 / £399 / AU$699, to sit comfortably within a premium space that includes much more expensive hits such as the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2 (at $799 / £629 / AU$1,299) and AirPods Max 2 ($549 / £499 / AU$999, although I've seen a few discounts on these MSRPs lately).
The excellent Sony WH-1000XM6 (also $449 / £399 / AU$699) are arguably Technics' chief competition, and this is likely why they've been released at the same price-point — but the superb September 2026 Sonos Ace Ultra can be yours for exactly this money too.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro also recently launched at just a shade cheaper than the Technics ($399 / £349 / AU$699) so, although certainly not in the budget headphones sector, Technics' pricing is hardly unreasonable.
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Specs
| Drivers | 40mm Magnetic Fluid Driver with pure carbon-fiber diaphragm and SST edge | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes (adaptive, tweakable static, ambient passthrough) | 
| Battery life | Up to 45 hours (ANC ON, AAC) / up to 90 hours (ANC OFF, AAC) Up to 30 hours (ANC ON, LDAC) / up to 60 hours (ANC OFF, LDAC) | 
| Weight | 306g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 with 3-device multipoint pairing, USB-C audio output at 24-bit | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz – 48kHz | 
| Waterproofing | No rating | 
| Other features | Dolby Atmos with head-tracking, LDAC support, USB-C Lossless audio up to 24-bit, triple-device multipoint pairing (LDAC off) | 
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Features
- Spatial audio with the option of Dolby Head Tracking
- Industry-leading simultaneous triple-device connectivity
- 8-tab EQ; ANC and Transparency modes both with 0-99 sliders
There are no hearing tests, hearing aid features or scope for nodding to either answer calls or respond to your voice assistant here and, honestly, I don't miss these features.
You will get wearer detection to pause your music, plus ANC that can either be set to 'Adaptive', to automatically adjust to your surroundings, or simply 'On' to tweak yourself. This is done on a little virtual dial within the easy-to-navigate (and easy-to-tailor, thanks to the option of prioritizing certain profiles on the home screen) Technics AudioConnect app.
For me, dialling up the ANC to 100% or thereabouts gives very good results. It dulls all but the really heavy crashes and clatters in my home office — even the sound of the microwave didn't creep in. I don't say it lightly either; Technics has done a great job with the active noise cancellation here.
Transparency? It also gets its own in-app dial, but here you can also choose between 'Attention', which is supposed to seek out voices and announcements around you, or 'Transparent', which lets in all ambient noise, to make you aware of where you are. For me, these are less successful. I certainly hear quite a bit more of my other half's lovely voice when selecting 'Attention' — and there's no hiss or tinniness to either the ambient sound or audio in my cans — but I still feel as if I need to remove them to hear him properly.
Although these headphones may seem relatively light on extras (there's no Sony 'Quick Attention' rival, to actively pipe a person's voice into your ear, and that is perhaps one perk I would have liked to see) the features you need are all here and, largely, they're implemented very well. The EQ graph is well-designed and, as well as presets for Bass+, Super Bass+, Vocal, Treble+ and Dynamic, you can create custom sound profiles on an 8-band tab.
And although I'd love Technics' excellent Sidetone tech to trickle from its earbuds to its cans as well as that magnetic fluid has, to hear my own voice better in calls, callers said my voice was nevertheless clear.
But I've saved one of the best (best!) features for last: triple-device connectivity. It simplifies life so much more than you might think not to have to keep disconnecting one device to add another when you regularly work on a tablet, a laptop and a phone!
I asked Technics recently why so few other companies are offering multipoint to three devices and was essentially told (I say 'essentially' only because I was talking to a Technics engineer through a Japanese translator, in Tokyo) that it isn't easy to get everything on a Bluetooth chipset, because you "need to be very organized".
So, the fact that when you connect to three devices simultaneously, you'll lose LDAC streaming quality, makes a lot of sense. Choose to forego Bluetooth entirely and you can listen via USB-C Lossless audio, although the headphones do need to be powered on for this.
A quick note on the Technics EAH-A1000's battery life: it's good rather than phenomenal. Up to 45 hours with ANC on sounds great, until you realize that's without LDAC (at which point stamina drops to 30 hours), but up to 90 hours without ANC and without LDAC is still a good chunk of time. To put that into perspective, Apple's AirPods Max 2 can only go for up to 20 hours with ANC on, but Cambridge's excellent P100 SE can last for up to 100 hours without ANC, or 60 hours with it — although it's worth noting that Cambridge hasn't disclosed how much aptX listening might affect things.
All in all, Technics has given us a well-rounded and beautifully presented feature set that does the essentials well, and even adds an extra device to your regular multipoint setup. The one fly in the ointment? A light-touch 'Transparency' profile that for me could use a bit of extra oomph.
- Features score: 4.5 / 5
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Sound quality
- LDAC support, plus Lossless via USB-C or 3.5mm bundled cables
- Exceptionally detailed audio for this level
- Also very occasionally a little too polite and lacking in bite
If you, like me, cue up Jamie T's 3310, the first track on his new album Ghosts (100 Days of Morning) you'll be very happy with these headphones. I defy you to knock the Technics EAH-A1000 while listening to more pared back intros and acoustic tracks. Here, the guitar sits beautifully under your left ear, textured and three-dimensional, and Wimbledon's finest rapper-slash-crooner might just as well be in the room, glancing at you as he sings about cider, the London district of Barnes, its cash-strapped cousin Twickenham, and how he longs to be 33 again.
As the track continues and the mix intensifies, you might feel as if you're missing an extra ounce of disillusion through T's petulant, unimpressed vocal though, and I'd agree. Deploying 'Bass+' in the EQ tab does help a little, but also puts you slightly further back from other frequencies in the mix. These are not the best choice for those who listen to heavier music or grime.
However, I've said it before and I'll reiterate here: there's nothing wrong with refinement and pulling back just a little to gain space, breadth and add a modicum of detail to every intake of breath and strum of a guitar. The issue here is that in easing off on the throttle for fear of overstating the low end especially, the Technics err just slightly in the opposite direction; if I'm being hyper-critical, they're just a touch too polite.
It's no huge issue, but it's my job to relay what I hear. Again, this will be a matter of taste and, depending on which genres of music you most enjoy, you may hear things while listening with these headphones that truly delight you. Stream Hotel California (I don't need to tell you the name of the LA five-piece who released it, do I?) and there's a stunning level of clarity to the shakers, guitars, bass and cymbals in the intro. Stream Bad Bunny's BAILE INoLVIDABLE and you may want just a little more good old fashioned sub-bass wallop.
Switch to B&W's Px8 S2 and there's an ounce more crispness through the leading edges of notes and more palpable dynamic nuance across the frequencies, which has me dancing rather than just nodding my head to Fontaines D.C.'s Favourite, but it's a close-run race — and given the fact that the B&W product is quite a bit more expensive, that's a big compliment for the Technics set of cans.
- Sound quality score: 4.5 / 5
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Design
- A very good-looking set of headphones
- The case is a winner too
- On-ear physical buttons occasionally fail to respond
My review sample is the classic black version rather than the new 'Platinum Greige' set, but both are incredibly stylish and promote no small sense of pride in ownership.
The case, bijou and useful though it is (and with a lovely bit of storage for your cables, which you'd think would be a given but isn't), is not imprinted with a Technics logo save for a demure mention on the zipper tag. This is because, and I'm quoting a revered member of the Technics design team here: "Everything at Technics must either be engraved onto the metal or embroidered to the fabric of a product: we do not print."
Everything has been finessed from the EAH-A800 and the look is far less bulky. At their unveiling, I was shown dozens of samples of potential top-plates for the ear cup: too shiny, too grooved, too smooth… this goes way beyond meticulous attention to detail. Technics wants us to love the look of them, and make no mistake, I do.
To circle back to the Magnetic Fluid Driver for a moment, the EAH-A1000 incorporates Technics' SST (Symmetrical Surround Technology) Edge — aka the same tech that's also used in the company's hi-fi flagship speakers — alongside the magnetic fluid-enhanced drivers that have been scaled up from Technics' earbuds.
What's under the hood is a pure rigid carbon-fiber diaphragm with dome shape and cone shape ideas (think a dish with a slight raise in the center), along with a redesigned acoustic control chamber, to better manage airflow. The EAH-A1000 also feature a new 'Baffle Flat Structure' to reduce "uneven surfaces around the driver, limiting unwanted reflections".
The arms of the headphones have been thinned, reshaped and refined since the EAH-A800, and I think it's a careful and chic solution. The movement of the arm is silent and the headphones have remained supremely comfortable during wear, throughout the course of my listening. Clamping force? Yes, it's here to promote passive isolation, but never to a fault. I think the fit is aided by the 13-degree angle of the ear cups, relative to the headband, implemented by the female Head of Design. Apparently, over 500 people tested them prior to landing on this specific degree, and half of those tested were women. Hurrah. (In case it needs to be said, women also like music.)
Any issues? One: the physical buttons located on the right ear cup. The one closest to the nape of your neck scrolls through ANC profiles; the central rocker can slide for volume and be pushed for playback control; the one nearest your cheek is for power and pairing. The volume rocker is great to use, but pushing it to pause music is a little more hit-and-miss if you don't press firmly, or don't make sure the rocker is truly central in its mounting. And the power button needs to pressed for two seconds to initiate powering off, but if you do this while removing them, in my experience it often doesn't work. It's a small issue, but one that obviously may affect battery life — and it doesn't help that my Cambridge reference headphones have a simple, reliable slider to switch them off.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Value
- Sonically bang on for the money
- They look and feel more expensive than they are
- Not as feature-stuffed as some rivals, though
If you value an expansive, detailed, insightful listen, you cannot do much better for the money. The ANC is also more than up to snuff and among the best-in-class, and they're light and easy to transport, with a useful but fuss-free case.
That said, you can better the EAH-A1000 just slightly for zealous energy and the kind of impact that makes you get up and dance to the music in your cans — and if you rely heavily on a 'Transparency' profile to cut through the noise, they won't be for you.
Nevertheless, if sound is king, you should add these to your test drive list.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the Technics EAH-A1000?
| Section | Notes | Score | Header Cell - Column 3 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Features | All killer, no filler. The essentials are here — and largely, they're very good too. Hearing tests though? No | 4.5/5 | Row 0 - Cell 3 | 
| Sound quality | Expansive and insightful, with lovely musicality. That said, they can sound just a little polite | 4.5/5 | Row 1 - Cell 3 | 
| Design | A beautiful set of headphones, only let down by the occasional lack of efficacy concerning the buttons on the ear cup. But that's a small issue | 4.5/5 | Row 2 - Cell 3 | 
| Value | They look so, so much more expesnive than they are, and the sound is more than worthy of the money | 4.5/5 | Row 3 - Cell 3 | 
Buy them if...
You want excellent ANC 
For this money, I think the ANC here is very effective — get it on, take the dial in the app right up and enjoy the cocoon of near-silence as your musical backdrop. 
You like to feel expensive
These headphones shine and reflect, but never in a trashy, 'look at me' way. They feel every bit as padded, light in weight and — hang it all — pricey as you want them to. 
You listen to acoustic tracks a lot 
LDAC support is here, if you can deploy it from your Android, and with it these headphones deliver guitars, strings and pared back vocals with depth, detail and care. 
Don't buy them if...
You rely on a decent 'Transparency' profile
There are two ambient profiles here, but neither is as easy to deploy or as effective at getting you in and focused on the conversation as Sony's 'Quick Attention' feature, say. 
You're all about that bass
It's not that the EAH-A1000 are shy on bass, especially, they're just a little polite with it. If you listen to a lot of grime or heavier hip-hop, they may not suit your tastes.
You want aptX and aptX HD
These are definitely headphones for a certain type of listener (one who values clarity and spacious detail in their music), which is perhaps why I feel the need to point out that you're not getting a few of the higher-res Bluetooth codecs, although LDAC is on the menu. 
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Technics EAH-A1000 | Sonos Ace Ultra | Nothing Headphone (1) Pro | Sony WH-1000XM6 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $449 / £399 / AU$699 | $449 / £399 / AU$699 | $399 / £349 / (approx. AU$655) | $449 / £399 / AU$699 |

To check the audio performance across the frequencies, I listened for many hours, in various environments, to my own reference playlists on Apple Music, Qobuz and Tidal, alongside TechRadar's reference tracks, and two of my favorite podcasts.
I’ve been testing audio products for well over seven years now, as a full-time job — first at our sister site What Hi-Fi? and now here at TechRadar. I know, tough gig (but someone has to). As a dancer, aerialist and musical theater performer in another life, I have always found that sound quality (in particular musicality and cohesion), fit and the user experience take priority for me in headphones, but having heard how wonderful ANC can be when done well, I know what I'm listening for there, too.

articles.title: NVIDIA RTX 5080 24 GB Reportedly Planned For Q1 2027, but Board Partners Are Still in the Dark
articles.text:
Monday, October 12th 2026
NVIDIA RTX 5080 24 GB Reportedly Planned For Q1 2027, but Board Partners Are Still in the Dark
Taiwanese outlet BenchLife has added more detail to last week's report that NVIDIA is pulling GB202 silicon away from the GeForce RTX 5090. According to BenchLife, board partners are no longer receiving GB202 chips for RTX 5090 production. The same applies to the China-specific RTX 5090 D and RTX 5090 D V2 variants. NVIDIA hasn't said anything officially yet. Apparently, the company doesn't see this as an end-of-life (EOL) move either, since the chips are simply being shifted to more profitable GB202-based RTX PRO cards like the RTX PRO 6000 and the recently unveiled RTX PRO 5500. In the meantime, any RTX 5090 cards still reaching shelves are built from chips partners already have. The card immediately sold out at Walmart for $4,299 last month, so buyers shouldn't expect prices to come down anytime soon.
The RTX 5080 part of the story is a bit more interesting. BenchLife says NVIDIA plans to launch an RTX 5080 with 24 GB of GDDR7 in the first quarter of 2027, replacing the current 16 GB model. However, board partners have yet to receive any development material for it. So far they've only been told verbally that it should arrive soon. That's odd, considering partners reportedly had RTX 50 SUPER silicon in hand back in July, before GDDR7 pricing put that launch on hold. We still don't know if the RTX 5080 24 GB and the long-rumored RTX 5080 SUPER are the same card. A Q1 2027 window would make CES in January a likely stage, though that's guesswork for now.
Sources:

articles.title: Dónde está la papelera de WhatsApp y cómo borrar archivos duplicados
articles.text:
La papelera de WhatsApp no existe como una carpeta convencional, pero la aplicación cuenta con una función para localizar y eliminar fotos, videos, documentos y archivos duplicados. La herramienta se llama Administrar almacenamiento y permite liberar memoria sin revisar cada conversación de forma individual.
La acumulación de contenido en chats, grupos y canales puede ocupar una parte importante del espacio disponible en el teléfono. Cuando la memoria comienza a agotarse, WhatsApp puede mostrar alertas, impedir la descarga de nuevos archivos o dificultar el envío de mensajes. Por ese motivo, la gestión del almacenamiento se ha convertido en una opción útil para identificar qué contenido ocupa más espacio y decidir qué debe desaparecer.
Dónde está la “papelera” de WhatsApp
La expresión “papelera secreta de WhatsApp” suele utilizarse para referirse a un apartado que no funciona como una papelera tradicional. Los archivos no quedan allí de forma temporal antes de borrarse. En realidad, Administrar almacenamiento reúne el material multimedia guardado por la aplicación y lo ordena según su tamaño, antigüedad o frecuencia de reenvío.
Desde ese menú es posible comprobar cuánto espacio utiliza WhatsApp en el dispositivo. También muestra los chats, grupos, canales y categorías que concentran más archivos. De esta forma, el usuario puede detectar conversaciones con muchos videos, documentos pesados, fotografías repetidas o notas de voz que ya no necesita conservar.
La aplicación incluye una opción destinada a los duplicados. Al identificar un archivo que aparece en varias conversaciones, se puede seleccionar “Eliminar todas las copias”. Esta alternativa borra el elemento elegido de los chats donde esté guardado y puede recuperar espacio en poco tiempo.
Antes de confirmar la eliminación, conviene revisar cada selección. Los archivos borrados desde esta sección pueden desaparecer de las conversaciones y dejar de estar disponibles si no existe una copia de seguridad o si no se guardaron antes en otro lugar.
Cómo vaciar archivos de WhatsApp en Android
En los teléfonos con Android, el acceso a la administración de archivos se encuentra dentro del menú principal de WhatsApp. El recorrido permite consultar el espacio usado y abrir cada conversación para eliminar contenido concreto.
Los pasos son los siguientes:
- Abrir WhatsApp.
- Pulsar el ícono de los tres puntos en la esquina superior derecha.
- Entrar en Ajustes.
- Seleccionar Almacenamiento y datos.
- Pulsar Administrar almacenamiento.
En la parte superior aparecerá el espacio que ocupa la aplicación. Más abajo, WhatsApp ordenará los chats, grupos, canales y archivos según el volumen de memoria que utilizan. El contenido puede filtrarse por tamaño, antigüedad o número de reenvíos.
Al abrir cada categoría, se pueden marcar fotografías, videos, documentos o notas de voz y pulsar el ícono de eliminación. Esta selección permite conservar lo necesario y retirar solo los elementos que generan un mayor consumo de memoria.
También es posible vaciar una conversación completa. Para ello, hay que abrir el chat, tocar los tres puntos, elegir Más y seleccionar Vaciar chat. La aplicación permite definir qué elementos multimedia se eliminarán durante el proceso.
En iPhone, el acceso comienza desde el perfil
En los dispositivos con iPhone, la ruta cambia en el primer paso. La función conserva el mismo objetivo: mostrar qué chats y archivos ocupan más espacio para facilitar la limpieza del teléfono.
El procedimiento es el siguiente:
- Abrir WhatsApp.
- Pulsar la foto de perfil.
- Entrar en Almacenamiento y datos.
- Seleccionar Administrar almacenamiento.
- Elegir un chat, canal o categoría.
- Marcar los archivos que se desean borrar.
- Pulsar el ícono de la papelera.
Desde esa pantalla se pueden revisar los archivos más pesados, los más antiguos o aquellos que fueron reenviados muchas veces. WhatsApp permite borrar fotos, videos o documentos específicos, además de retirar todo el contenido multimedia asociado con una conversación.
La opción de vaciar chats completos también está disponible. Antes de usarla, resulta aconsejable comprobar si la conversación incluye comprobantes, archivos laborales, imágenes familiares o documentos que no estén guardados fuera de la aplicación.
Borrar en WhatsApp no siempre elimina las copias del teléfono
Eliminar archivos desde Administrar almacenamiento libera espacio dentro de WhatsApp, pero no garantiza que desaparezcan las copias almacenadas en otras áreas del dispositivo. Una foto o un video que se guardó previamente en la galería puede continuar ocupando memoria aunque ya no figure en el chat.
Después de limpiar la aplicación, conviene revisar la galería, la carpeta de descargas y el administrador de archivos. Esa verificación permite detectar duplicados que siguen presentes fuera de WhatsApp.
También es recomendable revisar la descarga automática. Si la aplicación recibe y guarda de inmediato todas las fotos, videos y documentos de los grupos, el almacenamiento puede volver a llenarse en poco tiempo. Crear una copia de seguridad antes de eliminar contenido importante permite conservar los archivos relevantes.

articles.title: Bambu Lab officially teases its first 3D scanner — S1 3D set for launch in November 2026
articles.text:
Bambu Lab officially teases its first 3D scanner — S1 3D set for launch in November 2026
Bambu Lab's framework agreement with SCANOLOGY gives us a hint of what the scanner might be like and how much.
Bambu Lab has officially teased its S1 3D scanner, ahead of its planned release in November 2026. No details of the product have been released yet, but FCC filings and Bambu Lab’s partnership with SCANOLOGY may hint at the scanner’s capabilities and shared technology.
3D scanners are a niche within a niche, and not necessarily within the 3D printing niche either. 3D scanning is used in many fields, like game asset creation, texture assets, archaeology, prosthetics, and museum archiving; and the rise of 3D printing has created a small but growing demand in the form of reverse engineering automotive and various niche parts. However, because of PC requirements, the intensive and technical scan cleanup, and resurfacing in CAD programs, it remains a small niche; a niche currently being served by brands such as Creality with their CR-Scan line of 3D scanners, Revopoint’s Pop series, mini, and all-in-one MIRACO scanner, and SHINING3D’s Einstar prosumer-level 3D scanner.
Speculations in Bambu Lab’s own forums found FCC filings for a label and drawing of the scanner. The label shows a 60W-rated input, leading some to speculate a shared platform with SCANOLOGY’s 3DeVOK MT Gen2, a wired composite 3D scanner released in 2026, using both blue and IR lasers, and also has a rated input of 60W. The input rating doesn’t necessarily confirm that they share technology, but it does give a small hint of its potential capabilities, with the number of lasers and potentially a screen dictating the power requirements.
Considering the flat spot and the top of the handle on the FCC drawings, it looks like there may be a screen, possibly like the 3DeVOK MT Gen2. More importantly, the 60W rating with no hints of a battery on the label may mean this scanner will require a PC to operate. This is often a pain point, as you would either need a powerful laptop to bring while scanning, or use a really long USB cable to your PC. As for the price, the 3DeVOK MT Gen2 is officially priced at $8,299, which is a very high price point, further making it unlikely that they may share a platform if Bambu Lab wants to keep consumer-friendly pricing.

articles.title: Ledger-Wallets im Visier von Krypto-Kriminellen
articles.text:
Ledger-Wallets manipuliert: Krypto-Kriminelle sollen Millionen erbeutet haben
Mit „Not Your Keys, Not Your Coins“ haben Fans von Kryptowährungen einen wichtigen Schlüsselsatz geprägt. Wer Bitcoin und Co auf einer Börse oder Plattform liegen lässt, besitzt sie nicht wirklich, weil andere über die privaten Schlüssel verfügen. Demnach sind die Coins nur auf einer eigenen (Hardware-)Wallet wirklich sicher.
Millionenschaden durch manipulierte Wallets
Dieser Krypto-Grundsatz ist derzeit allerdings ordentlich ins Wanken geraten. Denn ausgerechnet Hardware-Wallets des bekannten Anbieters Ledger scheinen ein Sicherheitsproblem zu haben. Wie Computerbild berichtet, sollen Krypto-Kriminelle über manipulierte Ledger-Wallets mehr als 86 Millionen Dollar erbeutet haben.
Einige Branchenbeobachter:innen beziffern die Fehlbeträge sogar mit rund 93 Millionen Dollar. Zahlreiche Ledger-Nutzer:innen haben von entsprechenden Diebstählen berichtet. Allein 6,6 Millionen Dollar in Kryptowährungen sollen einer einzelnen Person abhanden gekommen sein.
Ledger untersucht Vorfälle in Asien
Ledger hat mittlerweile Untersuchungen eingeleitet. Ersten Erkenntnissen zufolge befand sich in mindestens einem untersuchten Gerät eine Hardware-Erweiterung, die wohl die beim Einrichten angezeigte Seed-Phrase abfangen konnte. Diese privaten Schlüssel dienen der Wiederherstellung des Zugangs zur Wallet – und öffnen Angreifer:innen das Tor zu den darauf verwahrten Kryptowährungen.
Eigentlich schien das Problem auf Asien und den dort tätigen Ledger-Händler Cryptbilis beschränkt zu sein. Dieser hat nach Aufforderung des Herstellers vorübergehend den Verkauf der Wallets eingestellt.
Berichte über Hardware-Implantat in Europa
Mittlerweile soll es aber auch aus Europa Berichte über manipulierte Ledger-Wallets geben. So teilte ein deutscher Nutzer via X Bilder einer mutmaßlich mit einem Hardware-Implantat versehenen Wallet, die er bei Mediamarkt gekauft haben will.
Eine Bestätigung des Herstellers gibt es dazu noch nicht. Laut Computerbild ist auch unklar, ob dieser Fall mit jenen in Asien zusammenhängt. Ledger, das die Fälle in Asien eingeräumt hat, erklärte, dass seine direkten Verkaufswege sicher seien.
Nutzer sollten neue Wallet einrichten
Sicherheitshalber rät das Unternehmen Nutzer:innen aber, ihre Kryptowährungen auf eine neue Wallet umzuziehen, bei denen sie die Seed-Phrase neu erzeugen lassen. Bevor aber nicht geklärt ist, ob auch Ledger-Wallets in Europa und Deutschland betroffen sind, sollten Nutzer:innen hierzulande diesen Rat mit Vorsicht genießen.

articles.title: « 123456 » : ce mauvais mot de passe est responsable d'une gigantesque fuite de données
articles.text:
Le Danemark a été victime d’une cyberattaque historique. La semaine dernière, le ministère du Numérique danois a révélé que des hackers sont parvenus à compromettre le registre civil danois (CPR). Dans le système informatique, ils ont pu consulter les noms, adresses et numéros d’identification de 8,8 millions de personnes. Il s’agit d’un « incident extrêmement grave », estime la ministre du Numérique, Christina Egelund. De l’avis du chercheur Jørn Guldberg, il n’y a « aucun précédent d’une fuite de données aussi importante venant d’une autorité publique ».
Quelques jours après l’annonce, nos confrères de Politiken, l’un des principaux quotidiens nationaux du Danemark, ont pu échange avec le pirate présumé à l’origine de l’attaque. Interrogé par le biais d’une messagerie chiffrée, le hacker affirme être l’auteur de l’attaque et dit qu’elle n’était « pas particulièrement difficile » à mener à bien. Pour prouver ses dires, le cybercriminel a envoyé un fichier de près de 8,8 millions de numéros CPR au média. Pour plusieurs experts, il est fort probable que le pirate dise vrai et soit bien impliqué dans la fuite.
À lire aussi : Fuite de données – la Cnaf suspend un site d’urgence après un « incident de cybersécurité »
Un mot de passe compromis à l’origine de l’attaque
Le cybercriminel fait une révélation étonnante sur le déroulement de la cyberattaque. Il prétend avoir d’abord utilisé le mot de passe compromis d’un ancien employé de Pays ApS, une petite entreprise danoise, autorisée à se connecter au registre national. Ce mot de passe n’était autre que le tristement célèbre « 123456 ». Avec ce mot de passe compromis, il a pu avoir accès au registre à partir du 10 septembre. Pendant plus de 21 jours, le hacker s’est servi dans la montagne de données sous ses yeux. Toujours selon ses déclarations, il a ensuite créé deux programmes informatiques pour organiser le vol. Le premier récupérait des informations dans le système CPR. Le second programme était taillé pour envoyer et stocker les informations sur un serveur externe.
Les journalistes de Politiken ont examiné les données issues de l’attaque pour confirmer les dires du truand. Elles montrent qu’au moins trois comptes utilisateurs de l’entreprise Pays ApS utilisaient « 123456 » en guise de mot de passe. L’un d’eux était même le compte administrateur de l’entreprise. Dans le sillage des révélations du pirate, Sophie Laursen, la directrice générale et propriétaire de Pays, a confirmé que « l’accès légal pour consulter des informations dans le système CPR a été détourné ».
À lire aussi : 730 millions de données volées – la police fait tomber Reacher, le moteur de recherche pirate de 3 ados
« Aucune sécurité, c’est une porte ouverte »
Interrogé par le média Berlingske, Jens Myrup Pedersen, professeur à l’Institut de génie électrique et informatique de l’université d’Aarhus, qualifie la situation de « désespérante » et voit « mal comment on pourrait avoir une sécurité plus mauvaise ». Il explique qu’un mot de passe comme « 123456 » est l’un des tout premiers code qu’un pirate va essayer pour tenter d’entrer dans un système informatique. Pour lui, ce n’était qu’une question de temps avant que les choses ne tournent mal.
« Il n’y a aucune sécurité, c’est une porte ouverte », tacle Jens Myrup Pedersen.
C’est loin d’être la première fois qu’un mauvais mot de passe a des conséquences désastreuses. On se souviendra notamment de l’affaire SolarWinds en 2020. Cette année-là, des pirates russes ont piégé une mise à jour du logiciel Orion de SolarWinds avec le malware Sunburst. Ils ont ainsi atteint les clients de l’éditeur, dont Microsoft, Google, Cisco et CrowdStrike. L’enquête a révélé que certains serveurs de SolarWinds étaient protégés par le mot de passe « solarwinds123 »… déjà divulgué en ligne des années plus tôt. Citons aussi l’affaire du compte Twitter de Donald Trump, qui était protégé par le mot de passe « maga2020! », soit le slogan de campagne « Make America Great Again 2020 ».
On vous invite évidemment à bannir les mots de passe trop simples, comme « 123456 », « password » ou votre date de naissance. Ceux-ci figurent en tête des listes testées en priorité par les pirates. Privilégiez plutôt des mots de passe longs, d’au moins 12 caractères, mêlant majuscules, minuscules, chiffres et symboles. Surtout, n’utilisez jamais le même mot de passe sur plusieurs services. En cas de fuite, un seul mot de passe volé pourrait ouvrir toutes les portes de votre vie numérique. On vous recommande idéalement de passer par un gestionnaire de mots de passe. Enfin, activez systématiquement la double authentification dès que c’est possible, de préférence par le biais d’une application ou d’une clé de sécurité plutôt que par SMS.

articles.title: TorrentClaw : ce moteur cherche les torrents infectés et découvre que VLC est souvent détourné
articles.text:
Des torrents malveillants utilisent une copie parfaitement légitime de VLC pour charger une bibliothèque infectée. Un moteur de recherche spécialisé en a repéré plusieurs dizaines en analysant près de 700 000 torrents.
Sur les sites de torrents, le nom d’un fichier ne garantit pas toujours que son contenu corresponde réellement à ce qui est annoncé. C’est précisément ce que cherche à vérifier TorrentClaw, un moteur de recherche lancé en février 2026 et dont l’index dépasse désormais les six millions de torrents.
Selon TorrentFreak, qui a interrogé ses développeurs, son outil TrueSpec rejoint temporairement les essaims BitTorrent, récupère généralement entre 10 et 20 Mo de données et utilise notamment FFprobe pour vérifier ce que contient réellement une vidéo. Les fichiers suspects peuvent ensuite être confrontés à VirusTotal.
34 malwares confirmés, dont 31 avec le même piège
Sur 687 057 torrents analysés, TrueSpec en a signalé 1 265 comme trompeurs, soit moins de 0,2 % : fausses résolutions, programmes déguisés en vidéos ou autres incohérences. Côté malwares, un premier bilan établi en juillet en recensait 6 450, mais beaucoup se sont révélés être des faux positifs, comme des scripts inoffensifs fournis par des fansubbers. TorrentClaw ne retient donc désormais que les cas confirmés par VirusTotal : il en reste 34.
Surtout, 31 de ces 34 infections suivent le même schéma. Le torrent contient un exécutable portant le nom d’un film ou d’un épisode récent, un fichier libvlc.dll et une véritable vidéo stockée dans un sous-dossier.
L’exécutable est pourtant une copie authentique de VLC, identique à celle distribuée par VideoLAN et correctement signée. Le piège se trouve dans la DLL placée à côté : lorsque VLC démarre, il peut charger cette bibliothèque et exécuter le code malveillant qu’elle contient. Cette technique est connue sous le nom de DLL side-loading. Elle consiste à profiter du fonctionnement normal d’une application légitime pour lui faire charger une bibliothèque malveillante placée au bon endroit. L’exécutable VLC lui-même n’est donc pas infecté.
The Boys, Frieren ou Dune utilisés comme appâts
Beaucoup de ces torrents reprenaient les noms de sorties populaires, notamment The Boys, Jujutsu Kaisen, Frieren, mais aussi Dune: Part Three ou Zootopia 2. Ils usurpaient également souvent les noms de groupes de distribution connus comme SubsPlease, ETHEL ou YTS afin de paraître plus crédibles. Parmi les 31 torrents utilisant le piège VLC, 15 étaient encore actifs début octobre, ce qui montre que la menace n’était pas seulement située au moment de l’analyse.
- Analyse avec plus de 70 moteurs antivirus
- Interface web simple et intuitive
- Possibilité de scanner des fichiers jusqu'à 650 Mo
Au-delà du caractère illicite du téléchargement d’œuvres protégées sans autorisation, ces torrents ajoutent ici un risque de sécurité supplémentaire. Un film ou un épisode vidéo n’a aucune raison de nécessiter un fichier .exe ou une DLL pour être lu. Si un torrent présenté comme une vidéo contient ce type de fichiers, c’est un signal d’alerte évident : mieux vaut ne rien lancer, même si l’exécutable porte le nom ou le logo de VLC.

articles.title: 5 Must-read lessons from Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly
articles.text:
5 Must-read lessons from Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly
Explore five lessons inspired by Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly, from believing in your dreams to embracing uncertainty and personal growth.
Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly important part of everyday life, changing how people work, communicate, and form relationships. But beyond questions of productivity and technological disruption lies a more personal concern: how might AI reshape human emotions, companionship, and our understanding of what it means to be alive?
In Endless Dream, speculative fiction writer Gigi Ganguly explores these questions through interconnected stories set across different points in the future.
The novel imagines societies where humans and artificial intelligence coexist in increasingly complex ways, examining themes such as AI companionship, grief, digital existence, loneliness, and belonging.
Rather than presenting technology as an uncomplicated solution to human problems or an inevitable threat, Ganguly uses imagined futures to explore the emotional and ethical questions that accompany technological progress.
5 Powerful lessons from Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly to reflect on
1. Human connection goes beyond technology
Technology can make communication easier, connect people across distances, and offer new forms of companionship. Yet the ability to communicate does not automatically guarantee that we feel understood or emotionally connected.
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly sophisticated, the boundaries between human interaction and digital companionship may become more complicated. AI systems might offer conversation, familiarity, and comfort, but questions about the nature of these relationships will remain.
Endless Dream invites readers to consider what makes a connection meaningful. The lesson is that genuine connection involves more than constant communication.
It requires us to think about trust, emotional understanding, vulnerability, and the needs that relationships fulfil in our lives.
2. Grief cannot always be resolved through technology
Grief is one of the most deeply personal experiences of being human. Losing someone can leave behind questions, memories, and a longing to reconnect with a person who is no longer physically present.
In a future shaped by advanced artificial intelligence and digital existence, technology might offer new ways to preserve memories or recreate aspects of a person's presence. Such possibilities could provide comfort, but they could also raise difficult questions about acceptance and letting go.
Would a digital recreation of someone we have lost help us process our grief, or make it harder to accept their absence? Could a simulation ever replace the complexity of a relationship shared with a living person?
These questions highlight the difference between preserving someone's digital traces and understanding the emotional reality of losing them.
The lesson is not that technology has no place in the grieving process. Rather, it encourages us to consider the limits of technological solutions when dealing with experiences that are fundamentally emotional and personal.
3. Progress raises new ethical questions
Technological advancement is often measured by what becomes possible. New systems can perform tasks more efficiently, expand human capabilities, and introduce entirely new ways of living.
However, the fact that something can be developed does not automatically mean that it should be used without careful consideration.
As artificial intelligence becomes more integrated into society, questions about responsibility, autonomy, privacy, and the treatment of non-human intelligence become increasingly important. The possibilities imagined in speculative fiction allow readers to examine these concerns before they become familiar features of everyday life.
Endless Dream creates space to consider how societies might respond when technological capabilities challenge existing moral assumptions.
The lesson is that progress requires more than innovation. It also demands thoughtful decisions about how new capabilities should be developed, governed, and used.
4. The search for belonging remains important
The world around us may change dramatically, but the desire to feel accepted and understood remains an important part of human experience.
People seek belonging through friendships, families, communities, and shared experiences. Yet loneliness can persist even in environments where communication is constant and opportunities to interact are abundant.
In futures where artificial intelligence becomes a regular presence in personal and social life, the meaning of belonging may become more complicated. Digital companionship might provide comfort, while new forms of existence could challenge traditional ideas about identity and community.
These possibilities encourage readers to think about whether belonging depends on shared biology, common experiences, emotional understanding, or something more difficult to define.
The lesson is that technological convenience cannot, by itself, answer every question about loneliness and identity. Understanding what makes us feel connected to others remains essential, regardless of how society evolves.
5. Being human means living with uncertainty
One of the defining characteristics of speculative fiction is its ability to imagine futures that challenge familiar assumptions. By placing recognisable emotions and dilemmas in unfamiliar circumstances, it allows readers to reconsider ideas they might otherwise take for granted.
Artificial intelligence, digital existence, and the possibility of radically different ways of living raise questions that do not always have simple answers. The boundaries between human and machine, presence and absence, or memory and identity may become increasingly difficult to define.
Instead of offering definitive solutions to every dilemma, stories about possible futures can encourage readers to remain curious and open to different perspectives.
Endless Dream invites reflection on what it means to live in a world where the familiar rules of existence may no longer apply in the same way.
The lesson is that uncertainty does not always need to be eliminated. Sometimes, acknowledging what we do not yet understand is the first step towards making more thoughtful decisions about the future.
Final thoughts
Endless Dream by Gigi Ganguly explores how AI could shape human relationships and future societies. Through themes of grief, belonging, connection and ethical innovation, the novel invites readers to reflect on what gives life meaning.
As AI evolves, these questions become more relevant. Technology may change how we communicate and experience the world, but imagining the future also means considering the values and human connections we want to preserve.

articles.title: Jev-like decision models are flooding the AI market, after researcher claims TypeSafe copied their research
articles.text:
Jev-like decision models are flooding the AI market, after researcher claims TypeSafe copied their research — Microsoft, OpenAI among companies releasing lightweight 'System One' AI models
Round and round the AI world goes.
Following the release of TypeSafe's Jev, many AI players have launched competitors, and many similar open-source projects from the likes of Microsoft, OpenAI, and many more have since emerged. Yet Nandakishor Mukkunnoth, of ConvAI Innovations, said that he'd come up with the base notions for Jev's architecture over a year before. So who copied who?
As a quick recap, Jev and its clones are APIs driven by decision models, for use in your own code. You feed them input data like a customer's online shopping transactions, alongside questions. For example: "is the user looking for a return?" for a yes/no answer, and "Which item are they referring to?" with a multiple-choice answer. A Jev-like AI model will answer each of the questions or choices with a probability that can then be used in your own "if" statements. While the concept by itself isn't strictly new, this practical application is indeed novel.
The release made a good portion of the internet abuzz, as the seemingly simple concept is extremely useful and neatly sidesteps the usual problems with trying to coax an LLM into giving a direct answer. There's no token-by-token text generation, no conversations, no re-feeding of conversation history, no feeding it gobs of information for context, and no conversational hallucination — just direct data in the form of probabilities. It's really fast too, answering questions in parallel, and exceedingly cheap compared to standard LLMs.
Along with Jev, TypeSafe also released a brief description of its System One architecture. Only days later, Nandakishor Mukkunnoth, founder of ConvAI Innovations, explained in a blog post that he'd actually "designed the Jev architecture one year back." He referred to his arXiv paper on SalesRLAgent, describing how he created a model for probability estimation, published on March 30, 2025. Along with the paper, he published his model weights and dataset. He later followed up with a September paper that more closely aligns with how Jev operates.
In his write-up, Mukkunnoth expressed his frustration, describing how he got overlooked "because [his idea] was built for a vertical use case," meaning SalesRLAgent was made to fix one specific problem, while TypeSafe made Jev a general-purpose decision engine. Notably, the company released Jev as a complete, hosted product, with its own servers, API, documentation, developer kits, and naturally, pricing.
Nevertheless, he said he opted to not remain bitter about the development, and ultimately released the open-source Laya roughly the same day. Laya is essentially a Jev-style model and interface that you can run on your own hardware, complete with multi-language support. Likely adding to the confusion, both TypeSafe and Mukkunnoth called their models "System 1/One" types, likely as a reference to Daniel Kahneman's book, Thinking, Fast and Slow, which describes System 1 as a faster, emotional mode of thought, whereas System 2 refers to slower, more logical thought.
Regardless, there was no stopping the hype generated by this new use case for AI, so players in this space did what they do best: copied the concept and rolled out their own services. In the space of only a few weeks after Jev was released, the world saw Microsoft Decision, OpenAI Decisions API, and Fastino Glide. Both Cloudflare Clef and Perplexity Decider arrived with open weights, meaning you can run them on your own gear, assuming it's up to the task. Over on the open-source aisle, there's Amazon's Strands Decider 2B, Kev, Von, Jeff, jevlike, SemIf, OpenJev, NanoJev, Ollaya, and many others.
Why so many? Well, because most of these projects, including the commercial ones, share the same root: taking an existing lightweight model, usually always a variant of Alibaba's open-source Qwen, and adding the extra layers that shape the input, output, and decision-making procedure. Mukkunnoth's Laya is based on encoder-only models from the Bert family, rather than an LLM like Qwen. And yet it's not too hard to imagine that many folks might have cribbed at least some notes from his work, given how quickly the alternatives materialized.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Embark Sees Arc Raiders Split into Separate PvE and PvPvE Camps After Upcoming Test
articles.text:
Monday, October 12th 2026
Embark Sees Arc Raiders Split into Separate PvE and PvPvE Camps After Upcoming Test
Almost since Embark Studios launched Arc Raiders, there has been a group of gamers calling for a greater emphasis on co-op PvE gameplay, with many asking the studio for separate PvE modes after the implementation of a new matchmaking system that prioritized player aggressiveness and matched players who were more likely to play co-op and avoid killing their fellow players. Ahead of a new PvE mode test, Arc Raiders executive producer, Aleksander Grøndal, has spoken in an interview with GamesRadar+ about the potential future of PvE in Arc Raiders.
In the interview following Arc Raiders's latest Frozen Trail update, Grøndal says comments that the introduction of a co-op-only game mode is potentially overdue, even if it is just a test for now, because the studio deliberated about whether or not it was going to "open this door" for a long time. When asked about a potential split between the PvE and PvP sides to Arc Raiders, the producer commented that "it's very possible." He continues, saying "I think the community is already split along those lines. If the game eventually will represent that? Quite possibly."He goes on to comment on the importance of respecting the game's community and how players want to play the game versus how the developers intended for it to be played.
I think it's important to respect how the players want to enjoy the game, even if it doesn't necessarily fully gel with what we thought the game was initially or how we designed the game to be initially. It's possible. Of course, it creates some challenges on our end. We need to figure out what we really mean by that.
He explains that the apprehension surrounding how a PvE-PvPvE split would affect the game is one of the reasons behind the limited-time testing that Embark is conducting in Arc Raiders in October.
I think there's a lot of valid concerns, and internally at the studio, that has been expressed, both sides of that coin. It's not like everyone was high-fiving Aleks when we introduced this idea to do this test. That's not the case. There were some real concerns there too. But at the end of the day, I really feel like we need to answer this question, at least to ourselves, and of course also to the players.
Source:
				GamesRadar+
