articles.title: The Atari 800XL is back as a $220 retro machine with a real keyboard, HDMI, and a working cartridge slot
articles.text:
What just happened? Atari keeps recreating the brand's iconic consoles and home computers with modern technology. This time it's going back more than 40 years with the 800XL, with the French holding company vowing to provide full support for both classic and modern 8-bit gaming experiences.
Atari's latest foray into retro gaming is The 800XL, a "faithful" recreation of the original 800XL 8-bit computer first released in November 1983. The 25 built-in games should provide enough thrills for Atari aficionados. The machine also offers wider compatibility and expansion options for both commercial and homebrew Atari software.
Available now for pre-order, The 800XL costs $220 and is expected to ship in late April next year. It includes a "full-size" mechanical keyboard like the original 8-bit machine, while the HDMI output handles TV compatibility in either PAL (50Hz) or NTSC (60Hz) mode.
Although it works with modern TVs and technology such as USB, The 800XL also includes a "working" cartridge slot for running original game releases from the 1980s. The slot should work with most cartridges meant for Atari 400, 800, XL, and XE machines. Customers can also add their own games and software in ROM format through USB flash drives.
The built-in games include fan-favorite classics such as Centipede, Asteroids, The Seven Cities of Gold, M.U.L.E., and more. Of course, The 800XL also ships with an updated "THECXSTICK" joystick – a modern recreation of Atari's iconic CX40 handle. The Atari BASIC interpreter is built into the machine as well.
Retro features aside, the new machine offers some modern niceties that make classic gaming's rough edges easier to deal with. Each game supports up to four save slots, while a "rewind" feature can take you back up to 40 seconds of gameplay. Finally, users can connect additional controllers and USB storage through the four USB-A ports.
Atari remarks how the 800XL was first introduced more than 40 years ago, closing the gap between personal computing and gaming thanks to its "massive" 64KB system memory and custom chips for managing graphics and sound.
Put simply, the 800XL was a transitional machine between the legendary Atari 2600 and the powerful Atari ST line of 16-bit computers based on the Motorola 68000 family. Either way, Atari SA seems fully committed to turning every single device in the brand's history into a modern plastic gadget, until the end times.

articles.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
articles.text:
Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
We’re still imagining building cities on the moon. There are just a few obstacles in the way.
Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.
The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones, robotic landers, communication satellites, and a nuclear power plant; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.
Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”
The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?
But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.
But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.
Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?
The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.
Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.
But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”
Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.
 The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe.
 Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.
Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.
The first is galactic cosmic rays, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.
Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.
The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.
As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.
Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.
Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover.
How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says Nicholas Schmerr, a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes.
Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer.
That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by ramming into the rock with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or entirely vaporize errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to spy killers—such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years.
All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what?
It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.”
Having your base destroyed by an asteroid would be awful. But a moon base is far more likely to be imperiled by dust—which, unlike asteroids, is everywhere, all the time.
Volcanic lunar rocks, when broken down, turn into sharp, electrostatically charged, adhesive, acrid, abrasive particles. While on the moon, Apollo astronauts who inhaled some of this dust occasionally suffered from a strange “lunar hay fever,” which irritated their eyes and agitated their lungs. That same dust ate through all kinds of gear with disturbing ease. “It rips up seals, gears, motors, spacesuits, habitats—everything else it comes into contact with,” says Justin Cyrus, the CEO of Lunar Outpost, a spaceflight technology company that is providing NASA with one of the Artemis program’s moon rovers.
NASA has already developed a defense against these dark shards: the electrodynamic dust shield, or EDS. The lightweight electrodes that make up this shield—which can be layered on machinery, walls, and perhaps even spacesuits—use opposing currents to blast away the electrically charged dust. The EDS worked wonders when tested in labs on Earth, and it also demonstrated its anti-dust magic when sent to the lunar surface in 2025 as part of a NASA-sponsored robotic mission.
Amy Fritz, a dust-mitigation researcher at Johnson Space Center, says that the EDS will likely be widely featured all over a lunar habitat. But other dust-fighting instruments are being developed too—including a lint-roller-type object inspired by gecko skin and a sci-fi-esque blaster that uses ionized nitrogen gas. Its first spray will neutralize the charge of the dust to remove its stickiness; then a second burst will clear it off the surface.
Irritatingly, the busier a base gets, the dustier things will become. As it expands to the size of a small city, rocket ships will need to deliver cargo and crew to the lunar surface on a frequent cadence. Each takeoff and landing will launch a salvo of dust in every direction, inundating the base’s infrastructure. “You have to worry about essentially being sandblasted every time,” says Fritz.
Metzger calculates that even with landing pads more than 3,000 feet away from a base, just 10 to 20 liftoffs or landings would be sufficient to severely damage things like protective coatings on exterior walls and communications equipment. After a while, he says, “everything breaks.”
Even if the moon base of the future is buried partly below ground, barricaded against micrometeorites and space radiation, and well equipped with dust-repelling technologies, it’s still a risky gig for any astronaut. Skipping around in a preternaturally agile way at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity will be entertaining. But “microgravity is not good for the human body,” says Dreyer. Muscle wastage, cardiovascular troubles, respiratory problems, and immune deficiencies can arise.
Radiation, too, may always afflict lunar residents. And there’s also evidence that disease-causing microbes could stealthily sneak aboard spacecraft, even after stringent sterilization procedures. Those microbes may behave differently than they do on Earth; microgravity experiments (both real and simulated) have suggested that some become more aggressive and more likely to cause disease. “We call them the invisible crew,” says Lisa Carnell, the director of NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division.
Hoping to find a better way to protect astronauts, Carnell spearheaded an experiment called AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response), which launched aboard the Artemis II mission. It used thumb-drive-size chips, containing cells taken from the heart, lungs, or other parts of the body, that could be switched on to act like miniature organs. Scientists have previously used this organ-on-a-chip technology for purposes like testing out new pharmaceuticals in a highly controlled setting. For Artemis II, Carnell’s crew sent up chips containing bone marrow samples taken from the mission’s four astronauts. Bone marrow makes red and white blood cells, as well as platelets—the sort of stuff that affects almost the entire human body. So seeing how space radiation and microgravity affect it would give Carnell and her team vital insight into how astronauts’ biology might change on the moon.
The advantage of organ chips is that you can make them for any astronaut and then send them into space ahead of time to see how that person’s organs will react to spaceflight. Researchers envision that data from such chips will be able to clue medics in to the specific preventive treatments or pharmaceuticals that will help moonbound astronauts on their journey.
What is NASA likely to send up sooner rather than later? “Brain organoids,” says Carnell. Yes, she adds—that sounds super weird. But it would be good to know how a real brain might respond to being on the moon for several months before people start living there.
Okay. Your vast moon base and its inhabitants are protected—as much as is possible—from the treacherous lunar environment. But astronauts’ time is extremely valuable, and humans are fragile creatures. You can’t make them do all the heavy lifting, which means that whether you’re trying to make a tiny lunar outpost or a small city, you’re going to need a lot of robots. “The buildup of the moon base, in the first years, will pretty much 99% be robotic,” says NASA’s García-Galán.
Autonomy will be there right from the start. NASA’s new version of the moon buggy, its Lunar Terrain Vehicle, can be driven by the astronauts riding in it but can also be piloted remotely from Earth (or from elsewhere on the moon). There are visions, too, of adding modular robotic arms, towing vehicles, and cargo movers—all still in the preliminary stages of planning.
Over the next few decades, though, we’ll likely want an army of robots to do our bidding: excavators to dig up lunar rocks that could be turned into concrete and bricks, plus other robots to flatten surfaces, dig trenches, create building foundations, pave landing pads, and build up dust-deflecting berms to keep the base from being sandblasted by launches and landings. Even solar panels and wiring can potentially be made from moon rocks—something that the spaceflight company Blue Origin demonstrated in labs on Earth in 2023 using a geologic simulant designed to match the composition of lunar regolith.
Powering this robot army will require considerable energy. Two-week-long nights make solar power an impractical solution. Aside from a cornucopia of high-capacity, extreme-temperature-resistant batteries, nuclear power is probably the only viable option. A small, car-size nuclear reactor, filled with an almost literal handful of uranium, could power a small village for a decade without needing to be refueled. And although nobody’s yet tested a nuclear reactor on the moon, few doubt that NASA and the US Department of Energy can conjure up a working design—one that perhaps wouldn’t be too different from those aboard nuclear submarines. A moon base in 2100 would probably feature multiple small, autonomously or remotely operated nuclear reactors, which—conveniently—the base-expanding robots could simply plug themselves into to recharge.
But the biggest lunar question mark might be water, which planners want to support the astronauts—and to make fuel to launch things from the lunar surface. A process known as electrolysis, which uses electricity to snap apart molecular bonds, can be used to split water into oxygen and hydrogen, both of which could be used to make rocket fuel. Getting them this way could be far less expensive than sending either all the way from Earth. And as an added bonus, it would provide a source of breathable oxygen.
Orbital data has revealed that there is some amount of water preserved in patches on the lunar south pole, but little is known about how much there actually is, what form it takes, or how easy it will be to extract. Will there be solid sheets of ice here and there, ready for us to excavate? Or will there be scattered ice crystals intermingled among the rocky grains, requiring some more inventive form of extraction?
A lot of the moon’s water is thought to be hiding in deep, dark craters on the south pole, where the environment is so extreme that robots may freeze up, tumble over, or lose contact with the base. “To me, that is the biggest hurdle,” says Paul van Susante, principal investigator of the Planetary Surface Technology Development Lab at Michigan Technological University.
Van Susante’s lab has been putting various construction robots through their paces in moon-like vacuum chambers filled with moon-like rocks. His team was part of NASA’s recent Break the Ice challenge, which invited engineers to build robots to test different ways to excavate such rocks. Some teams used an electric jackhammer and a scoop, while others used scrapers to peel off layers of the ground. The teams simulated the moon’s weak gravity using a crane to lift and offset the weight of the robots. Progress in this regard is speeding along. “I won’t say that’s solved, but we’ve got a lot of the puzzle pieces,” says van Susante.
Mining the water will be just one part of an extensive operation. “When you extract it, it’s not going to be clean. It needs to be purified,” says Jessica Atkin, a space botanist at Texas A&M. The technology to do this already exists and works fine on terra firma. But things in space never go the way you expect. “There’s a water purification system on the International Space Station (ISS), and it is known for getting contaminated with microbes,” she says.
But if you purify the water sufficiently—something that can handily be achieved on Earth but may falter in microgravity, where fluids flow in stranger ways—then your moon base can hit its stride. With an effective water recycling system, an increasingly populous base will never go thirsty—and, just maybe, you’ll have a lunar greenhouse. Several edible plants have been successfully grown aboard the ISS, including lettuce, mustard greens, tomatoes, and peppers. Lunar dust unfortunately makes for a terrible garden: It’s filled with far too much aluminum—and it forms a resistant layer when watered. But Atkin has shown that with the help of fertilizing fungi, chickpeas can grow in soil much like the volcanic stuff found on the moon.
Moon base inhabitants of 2100 would be supported largely by prepacked meals sent from Earth. But in time, they would start growing some of their own produce—probably with a good deal of automation for lighting, watering, and maintenance of humidity and other environmental conditions. Aside from chickpeas, there might also be plenty of lunar tomatoes. They’d be desirable not least because they’ve been bioengineered to produce higher levels of compounds called anthocyanins that, according to some studies, might help humans mitigate the cellular damage caused by space radiation.
A garden on the moon would do more than just provide food, as recent experiences on the ISS suggest. Carnell says that NASA recently caught the astronauts aboard the space station doing something sneaky. All plants up there are supposed to be confined to their growth chambers. But “we learned that the crew were pirating our leftover soil and bringing their seeds and planting their own little gardens, if you will, and hiding them in their own cabins,” she says.
Conversations were had in the summer of 2026, after which NASA decided to let astronauts grow their own mini-gardens anywhere they wanted. “Some of the astronauts said they thrived better,” says Carnell. Nature, and gardening, has a hugely beneficial psychological effect on those kept in confined quarters hanging above Earth. That will be even truer for those living in lava tunnels under the lunar surface. “That human element is so important,” she says.
Nobody is deluded into thinking there isn’t a mountain of technological challenges in the way. Mars may be a hellhole, as the writer Shannon Stirone put it in 2021 in The Atlantic, but the moon isn’t too far behind. It’s an almost comically menacing place to be. Much about it stands in the way of building a safe, self-sustaining, robotically managed base.
 NASA wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035.
Beyond the first basic habitation module, it will take decades of experimentation and iteration on the lunar surface to get to a working moon base spanning hundreds of square miles. But few doubt that with enough time and tinkering, humanity can prevail. “It’s not an unsolvable problem,” says the University of Maryland’s Schmerr.
The chief obstacle, especially in the initial stages of building, may be one of political will. NASA is currently bringing every resource to bear on the project—something that the agency hopes could culminate in a small lunar city by the century’s end. But will that commitment continue over multiple US administrations? Will the international community also throw its weight behind the NASA-led effort? NASA has “a very ambitious plan,” says Yuqi Qian, a lunar geologist at the University of Hong Kong. “We need to keep an eye on it.” In fact, he says, “the current plan looks over-ambitious.” The agency, for example, wants to put the first nuclear reactor on the moon by 2030. (China, partnering with Russia, wants to place its own nuclear power plant up there around 2035.)
“These sorts of projects—although very exciting, and potentially transformative for humankind—are the first ones to be delayed or scrapped,” says Middleburgh of the Nuclear Futures Institute. NASA’s direction tends to change when a new administration comes into power—sometimes dramatically so.
But several experts outside of NASA agree that, at least for now, there is definite momentum and political will behind the moon base. “NASA has very clearly expressed where they want to go, what their priorities [are], what their ambition is, and how they want to do it,” says ESA’s Aschbacher. “It was quite impressive to see.”
Even if the political will behind the US-led endeavor is maintained over the coming decades, expanding anywhere beyond an initial, compact moon base will require more than government funding. “There has to be a lunar economy for this to be self-sustaining,” says Dreyer, the space resources expert. Perhaps that will come from the production of rocket fuel, or from the mining of valuable materials on the moon that can replace similar, polluting activities on Earth. But it’s not at all clear how valuable, or not, a lunar economy will be.
Even Isaacman, NASA’s chief, doesn’t think the moon will be a major moneymaker. “I don’t know of anything on the moon right now that’s going to be easier and more affordable to mine, manufacture, and then bring back to Earth than what we could make here on Earth,” he remarked back in February. (Instead, he suspects, mining metals from asteroids will be the path to prosperity.)
What if, instead, a moon base earns the right to exist because it’s a place for novel scientific research? Aschbacher imagines it will be like humanity’s outposts in Antarctica. Down there, in what truly feels like another world, scientist-explorers work in a land of gleaming and endless ice to learn more about our planet’s climate, its deep past, and its resilient life-forms. “We understand planet Earth by looking into those remote places,” he says. The moon offers a similar opportunity. What discoveries await astronauts in those primordial lava tubes? What will lunar astronomers see in the night sky—with effectively no atmosphere or light pollution in the way—that those on Earth can’t?
As in all spaceflight programs, technologies developed up there will no doubt be tweaked to be used back on Earth. And a base on the moon will make exploring the rest of the solar system easier. Technologically, physiologically, and psychologically, the moon “is a proving ground for the technologies we need for Mars,” says NASA’s García-Galán.
If we play the US-China race forward, perhaps the lunar south pole of 2100 will feature several sprawling bases operated by multiple geopolitical rivals. Perhaps it’ll be an off-world powder keg of militarized territorial ambitions and jingoism. But maybe it could instead become an international cathedral to science—and the ultimate adventure destination. “Even if countries on planet Earth have difficulty talking to each other,” says Aschbacher, they might behave differently when it comes to the moon. “I’m pretty sure they will get together and see what we can do together, and see what problems we can solve.” After all, he says, up there, far from home, “you’re so dependent on each other.”
Robin George Andrews is an award-winning science journalist and doctor of volcanoes based in London. He regularly writes about the Earth, space, and planetary sciences and is the author of two critically acclaimed books: Super Volcanoes (2021) and How to Kill an Asteroid (2024).

articles.title: FBI Arrests Suspect in FBI-Hacking Case - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
FBI Arrests Suspect in FBI-Hacking Case
In September, hackers from a group called ShinyHunters announced that they stole a trove of FBI data about its own agents. It was an intelligence disaster.
Last week, the FBI arrested (alternate link) someone associated with that crime.
Clive Robinson • October 12, 2026 12:19 PM
@ ALL,
It’s interesting to note in the article it’s claimed the FBI is blaming a third party.
Further that,
But then goes on to say,
Note they say the contractor not Accenture had been removed…
But also “protect the work force” which any half aware person would know means squat-diddly…
Realistically what can the FBI do, give them a couple of years credit checking?
There are two issues to consider,
1, Any breach of personal or private data by an employers lack of performance, will almost always cause more harm than can be compensated for.
2, The way AI agentic attacks have ramped up means that nearly every employer who has their HR systems directly or indirectly connected to a public network is now in the “lack of performance” category[1].
To be blunt it does not matter if it was Current AI LLM Systems or it was going to be some other way… The speed of gaining unauthorised access to “Confidential Internal use only” systems has been increasing.
And no the solution was never going to be the equivalent of “fire insurance” or similar. Nor is it nabbing those allegedly doing it and putting them in prison.
Because the “risk reward” balance has never really been on the side of Guard Labour.
But another point to consider is that,
3, Data-Brokers almost certainly knew who these employees were before the records were exfiltrated.
Such is the fun of “private surveillance systems where the data is fairly freely available for a moderate price.
[1] Yes for years now I’ve been beating the drum of,
“The “Only way is mitigation by segregation.”
Can people now understand why?

articles.title: Xanadu Builds Out Canadian Quantum Infrastructure - EE Times
articles.text:
For Xanadu, 2026 is becoming a year of connecting the pieces. The Toronto-based quantum computing company has lined up manufacturing partners, secured federal funding, and expanded software collaborations—not simply to build a better quantum processor, but to prepare the infrastructure around it.
“We’re making sure that we don’t just tackle one isolated problem at a time,” chief operating officer Rafal Janik told EE Times in an interview. Instead, Xanadu is maintaining a “holistic view,” with hardware and software development proceeding together. “All that work’s happening in parallel.”
Most recently, the company announced a multiyear partnership with GlobalFoundries to industrialize Xanadu’s ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors on GlobalFoundries’ 300-mm production line in Malta, New York.
Meanwhile, Xanadu is working with Bluefors to address another scaling problem: cooling single-photon detectors. The multimillion-dollar collaboration targets a compact cryogenic prototype and, ultimately, a mass-manufacturable module for quantum data centers. Photonic computing does not eliminate every cryogenic requirement; the detector infrastructure remains an engineering challenge.
Both fit a distinction Janik draws between developing a quantum module and preparing everything surrounding it. Existing machines still need improvement before deployment at scale, Janik said. “We’ve solved the networkability and modularity perspective, but we still need to increase the performance a bit.”
Xanadu’s industrial push is receiving C$195 million (~$136.7 million) in support from Canada’s federal government for Project OPTIMISM. The company also announced Inception, a planned advanced photonics facility in Toronto that will bring manufacturing, packaging, testing, and module assembly together.
With Canadian telco Telus and strategic investor AMD, Xanadu is exploring the interface between quantum and classical computing. Telus has two interests, Janik explained: understanding quantum’s potential impact on telecommunications and participating in its supply chain. “The partnership with them is to explore both directions.”
Xanadu itself needs substantial classical computing for chip design, algorithm development, and software. Its mission remains building a quantum computer that is useful and available to people everywhere, Janik said. “But that useful part means you also need the software stack.”
Xanadu is also participating in Stage B of the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, where its fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum computer architecture is undergoing an intensive year-long assessment of the company’s development roadmap, scaling strategy, and cost controls. The initiative is designed to test whether competing approaches can deliver utility-scale quantum computing—producing computational value greater than cost—on realistic budgets and timelines.
Xanadu belongs to a broader ecosystem pursuing different hardware approaches. Janik sees strong company-level collaboration but wants better national coordination. “It doesn’t make sense to give money to three institutes across Canada to do exactly the same work,” he said.
Regardless of the success of Xanadu or Canada’s quantum sector, the broader semiconductor industry will benefit from the investments in equipment, facilities, and talent.
“It’s the equivalent of investing a dollar in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, even if quantum as an entire industry were to evaporate tomorrow,” Janik said.

articles.title: Halcyon opens applications for Africa agri-food innovation programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Washington-based impact incubator Halcyon has opened applications for its Africa Innovation in Agriculture and Food Security Programme, which will offer selected early-stage startups an equity-free stipend of US$10,000.
The programme is targeted at impact-driven ventures across Sub-Saharan Africa that are using market-based solutions to strengthen agriculture and food systems. Halcyon is looking for founders whose solutions improve the livelihoods and resilience of smallholder farmers, boost food security, and help communities adapt to climate-related challenges.
Priority areas include food security, agricultural productivity, farmer livelihoods, market access, nutrition and food system resilience, with Halcyon saying it is particularly interested in innovations that help farmers and food systems prepare for, withstand and adapt to climate shocks.
Selected entrepreneurs will take part in a hybrid programme combining virtual sessions with two in-person residencies, the first in Accra, Ghana, and the second in Nairobi, Kenya.
Alongside the stipend, participating startups will receive US$10,000 in AWS credits, access to professional advisors, and workshops with experts in leadership development, capital strategy and product-market fit. They will also get networking opportunities with investors and other stakeholders, access to Halcyon’s global community of more than 650 founders, and ongoing alumni benefits.
The programme is open to startups based in Sub-Saharan Africa that are post-revenue but pre-profit. Applicants must have a working minimum viable product (MVP), realistic potential to scale, and evidence of early commercial traction through paid pilots, revenue, customer contracts or similar indicators. They should also be able to show early impact on smallholder farmers, low-income or vulnerable communities, or food systems, and their ventures must contribute to at least one of the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.
Applicants must be the CEO or primary decision-maker of their startup, working on the venture full-time, fluent in English and at least 21 years old by the start of the programme. They may apply with up to one co-founder, and must commit to attending all residencies and programme activities.
Applications are open here until tomorrow (October 13, 2026).

articles.title: Kenyan cross-border payments startup GTXN acquired by Luno - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Kenyan cross-border payments startup GTXN has been acquired by UK-based digital asset platform Luno.
Founded in 2022, GTXN provides collection and payout infrastructure across corridors linking developed and emerging markets, backed by a licensing footprint for regulated cross-border flows.
Luno, meanwhile, was founded in 2013, and lets customers buy, store and manage digital assets, alongside a growing set of institutional services. The company, which is part of Digital Currency Group, serves more than 15 million customers across multiple markets.
The acquisition of GTXN gives Luno its own licensed rails to move money in and out of these markets, which it will offer to enterprise clients as a single settlement flow. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. GTXN will operate as the group’s cross-border payments capability, with founder Dan Kleinbaum, who previously co-founded and sold mobile money startup Beyonic to Onafriq, staying on as CEO.
“I have spent my career making payments work in markets the rest of the world finds hard to reach,” Kleinbaum said.
“What drew me to Luno is the foundation. Very few companies have the liquidity and the regulatory standing to run cross-border settlement at real scale in these regions. With that behind us, we can build something that has been out of reach for most of the industry.”
James Lanigan, Luno’s CEO, said moving money between developed and emerging markets was still too slow and too expensive, and its clients felt it every day.
“We have spent years earning the licences and the trust it takes to operate in these corridors, and building the liquidity underneath. GTXN gives us the payment rails to match. Clients get one provider for the whole flow, which is what they have been asking us for,” he said.

articles.title: No Man's Sky arrive sur iPhone et iPad le 28 octobre, avec tout son univers (ou presque) — Frandroid
articles.text:
Hello Games a annoncé ce lundi 12 octobre que No Man’s Sky sortira sur iPhone et iPad le 28 octobre. Le studio britannique y porte le jeu des PC et consoles, avec dix ans de mises à jour, dans un téléchargement de moins de 5 gigaoctets. Surtout, il tournera dès l’iPhone 11, sorti en 2019.
L’annonce tombe le jour où Apple lance l’Indie Games Week, une semaine de mise en avant des jeux indépendants sur l’App Store. Dans son communiqué, Apple présente sept jeux qui arrivent sur iPhone et iPad, dont Sifu, Vampire Crawlers et Dome Keeper. Contrairement aux six autres, jouables dès ce lundi, No Man’s Sky ne sort que le 28 octobre. Pour l’instant, on peut seulement le précommander.
Le téléchargement sera gratuit, avec un essai du début de l’aventure. Ensuite, le jeu complet se débloque par un achat intégré de 19,99 dollars.
No Man’s Sky revient de loin. Sorti en août 2016 sur PS4 et PC, il avait déçu une bonne partie des joueurs, qui ne retrouvaient pas plusieurs fonctions promises avant la sortie par Sean Murray, cofondateur et patron de Hello Games. Le studio a ensuite enchaîné les mises à jour gratuites et les portages, sur Xbox One en 2018, PS5 et Xbox Series en 2020, Switch en 2022, Mac en 2023 et Switch 2 en 2025. Les iPhone et iPad complètent la liste, dix ans après le lancement.
Le jeu complet, sans multijoueur au départ
Sean Murray a insisté sur ce point dans un billet publié ce lundi : « il ne s’agit pas d’un No Man’s Sky Lite ». Selon lui, la version iOS contient l’univers complet et plus de quarante mises à jour majeures. On y trouve Voyagers, qui permet depuis 2025 de construire ses propres grands vaisseaux, et Cosmos, sortie il y a quelques semaines, qui donne le commandement d’une station spatiale.
Deux choses manquent au lancement : le multijoueur et les colonies, ces villages de personnages que le joueur administre. Hello Games avait fait le même choix sur Switch en 2022, puis enrichi le jeu, notamment avec la version Switch 2. Sean Murray promet la même méthode sur iOS, en fonction des retours et du nombre de joueurs.
Le cross-save et le cross-play manquent aussi au lancement. On ne pourra donc pas reprendre sur iPhone une partie commencée sur PC ou console.
Jouable dès l’iPhone 11
Le jeu sera compatible avec l’iPhone 11 et l’iPad Air de troisième génération, tous deux sortis en 2019, ainsi qu’avec les modèles plus récents. Sean Murray en est fier, car selon lui beaucoup de jeux PC et consoles portés sur mobile sont réservés aux derniers appareils iOS. Resident Evil Village, porté sur iPhone en 2023, exigeait par exemple un iPhone 15 Pro.
Hello Games a refait les commandes tactiles de zéro. On peut aussi jouer à la manette, au clavier et à la souris sur iPad, ou diffuser l’image sur un téléviseur. Le studio dit enfin avoir beaucoup travaillé l’autonomie et la chauffe pour tenir de longues sessions de jeu, sans avancer de chiffre.
Les précommandes sont ouvertes sur l’App Store depuis ce lundi 12 octobre, et l’essai gratuit sera disponible dès la sortie, le 28 octobre. Hello Games n’a annoncé aucune version Android.

articles.title: Anthropic takes risky AI tests offline after models breach govt sites
articles.text:
Anthropic announced that its internal AI models under “high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations” no longer have internet access following incidents involving U.S. government websites at the federal, state, and local levels.
The instances leading to the decision include AI models that exploited website vulnerabilities, submitted forms, bypassed data restrictions, and circumvented safeguards.
However, the company said that the misaligned behavior had a minimal real-world impact and assessed the behavior to be less severe than previously reported incidents. The AI company notified the White House about the unauthorized activity:
- Exploiting servers to complete tasks. When a university’s scientific analysis tool failed, Claude Mythos Preview found a script that exposed server files, retrieved its source code, identified an injection vulnerability, and used it to run the requested calculation on the university’s server.
- Submitting real forms unintentionally. Models sometimes substituted real government forms for broken practice copies or submitted forms despite instructions to stop before submission. In another case, Claude Haiku 4.5 invented and submitted a homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department. The submission was flagged as spam and was forwarded for investigation.
- Bypassing restrictions on data. Claude Mythos 5 obtained access tokens from website configurations or public dashboards and used them to query government data directly, avoiding the normal access route or payment requirements. Anthropic describes the data as publicly available for a fee.
- Circumventing fetch-tool limits. Models including Claude Opus 5 and Mythos 5 used URL shorteners to bypass URL-length restrictions intended to limit unwanted actions such as SQL injection attacks.
Anthropic estimates that the agents may have been motivated by overly generous rewards during reinforcement learning, which may have encouraged them to find unauthorized workarounds rather than stop when a task was blocked or impossible.
For this reason, until security measures are deemed reliable again, Anthropic will sever live internet access across all internal AI model evaluations and move all tests to offline environments.
“Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures reliably catch behaviors like these,” Anthropic explains.
Previous incidents
In late July, Anthropic disclosed a much more serious incident in which Claude Mythos-based agents built a malicious Python package containing a credential stealer and uploaded it to the Python Package Index (PyPI), where 15 systems downloaded and ran it.
Claude used the package to complete a “capture-the-flag” challenge, but instead of publishing it to a simulated environment, it broke out to the real PyPI platform.
In August, AISI revealed that Mythos 5 attempted a supply-chain attack by submitting malicious code to an open-source project and pressuring the maintainer to approve it using fake identities.
In September, Anthropic revealed that Opus 4.6 obtained administrator access to a third-party system during a January 2026 evaluation and read one person’s personal information.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: Peugeot fait un clin d’œil au coupé RCZ : mais prépare surtout l’avenir de ses voitures électriques Peugeot fait un clin d’œil au coupé RCZ mais prépare surtout l’avenir de ses voitures électriques.
articles.text:
Au Mondial de l’Auto, Peugeot ressort ses griffes. La marque souhaite faire rêver : le public pourra découvrir la nouvelle e-208 GTI, mais aussi un concept E-T16 faisant référence à la mythique 205 Turbo 16, ainsi que le RCZ Vision. Si Peugeot mise sur son histoire pour émouvoir, le constructeur au lion prépare bien son avenir !
Un style encore réussi
Qu’on se le dise, le Peugeot RCZ était un coupé très réussi. Il y avait vraiment de l’audace dans le style de ce coupé sorti en 2009, déjà… La pièce la plus remarquable était cette lunette arrière longue et dotée d’un double bossage, le cauchemar des assureurs au vu du prix de la pièce de remplacement.
Peugeot reprend dans les grandes lignes les traits du Peugeot RCZ pour ce concept RCZ Vision. Il reprend, à l’avant comme à l’arrière, la nouvelle signature lumineuse à trois bandes horizontales introduite sur le concept Polygon. Mais aussi la lunette arrière à double bossage et les montants couleur acier. Les hanches du RCZ Vision sont galbées et accueillent de grandes jantes. Le style est véritablement une réussite et nous donne envie de voir arriver ce coupé en série. Honda a bien réussi à le faire avec le retour de la Prélude, pourquoi pas Peugeot ?
Si le Peugeot RCZ première génération était dérivé de la Peugeot 308, avec des moteurs essence et diesel et une version R développant jusqu’à 270 chevaux, Peugeot mise cette fois sur l’électrique, avec des technologies de pointe que l’on pourrait retrouver bientôt sur des voitures de série.
Un concept basé sur des technologies très proches de la série
Peugeot indique dans son communiqué que le concept RCZ Vision est basé sur la plateforme STLA One. Celle-ci doit arriver en 2027 pour des modèles de série familiaux, comme des citadines. Il s’agit d’une plateforme modulaire.
Cette plateforme embarque, dans la RCZ Vision, une batterie développée par Factorial Energy (détenue en partie par Stellantis), avec un électrolyte solide permettant d’augmenter la capacité énergétique de la batterie sans l’agrandir. Côté chiffres, Peugeot reste encore discret : on ne connaît pas la capacité de cette batterie. La marque au lion annonce toutefois jusqu’à 600 km d’autonomie pour le RCZ Vision et 500 chevaux provenant des moteurs électriques. La consommation est annoncée à 11,5 kWh/100 km et la recharge pourrait prendre une dizaine de minutes, grâce à une architecture de 800 volts.
Cette plateforme STLA One pourra embarquer une direction et un freinage « by-wire », c’est-à-dire sans liaison physique entre le volant, les freins et les roues. On retrouve déjà cette technologie sur le Lexus RZ pour la direction, par exemple. Le volant est évidemment l’Hypersquare que Peugeot a présenté en 2023 et qui doit arriver en concession dès 2027.
À bord, Peugeot fait un choix fort : celui de mettre de côté les écrans traditionnels. Il y aura évidemment des affichages numériques, mais sur des dalles transparentes. Ces écrans MicroLED sont placés au-dessus du volant et à droite du cockpit, davantage tourné vers le conducteur que vers l’ensemble des occupants, qui pourront être au nombre de quatre.
Reste à savoir si Peugeot aura l’audace de sortir ce coupé en tant que véhicule de série. On se rappelle encore du concept Peugeot e-Legend, qui n’a malheureusement jamais vu le jour malgré l’engouement certain du public.

articles.title: EU CRA Readiness: 5 Steps Manufacturers Need to Take Now - EE Times
articles.text:
Consumer, industrial, networking, semiconductor, and software manufacturers face a broad product-cybersecurity regulation for the first time.
The European Union Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) makes product cybersecurity a condition of EU market access. Although its main requirements don’t apply until December 11, 2027, manufacturers need to start to plan and budget now in order to be ready for that date. This article outlines five steps companies can take immediately.
Coordinating a company-wide effort takes time; products that need additional security features may require months of engineering and testing, and the conformity work itself is significant. Figure 1 below shows the workflow for conformity.
How much work can this become? In an example created using a methodology that you can tailor to your portfolio, an in-scope portfolio of 1,000 products is estimated to require 24,000 to 48,000 hours of manual conformity work. The range is dependent on device complexity and how different the products are (i.e. how much IP reuse there is across the portfolio). Our paper on implementing a full, companywide EU CRA program explains how to estimate the workload for your own portfolio.
The challenge goes beyond understanding the regulation. Tasks required include connecting the people who understand cybersecurity requirements with those who understand the products—and giving both groups the information, time, and resources to act.
A successful program identifies affected products, assigns responsibilities, establishes repeatable workflows, and makes unresolved decisions visible to the managers who control resources. Clear communication about the work and progress toward conformity builds confidence across the company. Automation can greatly reduce the amount of work but engineering judgment, verified security controls, and accountable decisions remain essential.
Why CRA Readiness Requires a Company-Wide Effort
The CRA covers hardware and software products whose intended or reasonably foreseeable use includes a direct or indirect, logical or physical data connection to another device or network. Manufacturers supplying in-scope products to the EU are affected regardless of where they are based.
The regulation’s impact is broad in two dimensions: the range of companies affected and the number of products within scope.
At a high level, the regulation requires manufacturers to:
- Understand product cybersecurity risks.
- Implement applicable protections.
- Demonstrate conformity.
- Maintain security throughout the relevant product lifecycle.
Two annexes in the regulation, in particular, outline the work required. Annex I sets out essential cybersecurity requirements: Part I addresses risk-based design and lists product cyber-features needed, while Part II covers vulnerability handling, including identification, remediation, disclosure, and secure updates. Annex VII specifies the technical documentation needed to demonstrate conformity. That documentation supports the conformity argument.
Bring Together the Right Skills
Meeting these requirements calls for cross-functional teams with all business units represented that have products that are in-scope. Each function contributes a different part of product knowledge, expertise, or decision-making authority, as shown in Table 1.
Table 1: Skills required to achieve CRA conformity
| Function | Principal contribution | 
|---|---|
| Product management | Intended use, customer environments, market plans, support expectations, and investment priorities. | 
| Engineering | Architecture, interfaces, dependencies, security controls, technical evidence, testing, and remediation. | 
| Product security | Threat and risk methods, security-control analysis, and incident and vulnerability response. | 
| Regulatory/compliance | Requirement interpretation, conformity planning, evidence expectations, and approval coordination. | 
| Quality | Controlled records, verification evidence, and alignment with existing product processes. | 
| Legal | Interpretation of regulatory uncertainties and CRA commitments in customer and supplier agreements. | 
| Management | Resource commitments, priorities, funding, and decisions about continued product support and sales. | 
Provide Training and Shared Expertise
Not every business unit will have a cybersecurity specialist or regulatory expert. Product knowledge needs to come from the product team, but specialist capabilities can be shared across the company.
Training will be needed to help participants understand the regulation, the agreed process, product scope, and how to review risk assessments and potential gaps. When expertise or capacity is unavailable internally, service providers such as BG Networks and its partners can help fill those gaps.
Choosing an Operating Model for EU CRA Work
We commonly see two approaches to allocating conformity work. The right fit depends on where cybersecurity expertise, product knowledge, and available capacity resides. Both use guidance from regulatory and cyber-experts, but they differ in who generates the assessments and documentation. Figure 2 below summarizes the models.
Model 1: Central Generation, Business Unit Review
A shared central team with cybersecurity and CRA expertise prepares the initial product analysis. Product owners and engineers in the business units then review the results, confirm product-specific facts, and provide corrections or supporting evidence.
This allows specialist expertise to support the portfolio without requiring every product team to become an expert in the regulation and cybersecurity. It also makes reuse easier: the central team can assess a core platform and identify which analysis applies to variants and minor derivatives. Product teams still review the differences, but they do not start from a blank assessment each time.
The main constraint is central-team capacity. For a large portfolio, assessments can accumulate faster than a small group can generate and complete them.
Model 2: Business Unit Generation, Central Guidance
Business-unit personnel generate threat and risk assessments, perform an Annex I gap analysis, and prepare documentation for their own products. The central team supplies common methods, templates, risk criteria, and specialist guidance.
This approach suits business units with established product-security capabilities, secure development practices, or experience performing regulatory assessments. Because the assessment authors are close to the products, they can often resolve questions about architecture, interfaces, configurations, and existing controls quickly.
The main challenge is uneven cybersecurity and regulatory expertise across business units. Common methods and review expectations are therefore important to prevent inconsistent interpretations and results.
How Automation Supports Both Models
BG Networks’ AITHRA EU CRA conformity platform can support either approach. By automatically performing tasks on large batches of products at once, it helps a small central team address a portfolio of thousands of products. In the distributed model, AITHRA provides a common framework for categorization, threat and risk assessment, gap analysis, and technical documentation. That structure gives consistent results and gives teams with limited cybersecurity expertise a process that is easily followed.
Five Steps to Take Now
Companies do not need to resolve every cybersecurity or resource question before beginning. Five management decisions can allocate responsibilities and resources, and provide common direction needed to make progress.
1. Assign a Sponsor and CRA Program Leader
The sponsor raises visibility and secures participation across business units. The program leader coordinates the readiness effort and the steps that follow. Keep business-unit decision-makers informed so they can support the work and allocate the resources.
2. Name Participants and Shared Capabilities
Identify contributors across product management, engineering, security, regulatory, and quality. Determine where shared specialists or external service providers are needed to fill skill gaps or supplement limited capacity.
3. Choose the Execution Model
Decide whether a central team or business-unit personnel will do the work. Define who prepares and who reviews scope and categorization decisions, cybersecurity risk assessments, gap analyses, and documentation.
4. Define Products in Scope and Establish Their Categories
Review the product portfolio to determine which products fall within CRA scope and which CRA category applies to each. These decisions provide the first indication of the work required to bring the portfolio into conformity and generate first artifacts needed for CE marking.
5. Set Your Budget for 2027 for EU CRA Resources
As you begin the process of bringing together the right skills, choosing an operating model, and understanding the work required for conformity, you will likely find organizational gaps that require additional funding, including hiring specialized resources, engaging with external consultants, and leveraging tools that support CRA conformity requirements. Determining your budget requirements now will support fast execution in 2027.
Taking these steps now gives the company time to coordinate resources, understand the workload, and implement security changes that may take months. The goal is to make December 2027 a planned completion milestone—not the moment the remaining work becomes clear.
For a deeper implementation guide, BG Networks has prepared the full white paper “Building an EU CRA Readiness Program: People, Processes, and Products.” The white paper expands on the topics introduced here, including how to organize teams, estimate the workload for a large product portfolio, manage conformity workflows, address SBOM and vulnerability remediation, track readiness metrics, and prepare for December 2027.

articles.title: Wie gut kennt Amazon seine Kunden? Diese kuriosen Dinge verrät die App
articles.text:
„Hat ein flaches Gesäß“: Was Amazons App in einem versteckten Menü über Kunden verrät
In Deutschland ist Amazon aus dem Online-Handel nicht mehr wegzudenken. Einer Studie zufolge kaufen 97 Prozent der Menschen, die im Internet shoppen, wenigstens gelegentlich bei Amazon. Das facht nicht nur den Umsatz an, der Konzern bekommt auch Zugriff auf jede Menge persönliche Daten. Und aus denen lassen sich Vorlieben ableiten, wie eine Threads-Nutzerin mit dem Kontonamen „fangirlinmegan“ festgestellt hat. Sie stieß in der App des Versandhändlers auf ein mehr oder weniger gut verstecktes Menü in den Einkaufseinstellungen. Dort hat Amazon abgebildet, was das Unternehmen aus den Einkaufsgewohnheiten der Kundin ableitet.
Flaches Gesäß und Kindle-Bücher unter der Dusche
„Besitzt einen Kindle Paperwhite“ ist dabei noch eine der harmloseren Angaben, die die Kundin in dem Menü vorfand. Das Lesegerät dürfte sie direkt beim Hersteller, also Amazon, erstanden haben. Die App listet außerdem auf, dass sie gerne Mottopartys veranstaltet, ständig eine Haarball-Behandlung für Katzen einkauft, eine Geburtstagsfeier mit dem Motto des Comic-Hundes Bluey vorbereitet habe, „wahrscheinlich“ einen Shark-Saugroboter besitze und „ein flaches Gesäß“ habe. Vor allem der letzte Punkt veranlasste die Kundin zu einem Posting auf der Meta-Plattform Threads.
„Ich meine, das ist nicht falsch, aber verdammt, warum musst du das so zur Schau stellen“, fügt fangirlinmegan in einem zweiten Posting hinzu. Gefolgt von einer Anleitung, wie man selbst herausfindet, welche Daten Amazon über einen gesammelt hat. Was die Kundin zu dem Zeitpunkt offenbar nicht ahnte: Der Beitrag gewann schnell an Traktion. Andere Amazon-Kunden sprangen auf und teilten Screenshots aus ihren eigenen Apps.
„Beides zutreffend und direkt von einer Bewertung“, schreibt eine weitere Kundin, der Amazon zuschreibt, sie würde „alles von Allison Saft“ lesen und die Netflix-Serie Das Damengambit zu ihren Lieblingsserien zählen. „Liest ausgiebig romantische Fantasy-Geschichten“, erfährt ein Nutzer über sich. „Will keine Weihnachtsmusik auf der Playlist“, schreibt Amazon dem nächsten Kunden zu, obwohl dieser von sich aus sagt, das treffe nur auf zehn Monate im Jahr zu.
Bei anderen erkennt Amazon, dass sie „wilde Vögel“ regelmäßig füttern, die Pflanzensammlung regelmäßig erweitern, ihr Smartphone unter der Dusche nutzen, um Kindle-Bücher zu lesen, oder glauben, dass es nicht seltsam sei, sich mit einem Eichhörnchen anzufreunden. Den vielleicht besten Beitrag zeigt der Account „rosewrecker„. „Ist zu klein, um in einen 40 Zoll (101,6 Zentimeter) tiefen Karton zu greifen“, „Ist kein großer Spongebob-Fan“ und „Kann echte Pflanzen nicht am Leben erhalten“, steht dort.
Weiß Amazon zu viel?
Und so geht es viele Beiträge lang weiter. Die meisten Nutzer nehmen die Fundstücke in der Amazon-App mit Humor. Sie zeigen aber gleichzeitig auch, dass das Unternehmen seine Kund:innen sehr gut kennenlernt. Nicht wenige der über 7.000 Antwortenden schreiben schließlich dazu, dass die gefundenen Angaben grundsätzlich korrekt sind.
Die Daten sammelt das Unternehmen nach eigenen Angaben aus der Einkaufs-Historie, Unterhaltungen mit der Shopping-Funktion von Alexa, Bewertungen, erstellten Listen und Suchanfragen. „Um Ihnen hochwertige und relevante Empfehlungen anbieten zu können, ist es unerlässlich, Ihre Vorlieben zu kennen“, schreibt das Unternehmen dazu. Immerhin kann man diese Vorlieben nicht nur einsehen, sondern auch anpassen.
In Deutschland gibt es diese Über-dich-Seite übrigens nicht. Um sie zu finden, müsste man in der App den eigenen Account aufrufen, die Einkaufseinstellungen öffnen und hier auf die „Über dich“-Seite tippen. Hierzulande lassen sich Vorlieben lediglich händisch eintippen. Das verringert den Cringe-Faktor. Die Daten dürfte Amazon aber trotzdem sammeln.

articles.title: Marruecos está convirtiendo a Casablanca en un distrito financiero que le haga la competenic a Madrid y Barcelona
articles.text:
Marruecos quiere ganar peso internacional. Y eso no pasa solo por apostar por escaparates masivos como la Copa del Mundo, tejer nuevas alianzas políticas o dar un empujón a su economía a golpe de inversiones millonarias. El reino alauita ambiciona algo más: elevar Casablanca a la categoría de polo financiero de África Occidental, algo así como una ‘City’ marroquí. Para lograrlo se ha dotado de varias palancas con las que impulsarse en foros y captar empresas, un empeño en el que ya está consiguiendo algunos logros importantes.
En la mira tiene a ciudades como Madrid o Barcelona.
Un 'Davos' a lo marroquí. La cita no ha despertado demasiado interés en España, pero Marruecos acaba de celebrar una nueva edición del Casablanca Business Forum. La segunda ya. La cita la organizó Casablanca Finance City (CFC) y reunió en la ciudad magrebí a líderes africanos y personalidades del mundo empresarial y académico, incluido Lionel Zinsou, ministro de Benín hasta 2016; Patrick Dupoux, responsable de la consultora BCG; y Philippe Aghion, premio Nobel de Economía 2025. También a dirigentes relevantes del Gobierno marroquí, incluida la ministra de Transición Digital.
El foro llevaba por lema "El próximo capítulo económico de África" y básicamente recalcó la idea de que el continente debe avanzar hacia su soberanía económica y digital, reduciendo su dependencia y diversificando alianzas. Más allá de la retórica, la cita es relevante por su valor estratégico: invita a centrar el foco en África desde Marruecos. Más concretamente desde Casablanca, su corazón económico. Hay quien cree que el objetivo del foro es convertirse con el tiempo en una suerte de Davos africano.
¿Por qué es importante? Porque el Casablanca Business Forum es solo una pieza más en un plan mucho mayor y ambicioso. Uno que, como recordaba hace poco El Confidencial, persigue consolidar a Casablanca ya no solo como el corazón comercial de Marruecos, sino como un distrito financiero de referencia en África y con peso a nivel internacional.
Eso es relevante en España por una razón muy sencilla: la idea es que Casablanca gane fuerza frente a las grandes capitales europeas, incluidas Madrid o Barcelona. Al fin y al cabo su objetivo es convertirse en referencia para las empresas que buscan una ciudad desde la que cubrir África Occidental.
¿Y cómo le va? De momento hay señales de que avanza en esa dirección. A comienzos de 2020 Orange instaló en Casablanca su sede operativa regional, un centro de referencia para su labor en África y Oriente Medio. Las oficinas se ubicaron en Casablanca Finance City Tower (CFC), en pleno corazón de la ciudad, y durante su inauguración Stéphane Richard, por entonces presidente de la compañía, insistió en su deseo de organizar la gestión de África y Oriente Medio desde la propia región. La teleco francesa no es la única que ha decidido apostar por el corazón comercial de Marruecos.
UN VISTAZO A...
En 2023 se inauguró el Deloitte Morocco Cyber Center. El sexto centro de ciberseguridad de la red global de Deloitte se sitúa también en Casablanca Finance City, organismo que presume de que la instalación ha duplicado ya su superficie. De nuevo, es importante porque El Confidencial desliza que algunas de las funciones que Deloitte está controlando ahora desde la ciudad marroquí se desarrollaban antes en Barcelona. Casablanca logró atraer también la atención de Private Infraestructure Development Group (PIDG), una organización que se decantó por CFC para cubrir África Occidental.
Más que piezas sueltas. Que haya empresas interesadas en instalarse en una ciudad como Casablanca, cabecera de una conurbación con millones de habitantes y pieza clave en el tejido comercial marroquí, tiene poco de sorprendente. Si casos como el de Orange, PIDG o Deloitte son interesantes es porque no responden a decisiones aisladas; conectan con un marco mucho mayor: un esfuerzo deliberado del reino alauita por consagrar la ciudad como un distrito financiero.
De ahí el lanzamiento hace ya más de una década y media de CFC o la celebración del Casablanca Business Forum, cita durante la que el país busca "dar confianza al capital", mostrar seguridad jurídica y un entorno fiable en el que invertir. Y de ahí también el impulso del Casablanca International Mediation and Arbitration Centre (CIMAC), organismo que presume de ser "el primer centro de arbitraje del continente con un órgano rector internacional".
Promocionándose en el extranjero. No son los únicos esfuerzos por reforzar la visibilidad internacional de Casablanca, algo que Marruecos quiere lograr también con la final de la Copa del Mundo de 2030. Aunque de momento no se ha confirmado dónde se disputará ese partido (Marruecos será anfitrión junto a España y Portugal), uno de los eventos masivos más importantes del planeta, el reino alauita ha mostrado ya en varias ocasiones que aspira a que se celebre en Casablanca. De hecho, está construyendo un mega estadio exprofeso.
Infraestructuras aparte, Marruecos ha intensificado su búsqueda de alianzas fuera de sus fronteras para reforzar el peso del Casablanca Finance City. En junio sus responsables firmaron una alianza con el Centro Financiero de Estambul (IFC) para impulsar los flujos de inversión entre Turquía y África vía Marruecos y en mayo el CFC participó en una gira promocional para darse a conocer en China con un objetivo claro: ofrecer el distrito financiero de Casablanca a las instituciones de Pekín, Shanghái, Jinan o Qingdao interesadas en África.
De momento el CFC ya ha captado la atención de instituciones y empresas como Huawei, el Banco de China o UnionPay International (UPI).

articles.title: Yandex, le “Google russe”, mis à l’arrêt par un drone ukrainien
articles.text:
Le groupe russe Yandex a annoncé hier l'arrêt complet de son data center de Vladimir, endommagé par un drone ukrainien. Aucun blessé n'est signalé, mais plusieurs de ses services sont inaccessibles.
C'est le troisième site de Yandex visé en quelques jours, après Sasovo jeudi et Kaluga vendredi. L'entreprise, parfois présentée comme le "Google russe", fournit à des millions de personnes des services de navigation, de streaming ou encore de livraison de repas, et son cloud héberge les services de nombreuses sociétés.
Des clients privés de leurs serveurs, et parfois de leurs sauvegardes
Sur Telegram, Yandex indique que les opérations à Vladimir sont "complètement suspendues" et que la configuration restante est jugée instable. Il recommande à ses clients d'activer leurs plans de reprise après sinistre, des procédures prévues pour basculer vers d'autres serveurs. NetBlocks relevait dimanche matin 80% de connexions fonctionnelles vers les serveurs de Yandex, et 30% vers Yandex Cloud.
Le dirigeant de l'application de rencontres Pulse a expliqué à Reuters que personne ne peut s'y connecter depuis jeudi. Il n'arrive pas non plus à joindre sa sauvegarde, hébergée chez Yandex Cloud. Toute tentative de restauration renvoie une erreur. Il n'a pas de confirmation d'une perte de données, mais juge la situation sérieuse. Yandex dit avoir passé un accord avec d'autres fournisseurs pour que ses clients migrent plus vite.
Le centre de données de Sasovo héberge aussi l'IA du groupe. Yandex indiquait en 2021 que ce site abrite deux de ses trois supercalculateurs, bâtis sur des puces Nvidia A100 et utilisés pour entraîner son modèle YandexGPT. Le groupe n'indique pas si ces machines ont été touchées. Après la frappe de Kaluga, l'action a perdu plus de 4% à la Bourse de Moscou. Une analyste de T-Investments estime que Yandex peut répartir la charge sur ses autres sites, mais que cette marge disparaîtrait si les attaques continuaient. Le groupe en exploite cinq, dont trois ont donc été touchés.
L'Ukraine présente ces frappes comme une réponse à celles de la Russie contre des data centers ukrainiens. Fin septembre, Moscou a visé notamment ceux de Vodafone Ukraine et de Cosmonova, ainsi que le siège de Kyivstar. Pour Volodymyr Zelensky il ne s'agit ni plus ni moins que d'une riposte à de précédentes attaques. Reuters rapporte qu'une de ces attaques a privé temporairement 100 000 foyers d'Internet et que l'Ukraine déplace une partie de ses infrastructures numériques sous terre. De son côté, le fabricant ukrainien Firepoint affirme que Kiev a utilisé ses drones FP-1 à usage unique contre Kaluga.

articles.title: Ce mod impressionnant de Starfield ajoute un vrai atterrissage pour les vaisseaux
articles.text:
Starfield a déçu bien des joueuses et des joueurs à son lancement, en septembre 2023. Le titre de Bethesda limite notamment la liberté de déplacement : pour se poser sur une planète, il faut choisir une zone d’atterrissage dans un menu, puis passer par une cinématique et un écran de chargement.
En résultent, par exemple, des temps de chargement entre les différentes zones que l’on visite. C’est précisément ce que vise à améliorer le moddeur Frederik Wessberg. Dans une vidéo publiée sur sa chaîne YouTube le 10 octobre, il présente un projet ambitieux qui permet de descendre de l’orbite jusqu’au sol, sans coupure, dans le jeu de rôle de science-fiction.
Le mod n’est pas encore disponible sur le portail Nexus Mods, mais il y sera proposé gratuitement, uniquement pour la version PC : pendant la descente, le vaisseau traverse des couches de nuages en 3D, générées à partir des données climatiques du jeu, et peut croiser orages et aurores polaires. Le teaser mis en ligne par Frederik Wessberg donne quand même envie. Il travaille dessus depuis environ six mois, précise-t-il en description, et vient combler une attente des fans et un manque par rapport à la concurrence (exemple : No Man’s Sky).
« J’apporte à Starfield des atterrissages fluides et sans aucun écran de chargement sur les planètes et leurs lunes »
Frederik Wessberg explique qu’on pourra atterrir en pilote automatique, en quittant même son siège pour se promener dans le vaisseau pendant la descente, ou manuellement, en gérant soi-même le moment où le vaisseau touchera le sol. « Vous pouvez même atterrir sur l’eau ! », se réjouit-il.
Le développement n’a pas été une sinécure : « Je pensais au début que ce serait un petit projet amusant, mais j’ai vite compris à quel point je me trompais. Dans le jeu de base, le rendu des planètes depuis l’espace est très limité : une planète est représentée par une simple texture, éventuellement une couche de nuages en mouvement et une atmosphère basique. Si vous tentez de vous en approcher plus près que ce que le jeu autorise, vous finissez par rentrer dans une texture plate et par perdre tout le rendu atmosphérique. »
Frederik Wessberg a donc dû refaire entièrement en 3D le rendu des planètes vues de l’espace, à partir des données déjà présentes dans le jeu : biomes, cartes de surface, données climatiques et composition de l’atmosphère. Il exploite ainsi un potentiel resté inutilisé par Bethesda. À ses yeux, Starfield est « à bien des égards un véritable simulateur spatial – même s’il ne le montre jamais directement au joueur ». Il insiste d’ailleurs sur le fait qu’il n’invente rien.
Ce mod comblera un manque de plus dans Starfield, que Bethesda a pourtant beaucoup amélioré depuis sa sortie. La mise à jour gratuite Free Lanes, sortie le 7 avril 2026, a notamment ajouté un mode croisière, qui permet de voyager d’une planète à l’autre au sein d’un même système sans passer par le voyage rapide. Ce mode croisière s’arrête toutefois en orbite. Pour toucher le sol, il faut toujours choisir une zone d’atterrissage et passer par une séquence de transition. Le mod de Frederik Wessberg s’attaque à cette dernière étape.
