articles.title: IonQ to Acquire Zero Trust Firm Elisity for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.text:
IonQ on Monday said it signed a definitive agreement to buy Elisity in a stock-only transaction worth up to $1.3 billion.
Up to $150 million of that amount is earnout consideration, contingent on how Elisity’s business performs. IonQ expects to complete the acquisition in the fourth quarter of 2026.
The number of IonQ shares issued will depend on the company’s volume-weighted average price over 20 trading days ending shortly before closing, but the price will be kept between $33.07 and $49.61.
Founded in 2019, Elisity sells software that restricts which users, devices, workloads and AI agents can communicate on enterprise networks, based on least-privilege policies. A component called IdentityGraph combines what Elisity collects itself with data from partner tools, including identity, asset and risk details, to guide access decisions.
According to IonQ, Elisity has more than 100 customer deployments. The startup raised more than $70 million.
IonQ’s portfolio spans quantum computing, networking, sensing and security, and the company already offers post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD). It plans to use Elisity’s customer and CISO relationships to reach more enterprise and government buyers for those technologies and its quantum computing products.
The two companies plan to add cryptographic inventory and risk data to IdentityGraph. The goal is to help organizations decide which post-quantum upgrades to tackle first, weighing business risk and the criticality of affected operations.
“Access controls reduce exposure; cryptographic upgrades would address the underlying weaknesses,” Elisity CEO James Winebrenner wrote in a blog post on the deal. In a press release, he noted: “Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running.”
IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi pointed to Q-Day, the point at which quantum computers could break widely used public-key encryption. “Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted,” he said. IonQ also cited recent White House executive orders promoting quantum technology and pushing federal agencies to adopt PQC sooner.
Once the deal is completed, Winebrenner and Elisity’s existing management team will remain in charge of the business.
SecurityWeek’s cybersecurity M&A tracker has cataloged roughly 300 deals to date in 2026.

Despencou: Galaxy A57 (256 GB) cai 55% e tem bom custo-benefício
Samsung Galaxy A57 5G de 256 GB com tela AMOLED de 120 Hz e câmera de 50 MP recebe melhor oferta histórica com cupom no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy A57 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 1.810 no Pix com cupom PROMODEHOJE no Mercado Livre. O celular da Samsung com câmera wide de 50 MP e tela Super AMOLED+ de 120 Hz está pelo menor preço já registrado, com desconto de 55% sobre o original de R$ 3.999.
O Galaxy A57 é o celular de melhor relação custo-benefício do mercado, graças ao chip Exynos 1680 de 4 nanômetros e 8 GB de RAM LPDDR5X, que permitem rodar apps em multitarefa e soluções do Galaxy AI. Os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno razoável para guardar fotos e vídeos.
Seu kit de câmeras é formado por uma wide de 50 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 12 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, uma macro de 5 MP para aproximações de elementos pequenos com qualidade, e uma frontal de 12 MP que tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
A tela de 6,7″ conta com a tecnologia Super AMOLED+, evolução sutil da Super AMOLED que melhora a qualidade na reprodução de imagens. Sua taxa de atualização 120 Hz e o brilho de até 1.900 nits a permitem reproduzir imagens com alta fluidez nas transições, além de ter visibilidade garantida em qualquer ambiente.
O corpo de alumínio do A57 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+, resistente contra pancadas e quedas. A certificação IP68 confere proteção adicional contra poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste por até dois dias de uso, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W via USB-C o permite receber uma carga de 60% em apenas 30 minutos, recurso ideal para usuários que não querem se preocupar com tomadas e powerbanks.
O Galaxy A57 de 256 GB (R$ 1.810 no Pix com cupom PROMODEHOJE) está sendo atualizado para o Android 17 e deve receber mais cinco updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Samsung possui conectividade 5G, Bluetooth 6.0, NFC e Wi-Fi 6E.

articles.title: Gaius Capital closes debut fund at €50 million, raises another €6 million via co-investment vehicle | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Gaius Capital, a Berlin-based private equity firm focused on business succession in the DACH Mittelstand, has announced the final close of its debut fund, Gaius Nachfolgekapital I, at €50 million.
The oversubscribed fund hit its hard cap alongside an additional €6 million raised through a co-investment vehicle, bringing the total capital secured to €56 million. The final close comes just four months after the fund’s first close at €40 million in June.
“We are very grateful to our investors for their trust and support throughout this journey. Reaching the final close at our hard cap, with significant demand from an experienced institutional investor base, is a strong endorsement of our strategy and the opportunity we see in Mittelstand succession,” said Jan Mickel, Founding Partner, Gaius Capital.
Founded in 2025 in Berlin by Mickel, Joscha Radeck, and Dr. Lukas Klipper, Gaius Capital is an independent investment firm that pursues a scalable buy-and-build strategy in the micro- and small-cap segments of the Mittelstand. The firm partners with founder- and family-owned businesses to provide collaborative succession solutions, seeking majority stakes in profitable mid-sized service companies.
The primary focus of the firm is insurance and financial services, industrial services, healthcare, and testing and inspection, across three German-speaking regions: Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Unlike a conventional acquirer, Gaius also offers entrepreneurs the option to participate in the value created through a group sale via its Gaius Seller Consortium model, allowing founders to retain an economic stake in the combined entity they help build.
Since its first close, Gaius has already begun executing its strategy through its inaugural succession platform, Praevidentia Group, aimed at the insurance broking sector in Germany. The firm recently launched Alpiora Group, its second succession platform, focused on insurance advisory and brokerage in Switzerland.
Its website mentions additional succession platforms being built across sectors, including outpatient care, wealth management, compliance, and medical technology testing.
“With the fundraise successfully completed, our focus is now on deploying capital thoughtfully and building lasting partnerships with entrepreneurs across the DACH region,” added Mickel.
The firm also revealed that more than 90% of the commitments to the fund came from institutional investors across Germany, France, the Benelux region, the United States, and the United Kingdom. With the fund closed, Gaius Capital says its priority is to identify and build succession platforms in resilient-growth service industries across the DACH region. Alongside Gaius Nachfolgekapital I, the firm also manages Gaius Unternehmerkapital I, its other active fund vintage from 2025.

articles.title: Ajouter du stockage à son Chromebook : la SanDisk Ultra 128 Go avec adaptateur SD est à 24,99 €
articles.text:
La carte microSDXC SanDisk Ultra 128 Go pour Chromebook est à 24,99 €
La SanDisk Ultra 128 Go pour Chromebook propose jusqu’à 140 Mo/s en lecture, une certification A1 et un adaptateur SD pour les lecteurs compatibles.
Amazon propose la SanDisk Ultra microSDXC 128 Go pour Chromebook à 24,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 32,99 €. L’écart atteint 8 €, soit environ 24 %. Cette offre concerne la carte neuve avec adaptateur SD, expédiée par Amazon. Elle peut servir à conserver des documents, des photos ou des vidéos sur un support amovible.
Une carte de 128 Go certifiée pour les Chromebook
Cette version de la SanDisk Ultra a été testée et certifiée pour fonctionner avec les Chromebook. Elle permet d’ajouter du stockage aux modèles équipés d’un lecteur compatible, notamment pour garder des fichiers accessibles hors connexion. Sa capacité nominale est de 128 Go ; l’espace réellement disponible après formatage est inférieur.
La mention Chromebook ne la réserve pas à ces ordinateurs : il s’agit d’une carte microSDXC UHS-I, utilisable avec d’autres appareils prenant en charge ce format et cette capacité. Il faut donc vérifier les caractéristiques du lecteur avant l’achat, particulièrement sur les équipements anciens.
Jusqu’à 140 Mo/s en lecture, avec un adaptateur SD fourni
SanDisk annonce une vitesse de lecture pouvant atteindre 140 Mo/s pour cette capacité. Ce maximum nécessite un appareil compatible avec la technologie utilisée pour dépasser le débit standard UHS-I. Les résultats varient selon le lecteur, l’interface et les conditions d’utilisation. La vitesse d’écriture est inférieure : les 140 Mo/s ne s’appliquent donc pas à tous les transferts.
La carte porte les classifications A1, Class 10 et U1. SanDisk la destine notamment au stockage de fichiers, aux applications Android compatibles et aux vidéos Full HD. La prise en charge de ces usages dépend également de l’appareil qui accueille la carte.
L’adaptateur SD fourni permet de l’insérer dans un lecteur au format SD classique prenant en charge les cartes SDXC. Il facilite ainsi le passage entre différents lecteurs, sans modifier la capacité ni les performances intrinsèques de la carte.

articles.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
articles.text:
No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.
Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.
“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we’ve seen usually happens away from workers—you’re taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you’re doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”
In many ways, robotics and AI are well suited to the relentless pace of work that is already happening inside e-commerce fulfillment centers. Amazon’s promise of speedy deliveries for its 200 million Prime subscribers in particular requires hundreds of thousands of human employees to speedily assemble and ship out customer orders that often combine a dizzying array of products.
Much of the work in fulfillment centers also frequently involves “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks that people may prefer to hand over to robots. The injury and illness rate for workers in the US warehouse sector has typically been more than double the average across all industries, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
“You have almost 2 million people working in the warehousing sector in the United States, and it’s characterized by very high turnover and very high workplace injury rates,” said Greenwood.
But robots are still far from capable of handling the many different tasks that human workers can perform. So Amazon still has a massive human workforce working in tandem with the company’s growing fleet of wheeled robots and robotic arms—and workplaces can get complicated when humans are expected to keep pace with robotic counterparts.
Amazon’s robotic era
Amazon has rapidly built its robotic fleet following the pivotal decision to acquire the robotics company Kiva Systems in 2012. Kiva was among the earliest companies to pioneer wheeled mobile robots that bring racks of items to warehouse workers, instead of requiring people to continually walk around grabbing items off of shelves inside fulfillment centers.
Since the acquisition, Kiva was renamed Amazon Robotics and has focused on deploying an array of mobile robots and robotic arms that Amazon primarily manufactures in-house at facilities in Massachusetts. This year, the company also announced it would build additional production factories in Austin, Texas, and Greenwood, Indiana, to churn out even more robots in the future.
“There’s a theme of how we look at the challenges that we can help our associates and our employees with, and how we can make our customers’ lives better through these technologies,” Scott Dresser, vice president of Amazon Robotics, told Ars. “Each step of the way, [we are] tackling a hard or deep set of technical challenges to achieve that goal.”
Most of Amazon’s million-robot fleet still consists of those wheeled mobile robots. The company claims that its robotic Sequoia system can identify and store items up to 75 percent faster at fulfillment centers by coordinating swarms of such robots. Hercules and Titan robots, the size of a pool table or a baby grand piano, respectively, roam warehouse aisles to retrieve tall fabric shelving units called pods packed with plastic tote crates and bring them to human employees at various workstations.
Such mobile robots typically follow grid lines of stickers laid out on the floor and stay within fenced-in areas away from human employees. But the newest mobile robot, called Proteus, has sensors that allow it to operate safely around humans and other objects in a more free-roaming role.
Those swarms of mobile robots traveling through narrow lanes between rows of storage pods can also sometimes create robotic traffic jams. That is why Amazon began coordinating its robots using a suite of AI foundation models collectively named DeepFleet, which can help predict potential robot congestion ahead of time.
More recently, Amazon has been deploying a growing number of robotic arms that can grab items stowed high up inside inventory pods, sort packages and place them in carts or on top of mobile robots, and handle the many different individual products that Amazon customers order when shopping online.
The company expects to more than double its existing fleet of robotic arms this year, according to Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky in a July earnings call. When Ars sought clarification, Dresser described the current number of deployed robotic arms as being in the single-digit thousands.
A robotic arm system called Cardinal uses a suction system to grab boxes from a pile of Amazon packages and stack them inside a rolling cart.
A robotic arm system called Cardinal uses a suction system to grab boxes from a pile of Amazon packages and stack them inside a rolling cart.
Credit:
Amazon
The robotic arms race
Amazon first bought third-party robotic arms to help lift and stack heavy pallets and bins inside its fulfillment centers. But the first robotic arm developed in-house by Amazon Robotics to sort individual mailer envelopes and boxes from cluttered piles, called Robin, began testing in 2021 before debuting at a facility in Lakeland, Florida, in 2022.
“With Robin, it was really that first attempt at taking a number of customer orders all in a jumble and building the advanced robotics to identify the items in that scene, to strategize on how to pick them up and build a motion plan that would be successful in placing it down on one of our mobile drive units,” Dresser explained.
The robotic arm uses eight suction cups to pick up individual packages. But before it takes any action, the robot’s software analyzes a top-down view of the conveyor belt cluttered with packages and quickly ranks possible picking actions.
In a 2023 research paper, the Amazon Robotics team described having developed several picking strategies for the robots to follow early on—but each had its own limitations. One strategy that prioritized picking larger packages encountered challenges when smaller packages lay on top of or overlapped with larger ones. Another strategy that favored picking up packages near the top of piles would fail in practice to retrieve “unreachable picks” and partially buried packages.
Improvements came from replacing such hand-crafted algorithms with an AI approach known as machine learning. The machine learning model initially trained on more than 394,000 picking actions from deployed robotic arms to estimate pick probabilities of success, and then used an online pick ranker to prioritize optimal actions for the Robin robots.
The best machine-learning method in that trial achieved a 93.73 percent success rate compared to 92.28 percent success for the best-performing traditional algorithm. That may seem trivial at first glance, but it meant the machine-learning method resulted in about 16,500 fewer failed picks than the traditional method during a work period involving more than 1 million total picks. That matters for an operation like Amazon’s that prioritizes speed and efficiency at scale.
The Amazon Robotics team further showed how such a machine-learning method could reduce the failed pick rate by 20 percent during an experiment involving 2 million picks by robotic workstations set up to resemble the operations of Amazon’s Robin fleet. They presented this work at the International Symposium on Experimental Robotics in July 2025.
Next up was Cardinal, a robotic arm that can place packages weighing up to 50 pounds into wheeled carts that are eventually brought to Amazon trucks waiting in loading docks. These robots first began operating at a facility in Nashville, Tennessee, in November 2022.
“Think of it as a game of Tetris: You’re sorting packages, and you’re placing them into the cart, and you want to be able to pack that as densely as you possibly can,” Dresser told Ars. “Dense containers are great from a sustainability perspective and from a transportation cost perspective.”
Cardinal built on lessons learned from Robin’s development in picking up and manipulating packages, while adding the capability to densely pack customer orders into the carts. Amazon has just started to deploy Cardinal in larger numbers and will continue to do so over the next several years, Dresser said.
A robotic arm system called Sparrow can handle millions of different products while packing container-size totes.
A robotic arm system called Sparrow can handle millions of different products while packing container-size totes.
Credit:
Amazon
AI-driven robot successors
Robin and Cardinal can handle several dozen package variations. But the newer Sparrow robotic arm was developed to tackle an even more challenging task—handling the hundreds of millions of products of varying shapes and sizes that can go into customer orders.
Specifically, Sparrow focuses on consolidating items from partially filled container-size totes to create densely packed totes. When items get picked out as customer orders are being fulfilled, Sparrow continually refills the totes.
“When we think about how AI applies to the physical space in robotics, Sparrow was really the first place where we truly deployed foundation models that enabled us to deal with that high diversity of products,” Dresser told Ars.
Such foundation models have helped the Amazon Robotics team to efficiently identify and classify those hundreds of millions of items to develop new robotic strategies for grasping them, Dresser explained. They also eliminated the need for manually coding every single item.
More recently, the Amazon Robotics team has created a foundation model for robotic perception that can handle new, never-before-seen products that may end up in Amazon fulfillment centers. The team also developed a generalized action model compatible with different types of robotic arms that may use varying combinations of suction and finger grasping.
“If you need to build ad hoc perception models for every such task and embodiment, that just doesn’t scale,” Kapil Katyal, a senior applied science manager at Amazon Robotics, said during a presentation attended by Ars at the Intelligent Robots & Systems conference held in Pittsburgh on September 29.
“So one of the initiatives we took up in our team was to design a foundation model which could work for any new embodiment of robots that we deploy, and across all of the perception tasks that we need to perform over those,” Katyal said.
Most of the robotic arms have relied primarily on vision. But Amazon’s newest robotic arm, Vulcan, is the first to combine vision with force feedback sensors capable of providing a sense of touch. This enables the robot to accurately pick out or stow away items within the fabric-covered inventory pods.
“You need to be able to insert an item, create space, or pull something out,” Dresser said. “Those are really hard things to do with traditional non-touch-based systems today, like the suction-based systems that are part of Sparrow.”
Vulcan initially began operating at Amazon fulfillment centers in Spokane, Washington, and Hamburg, Germany, starting in 2025. It is not widely deployed yet, but Dresser said the company expects to scale up use of this robotic arm in 2027.
The Vulcan robotic arm has force-feedback sensors that provide a sense of touch as it picks and stows items in tall inventory pods.
The Vulcan robotic arm has force-feedback sensors that provide a sense of touch as it picks and stows items in tall inventory pods.
Credit:
Amazon
Parsing the human impact
Each new robot has benefited Amazon’s human workforce, according to the company. For example, Vulcan focuses on picking and stowing items located in the top rows of inventory pods that would otherwise require a person to use a step-ladder, along with handling items located just above the floor. That enables employees to focus on picking and stowing items that are within more comfortable reach.
But investigations by labor advocacy groups, journalists, and the US Congress have painted a less rosy picture of Amazon’s automation drive over the years. The Strategic Organizing Center (SOC), a coalition of trade unions headquartered in Washington, DC, published reports in May 2021 and April 2022 showing higher injury rates at Amazon’s robotic warehouses compared to non-robotic warehouses. That analysis drew on injury data reported by companies to the US government from 2017 through 2020.
“Amazon likes to talk about its latest robots because it doesn’t want to talk about the tens of thousands of Amazon workers who are injured every year due to Amazon’s obsession with maximizing speed and minimizing costs,” Joan Moriarty, director of strategic research and Campaigns at SOC, said in an email to Ars.
The organization also gathered nearly 1,000 responses from Amazon workers in an online survey conducted in February 2021. “Workers consistently report that the presence of robots increases the pace of work expected in Amazon facilities, forcing them to make fast, repetitive motions, substantially increasing the risk of injury,” Moriarty said.
The US Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) also conducted a 2024 investigation led by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt). The committee’s report noted how Amazon’s internal data also suggested a link between robotic productivity and increased pressure on human workers, leading to higher injury rates.
Amazon has described these reports as flawed and being reliant on older data predating the deployment of its most modern robots, including the robotic arms that became operational over the past several years. The company also touted improvements in its overall workplace injury rates without detailing any potential differences between robotic and non-automated warehouses.
“All of these claims ignore the fact that since 2019 our Global Recordable Incident Rate has improved 43 percent and our Global Lost Time Incident rate, which includes the most serious injuries that require employees to take time away from work, has improved 70 percent,” an Amazon spokesperson told Ars. “Our consistent year-over-year improvements have worked in parallel with our robotics growth across our operations network.”
The most nuanced findings on Amazon’s automation drive may come from a research study published in the journal ILR Review in April 2025. That analysis showed Amazon’s robotic warehouses had a 40 percent decrease in severe injuries compared to legacy fulfillment centers—which suggests some benefits from having robots take on the most physically challenging and risky tasks.
However, the same study also found that robotic fulfillment centers had a 77 percent increase in less severe injuries associated with physical strain from repetitive motions.
“At least one of the mechanisms by which this appears to be manifesting is through the pace of work, in that pick rates for the robotic fulfillment centers are off the charts higher,” said Greenwood at George Mason University, who was one of the paper’s coauthors.
A faster pace of work driven by partial automation could mean “the robot is dictating the pace of work” and spurring human employees to perform certain repetitive actions more quickly, Greenwood told Ars. “That appears to be what’s driving the strains and the sprains that we observe,” he said.
The study drew in part on Amazon company data obtained by journalists at Reveal and The Center for Investigative Reporting, covering weekly data at more than 150 Amazon warehouses from 2016 through 2019. Although the data is older, Greenwood said the findings are still relevant to Amazon’s ongoing automation efforts.
“I haven’t seen a tremendous amount of evidence to suggest that these dynamics are changing, inasmuch as you still have a tremendous amount of turnover in the warehousing context—and that’s not just Amazon,” Greenwood said.
Greenwood and his colleagues also analyzed online comments posted on Reddit by Amazon fulfillment center employees. In those comments, Amazon employees described work at robotic fulfillment centers as being less physically stressful but also mentally exhausting because of the physical repetitiveness and faster pace associated with higher productivity expectations.
Amazon has opened new roles for employees to build and maintain mobile robots and robotic arms.
Amazon has opened new roles for employees to build and maintain mobile robots and robotic arms.
Credit:
Amazon
The future of work
An obvious question is whether automation efforts by Amazon and other companies will end up replacing some potential human hires with robots. For its part, Amazon has touted the robotics push as providing new job opportunities for human employees. Fulfillment centers with advanced robotics typically require 30 percent more employees working in reliability, maintenance, and engineering roles, and the new facilities for manufacturing additional robots will also supposedly bring more than 300 jobs each.
“As we recognize that each of these robotics [developments] can change the nature of work, we’re providing opportunities for our employees to upskill and learn some of these things,” said Dresser at Amazon Robotics. “We’ve actually increased the number of robotic maintenance technicians that we have in the network by over 30 percent, and that is a much higher-skilled, higher-compensated job.”
The company has also described its automation efforts as going hand in hand with a growing business that needs more human employees. “As we’ve deployed robots over the past decade, we’ve seen our operational footprint grow, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs as we expanded our network,” the Amazon spokesperson told Ars.
However, there are apparently internal discussions within Amazon about robots potentially reducing the need to hire humans. In October 2025, The New York Times reported on internal strategy documents suggesting that the robotics push could allow the company to reduce projected hiring needs in the United States by more than 160,000 people by 2027 and 600,000 people by 2033. (An Amazon spokesperson responded at the time by saying the documents reflected the views of just one group inside the company.)
Even as Amazon looks to build out its robotic fleet beyond the million-robot mark, discussions about the company’s workplace safety and working conditions are unlikely to go away. Although just a very small fraction of Amazon’s hundreds of thousands of employees have unionized in the United States, labor unions have “traditionally served a very good role in terms of improving worker safety,” Greenwood said.
“Now, obviously, I understand that firms are not always excited to engage in that conversation, and I can’t say that would solve the problem here,” Greenwood told Ars. “But developing a better relationship between management and labor is usually the best path forward to try to figure out how to reduce these injury rates, which would have benefits for Amazon as well.”
The first Amazon Labor Union that was organized among workers at a warehouse in Staten Island, New York, in April 2022, has been pushing what it describes as a Safety Bill of Rights that outlines changes it would like to see to make their workplace safer. The image that accompanies the document declares: “We are not robots.”
Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English.

articles.title: AMD Unveils Helion Rack Designed for Agentic AI
articles.text:
Monday, October 12th 2026
AMD Unveils Helion Rack Designed for Agentic AI
AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today introduced the AMD Helion agentic AI rack, an open blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure based on an Open Compute Project spec-design and powered by AMD compute.
Building on the open-platform approach of the AMD Helios rackscale solution, AMD Helion is designed to provide partners and customers with the flexibility they need for agentic AI infrastructure. With AMD Helion, customers can match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform.
Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD"Agentic AI is not a single workload. It spans personal agents, enterprise applications, code execution and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements. To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power."
AMD Helion's OCP spec-based rack blueprint supports open software and can come in flexible configurations, including liquid- and air-cooled versions, allowing customers to create virtually any configuration needed for their needs. Some examples of this include:
- A CPU-only rack powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors that can support up to 32,768 CPU cores. This rack is designed for hyperscale customers, providing dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.
- An all-in-one rack that combines AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform. This rack is designed to provide partners and customers an all-in-one concept for enterprise agentic AI.
AMD Helion enables customers to deploy agentic AI in the IT infrastructure they already have, turning existing investments into a foundation for new AI capabilities. Partners can tailor CPU and GPU configurations to customer workloads, matching agent execution, model inference and supporting compute to each deployment's performance, power and cost requirements.
AMD plans to contribute the AMD Helion specification to OCP, making it available to the community for further development and adoption. AMD Helion agentic rack configurations are currently under development with ecosystem partners and are planned to be available in November 2026.

articles.title: Hackers invadem geladeiras de supermercados na França e causam incêndios
articles.text:
Hackers invadiram sistemas de refrigeração de supermercados na França durante a noite, elevando a temperatura de equipamentos a 50 °C e provocando incêndios e perdas de alimentos. O ataque, confirmado em 12 de outubro de 2026, atingiu centenas de lojas e levou as autoridades francesas a investigar a origem da invasão e a possibilidade de novos incidentes.
A Procuradoria de Paris classificou o caso como um ataque cibernético de grande escala contra refrigeradores conectados de diferentes redes varejistas. Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché e Cooperativa U estão entre as empresas afetadas. O governo francês também avalia se outros países podem enfrentar problemas semelhantes. As informações são da Reuters.
Ataque afeta redes de supermercados
O Carrefour informou que 80 de suas lojas foram atingidas, enquanto a Monoprix relatou impactos em 5% de suas unidades. Já a Les Mousquetaires, proprietária da rede Intermarché, afirmou que os refrigeradores de cerca de 150 estabelecimentos foram aquecidos a 50 °C durante seis horas.
Segundo um porta-voz da empresa, todos os alimentos armazenados nos equipamentos afetados foram descartados para evitar riscos sanitários. O presidente-executivo da Cooperativa U, Dominique Schelcher, também confirmou que um supermercado da rede foi atingido.
O primeiro-ministro francês, Sébastien Lecornu, determinou que a Agência Nacional de Segurança dos Sistemas de Informação da França (ANSSI) investigasse o caso. As autoridades também verificam se outras empresas francesas podem estar vulneráveis.
Falha em software pode ter facilitado invasão
Os sistemas de refrigeração de supermercados costumam ser controlados por painéis conectados à internet. A tecnologia permite que empresas de manutenção ajustem remotamente o funcionamento de geladeiras e freezers, mas também pode abrir brechas de segurança.
Segundo uma fonte próxima ao governo francês, a ANSSI identificou uma vulnerabilidade em um software fornecido pela empresa dinamarquesa Danfoss. A fabricante afirmou estar ciente dos incidentes na França e disse que os sistemas afetados utilizavam versões desatualizadas de firmware, software que controla o funcionamento dos equipamentos.
A Danfoss declarou que recomenda aos clientes manter os sistemas compatíveis atualizados e substituir soluções antigas por versões mais recentes. Ainda não foram divulgadas estimativas do prejuízo total causado pelo ataque.
A Federação do Comércio e da Distribuição da França (FCD), que representa o setor varejista, cobrou transparência da fabricante sobre o incidente. Segundo a entidade, os supermercados trabalham para proteger os consumidores e restabelecer as operações. Algumas lojas afetadas já haviam retomado as atividades.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Open-source project moves one step closer to letting you run PlayStation 5 games natively on PC
articles.text:
What we know so far: The open-source AnyPS5 project has taken a major step toward its goal of letting gamers run PlayStation 5 games natively on Windows and Linux PCs. Hosted on GitHub, the project now reports 100% GPU shader instruction coverage, with all 1,166 tracked AMD RDNA 1 and RDNA 2 instructions implemented, thanks to contributions from more than 100 (human) developers alongside AI-generated code.
AnyPS5 has successfully decoded the GPU instruction set used by the PS5's "Oberon" SoC, which pairs an 8-core AMD Zen 2 CPU with a custom RDNA 2 GPU. The developers note, however, that only instructions recognized by the decoder were counted, while decoded opcodes absent from AMD's public list were not.
It's also worth noting that the system libraries aren't fully translated yet, with the latest data showing 3,052 of 3,535 functions, or 86.34%, implemented. The developers clarified that the list only covers functions already declared in the project's core/libs/prx directory and doesn't account for every function exported by the PS5 firmware..
For those unfamiliar, AnyPS5 is a compatibility layer that lets PS5 binaries run natively on PC by converting executables built for the PlayStation 5 into formats Windows or Linux can read, much like Wine or Proton. It works by translating the PS5's proprietary API calls, such as those for graphics, audio, or user services, into native calls on Windows and Linux.
The project's founder, who goes by the online handle boykopovar, explained that AnyPS5's core/libs/prx directory covers only low-level system libraries, such as libSceAgc, that interact directly with the hardware or the operating system kernel. It does not bundle engine-level middleware, modules shipped separately with games, or SDK libraries that merely wrap other system libraries.
While full support for the entire PS5 library is still some way off, at least one PS5 game, the 2D platformer Dreaming Sarah, has been shown running at a stable 60 FPS on PC through AnyPS5. It's a relatively lightweight title that requires very little CPU or GPU power, but the developers believe they'll be able to add support for more demanding games soon.

articles.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
articles.text:
The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
Massive tree-planting programs lead to unhealthy monocrop plantations. Daisy Dent aims to help forests rebuild themselves.
In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.
Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.
Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.
That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba, hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.
The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.
Filling in the gaps
Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees, after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way?
While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs, Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land.
Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow.
In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.
The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.
For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia-dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.
To plant or not to plant
Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun.
Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest.
“Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.”
In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery. They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife. They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration. Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent. Many sites are too degraded.
 Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness.
The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches. Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains. Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting.
Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent. For instance, they want to understand if solitary standing trees, often left by ranchers to shade cows, help sites regenerate faster. Those insights can help Ponterra sell high-quality credits and avoid the embarrassing pitfalls that can lead fresh plantations to literally go up in smoke. While credits can be bought for as little as $5 per metric ton, corporate giants such as Microsoft—one of Ponterra’s clients—have paid more than 10 times as much for high-quality removal.
There are plenty of places where a level of natural regeneration can work well. So far, millions of hectares of rainforest are naturally regenerating in Brazil, according to the Brazilian Restoration and Reforestation Observatory. Still, Dent is mystified as to why the people in charge of large-scale projects continue to think the best solution is the one that imposes humans’ will on the landscape.
The conversation may be shifting. As droughts hit Latin America, policymakers and carbon creditors might be forced to face the shortcomings of cookie-cutter plantations. “You have much reduced resilience in the system when it comes to extreme events like droughts or floods or extreme heat or pathogens,” Dent says. The coming year’s “mega El Niño” could be a moment of reckoning, she says: “I think there’s an increasing recognition that we can’t just plant trees. We have to rebuild a system.”
Matthew Ponsford is a freelance reporter based in London.

articles.title: Guía para perezosos: los mejores estrenos en streaming para ver ya mismo
articles.text:
Nadie lo duda: el streaming llegó para cambiar el mundo del espectáculo. Y hacerlo, demostrando que la cultura pop puede democratizarse y hacerse más accesible. Todo, teniendo como mayor ventaja la accesibilidad inmediata y la comodidad. A diferencia de los formatos físicos o las descargas tradicionales, las plataformas han demostrado un principio básico. A saber: que personalizar la experiencia cinematográfica y televisiva puede ser el punto central de una revolución a todo nivel.
Algo que ha ocurrido a lo largo de la última década. Los servicios por suscripción permiten no solo una multiplicidad de opciones que para las salas del cine o el cable son impensables. También, convertirse en una vitrina para todo tipo de producciones que, de otra forma, jamás encontrarían un nuevo público. Lo cierto es que el streaming demostró la capacidad de internet para desaparecer distancias y llevar la cultura a todas partes. Pero además, permitir que el mundo del espectáculo encontrara una nueva audiencia, mucho más amplia y nutrida.
Pero, por supuesto, todas esas estupendas ventajas tienen un gran inconveniente. Y se trata de la gran cantidad de contenido semanal que las plataformas agregan a su catálogo y que hace casi imposible estar al tanto de las novedades. Si ese es tu caso, esta lista es ideal para ti. Te dejamos una guía para perezosos: los mejores estrenos en diversas plataformas para ver ya mismo. De una adaptación que sorprende por su calidad, a un spin-off de una popular serie, a las más recientes películas al alcance de un clic. Todo para los amantes del buen cine y de la televisión de altura que no tienen el tiempo para rebuscar en las colecciones de streaming.
Netflix
Al este del Edén
Esta adaptación de la clásica novela de John Steinbeck tiene mérito por partida doble. En especial, porque la miniserie de 7 capítulos toma la historia y explora en sus complejidades con cuidado. Y de hecho, de forma más amplia que el clásico de Hollywood de 1955. Creada por Zoe Kazan, esta ambiciosa reinterpretación narra la profunda e intrincada saga de la familia Trask. La historia gira fundamentalmente en torno a Adam (Christopher Abbott) y Charles Trask (Mike Faist). Estos, dos hermanos de personalidades opuestas cuyas vidas cambian radicalmente por un giro del destino. Acoger a la enigmática Cathy Ames, interpretada magistralmente por Florence Pugh.
Cathy representa una de las figuras más oscuras de la literatura, una antiheroína implacable que siembra la discordia y destruye los lazos familiares. A través de este tenso escenario, la trama explora la dolorosa herencia familiar y la eterna lucha existencial entre el bien y el mal. Al revivir el mito bíblico de Caín y Abel, la narrativa desentraña los destructivos celos fraternales y la incansable búsqueda de redención. Ideal para los que amaron la primera adaptación y que buscan una versión más profunda de la clásica histórica.
El viudo: hasta que la muerte nos separe
Podría parecer otro de los ya clásicos true crime de la plataforma, pero en realidad es más que eso. Dirigido por Chris Smith, este documental que acaba de llegar al streaming asombra por su capacidad para indagar en el horror. Para eso, producción desentraña la escalofriante historia real de Thomas Randolph. Este, un hombre que ocultó un siniestro historial criminal detrás de una fachada de encanto, carisma y manipulación psicológica.
Para eso, el argumento sigue de cerca una exhaustiva investigación de tres décadas liderada por el periodista Dan Slepian. Eso, junto al detective de homicidios Dean O’Kelley. El detonante principal ocurre en mayo de 2008, cuando la sexta esposa de Randolph, Sharon Causse, muere en su hogar. Thomas alegó ante las autoridades que un intruso enmascarado la había asesinado y que él se defendió matando al asaltante. Sin embargo, las pericias destapan un macabro patrón. Randolph es sospechoso de estar involucrado en la muerte de cuatro de sus seis esposas con el único objetivo de cobrar millonarias pólizas de seguro de vida. Lo demás es un caso tortuoso que te dejará desconcertado por su complejidad y situaciones inesperadas. Una opción en streaming ideal para los fanáticos de los crímenes sin resolver.
Unabomber
Dirigida por el cineasta danés Janus Metz Pedersen, la cinta aborda el oscuro origen de Theodore Kaczynski. Por si no lo recuerdas, uno de los terroristas domésticos más notorios y peligrosos en la historia estadounidense. Pero antes de serlo, era un matemático prodigio considerado un alumno brillante. Un punto conocido y que la cinta toca de manera inquietante.
Por lo que la trama explora toda su etapa universitaria como estudiante superdotado en Harvard durante finales de los años cincuenta. Allí, el frágil protagonista (Jacob Tremblay) se convierte en el sujeto principal de crueles e impactantes experimentos psicológicos secretos de control mental. Todos dirigidos por el profesor Henry Murray (Russell Crowe) en lo que parece ser el detonante del aislamiento social y la paranoia del futuro terrorista. Peor aún, el punto central de la extrema radicalización ideológica que posteriormente lo llevaría a aislarse en una cabaña rústica de Montana. Todo para planificar sistemáticamente su campaña criminal contra el progreso moderno de este mundo actual y contemporáneo. Una producción curiosa en el mundo del streaming actual.
Prime Video
Carrie
A tiempo para octubre, llega una nueva adaptación de Carrie de Stephen King al streaming. Más interesante todavía, creada y dirigida por Mike Flanagan, conocido por su impecable punto de vista de la obra del escritor. Y Carrie es, de hecho, un interesante experimento para tomar la historia clásica de terror y llevarla a otro nivel. Para eso, el relato traslada su premisa al mundo contemporáneo. Pero además, reinventa a su protagonista titular.
Esta vez, Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) debe enfrentar la reciente muerte de su padre. Además, su abrupta inserción en el hostil ecosistema de la educación escolar pública. Pronto, la protagonista se convierte en el blanco de un brutal y despiadado escándalo de ciberacoso viral que sacude por completo a su comunidad estudiantil. Lo que la forzará a lidiar con toda la humillación sistemática mediada por las redes sociales y teléfonos móviles de la era digital. Todo, mientras experimenta en plena adolescencia el despertar violento de sus destructivos poderes telequinéticos. El resto de la historia ya la conoces, pero esta vez te parecerá un poco más agobiante. Y en especial, disfrutando de las ventajas de tiempo de las series en streaming.
La hipótesis del amor
¿Eres amante de los ya conocidos fanfics de internet? Esta película es para ti. En especial, porque está basada en la obra homónima de Ali Hazelwood, que causó furor desde su publicación. Pero esta adaptación de Claire Scanlon es, además, una caja de sorpresas románticas para los amantes de las romcom.
Para eso, la historia sigue a Olive Smith (Lili Reinhart). Olive es una brillante candidata a un doctorado en biología dentro de la prestigiosa Universidad de Stanford. Además, es una que prefiere enfocarse por completo en sus rigurosas investigaciones sobre el cáncer pancreático antes que en los asuntos románticos. Sin embargo, la trama da un giro imprevisto cuando ella decide besar de forma impulsiva al primer hombre que se cruza en su camino. Todo, con el único objetivo de convencer a su mejor amiga de que ha superado una vieja relación del pasado. Para su enorme sorpresa, ese enigmático extraño resulta ser el doctor Adam Carlsen (Tom Bateman). Este, el profesor adjunto más intimidante, frío y temido de todo su departamento académico universitario. Ya sabes cómo terminan ese tipo de historias.
Neagley
Si eres amante de la acción, esto es para ti. Creada por Nick Santora y Nicholas Wootton, es el spin-off del universo de Reacher. Para eso, la trama se enfoca por completo en Frances Neagley (Maria Sten). Por si no lo recuerdas, la brillante investigadora privada de Chicago y antigua sargento de la Unidad de Investigaciones Especiales 110 del Ejército. Pero alejándose del estilo de Reacher, la historia tiene un tinte marcadamente personal.
Por lo que comienza cuando Frances se entera de la muerte sumamente sospechosa de Tommy Crane, un querido amigo de su infancia. Decidida a hacer justicia por cuenta propia, se sumerge en una peligrosa investigación que la lleva a infiltrarse en la granja Echo Canyon. Esta, una misteriosa comuna rural con tintes de secta liderada por el amenazante Lawrence Cole (Damon Herriman). Ideal para los amantes de la acción trepidante y en busca de opciones en streaming.
HBO Max
Backrooms
Ahora bien, si estás buscando en streaming buen cine para ver, HBO Max es tu opción. Y mucho más con sus novedades. Lo que incluye un éxito de 2026 que ya se considera un hito en el cine. En específico, porque marca el histórico debut del joven prodigio de veinte años Kane Parsons, de apenas veinte años. Pero en realidad, Backrooms es mucho más que solo un dato anecdótico. Es una de las primeras películas que dialoga con la generación Z.
Eso, al profundizar en el terror analógico nacido originalmente del folclore de internet y las leyendas urbanas de las creepypastas de 4chan. Por lo que la enigmática trama se enfoca en Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), un arquitecto frustrado que comienza una travesía por lo sobrenatural. Eso, cuando accidentalmente descubre una misteriosa e imposible puerta resplandeciente en el sótano de una tienda de muebles cotidianos. Una inspirada película de terror que se vuelve cada vez más siniestra a medida que se hace más críptica.
Linternas
DC está de celebración y el motivo es obvio: el legendario Linterna Verde llegó a live-action esta vez en una brillante y elegante serie. Co-creada por los renombrados guionistas Damon Lindelof, Chris Mundy y Tom King, es además una mirada madura al mundo de los superhéroes. Por lo que la trama se distancia por completo de las clásicas aventuras espaciales de los cómics tradicionales para ofrecer un thriller policíaco. Uno, además, sombrío, fuertemente inspirado por el tono rural y la atmósfera de misterio psicológico de producciones como True Detective.
Para eso, la historia sigue a Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) en una investigación en la América profunda que le llevará a su propia muerte. Todo, mientras intenta entrenar a John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), un hombre en busca de su destino. Si lo tuyo son las historias de superhéroes, pero a un nivel por completo nuevo, esta es tu elección en streaming.
Supergirl
Lo sabemos: la película naufragó en taquilla y en crítica. Pero quizás, merezca una segunda oportunidad. Y la acaba de encontrar en el streaming. Dirigida por Craig Gillespie, el relato sigue los pasos de Kara Zor-El (Milly Alcock), quien ofrece una versión sumamente rebelde y profundamente traumatizada por la trágica destrucción de Krypton.
Mientras celebra su cumpleaños número veintitrés en un lejano planeta bajo un sol rojo que anula sus asombrosos poderes, Kara deberá repensar su vida. Además, comenzar un vertiginoso viaje de carretera espacial envuelto en dolor, ira y venganza personal. Con fallas de guion, una historia un tanto desordenada y problemas de edición, no es la mejor obra de DC. Pero tiene un espíritu subversivo que quizás te sorprenderá y que su llegada al streaming te ayude a disfrutar.

articles.title: Elon Musk has donated over $276 million to Republican midterm efforts
articles.text:
Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire.
Elon Musk has donated over $276 million to Republican midterm efforts
He’s by far the biggest known midterm donor.
He’s by far the biggest known midterm donor.
He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including:
- $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund super PAC for House Republicans
- $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, supporting Ken Paxton’s Senate Seat bid in Texas
- $10 million to the Republican Governors Association
- $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association
The roughly $366 million that Musk has donated to federal committees over the entire 2025-26 election cycle is significantly higher than the $290 million he gave out in 2024 to help President Trump return to office, when he pledged to spend “around $45 million a month.” That’s despite Musk announcing in May last year that “In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.” He’s consistently failed to stick to that promise so far.

articles.title: PaidHR finds 46 of 100 Nigerian workers earn below $150 monthly
articles.text:
46 out of every 100 Nigerian workers earn below ₦200,000 ($150) monthly, according to a new salary report by PaidHR, a Nigerian human resources and payroll startup.
The report offers a visual of what employers pay employees in Nigeria’s formal labour market. PaidHR said it analysed payroll records for more than 25,000 workers across over 400 Nigerian employers, using a July 2026 snapshot of active employees on its platform.
The findings show a wide gap between the lower and upper ends of the salary scale. Of every 100 workers in the dataset, 46 earn below ₦200,000 ($150) a month, while 10 earn at least ₦1 million ($751.93).
“The shape of the distribution suggests that Nigeria’s formal workforce is not one evenly distributed middle class; it is increasingly a two-tier labour market,” Seye Bandele, PaidHR’s co-founder and chief executive officer, told TechCabal in an interview. “A large group is clustered around relatively low wages, alongside a much smaller professional group earning substantially more.”
Nigeria’s labour force participation rate rose to 79.5% in Q2 2024, and formal employment accounts for about 7.0% to 7.3% of the total employed workforce. However, only a fraction of the workforce earns a regular wage from an employer, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). For these workers, earnings depend on their job, experience, industries, and how their employers value their skills.
The report’s anchor is the median, the worker standing in the middle when every salary earner is lined up from lowest paid to highest. That worker earns ₦217,000 ($163.17) in monthly gross and takes home ₦199,972 ($150) after deductions, such as pension contributions, income tax, and other payroll deductions.
At the bottom of the scale, the report noted that 10 out of every 100 workers in the dataset earn below ₦70,000 ($52.64), Nigeria’s national minimum wage, signed into law in 2024.
As Nigeria’s cost of living increases, fuel prices have pushed up transport costs, while food, rent and electricity bills compete for a share of monthly income. Inflation has eased from its recent peak, but lower inflation does not mean prices have returned to where they were before.
The report’s findings also question the value of sustained loyalty to a single employer. Career progression has been built around accumulating experience that will eventually lead to higher pay. PaidHR’s data suggests salary growth is strongest during the first few years with an employer, before slowing down.
Workers with less than a year at their current job earn a median salary of ₦181,235 ($136.28). Pay rises with tenure and peaks around the five-year mark, when the middle worker earns about 47% more than someone at entry level. After that, the gains become much less consistent.
PaidHR’s report describes this as the five-year wall. It is the point at which staying longer with an employer no longer delivers the same salary gains as in the early years.
“The interesting thing is that experience itself stops being enough to generate significant salary growth,” Bandele said. “The report’s explanation is that the market regularly reprices jobs, but employers do not necessarily reprice their existing employees at the same pace. As a result, someone who stays in the same organisation can become underpaid relative to what the market is willing to pay for their experience.”
An employee who joined a company five years ago may have received annual raises, but a new hire entering the same role is being recruited at the current market rate. If the market has moved faster than the company’s salary reviews, the new employee can arrive on a salary that the existing worker has taken years to reach.
PaidHR argues that this creates an incentive for workers to look outside their current organisations when they want a significant salary increase, as workers may find bigger salary gains by changing employers or moving into a higher-paying industry.
The report suggests that two workers with similar skills and experience can earn very different salaries because their employers operate in markets with different capacities and willingness to pay.
“Where you work changes what you earn as much as what you do,” Bandele said.
PaidHR’s sector data shows that the middle salary in fintech and technology is ₦418,916 ($315), compared with ₦80,000 ($60.15) in retail, hospitality and leisure. Banking, lending and financial services sit at ₦230,491 ($173.31), while healthcare and pharmaceuticals have a middle salary of ₦169,423 ($127.39).
The gap suggests that workers with similar skills may have very different earning prospects depending on the industries in which they work. Nigeria’s technology and fintech companies have attracted substantial venture funding over the past decade, helping some employers build products and compete for specialised talent in a global market. However, the funding does not automatically translate into higher salaries.
The report also identifies a gender gap. The middle woman in the dataset earns ₦192,089 ($144.44) a month, compared with ₦238,103 ($179.04) for the middle man. That means women earn about 81 kobo ($0.00061) for every ₦1 ($0.00075) men earn at the middle of the salary scale. The report does not establish the causes of the gap, but the differences within individual companies suggest that it cannot be explained solely by men and women working in different industries.
Taken together, the findings suggest that workers’ positioning in the labour market shapes salary growth. Experience matters, but it may not be enough to secure higher pay; skills matter, but the same skill can command different salaries in different industries, while staying with an employer can become costly if salary reviews do not keep pace with the market.
PaidHR’s forecast projects that the middle salary could rise from ₦217,000 ($163.17) in 2026 to ₦380,000 ($285.73) by 2030, assuming annual salary growth of roughly 15%. Still, a higher salary does not equate to greater purchasing power. If the prices of food, transport, housing, and other essentials rise as fast as, or faster than, wages, workers may earn more without being able to afford much more.
