articles.title: Coding agents made building easy. Platform teams that build from scratch are 3.5x more likely to lack a strategy.
articles.text:
Coding agents made building easy. Platform teams that build from scratch are 3.5x more likely to lack a strategy.
Build-or-buy is usually framed as an engineering trade-off, where developer time is weighed against integration and migration overhead, and control against the maintenance burden of a bespoke build. When we put together the 2026 Future of Platform Engineering report, we weren’t trying to settle the trade-off; we were trying to find out whether platform feature-sourcing decisions revealed anything about the platform team. It turns out it does. Across responses from 379 platform professionals, we found that teams predominantly building from scratch are less likely to have a clear strategy in place and to meet fewer of their platform goals.
This question has changed considerably with AI. Agents have made building easier than ever; an internal tool that once took months to build can now be put together in a day. But AI removes the effort of writing code, not the work of owning it. The maintenance, upgrades, and governance that come with a scratch-built feature remain, while the volume of change moving through the pipeline increases. That makes build-versus-buy a sharper strategic question than ever.
We asked platform teams how they support each feature they own: built from scratch, built on an existing template, or bought as an underlying tool. Teams whose dominant approach is building from scratch are far more likely to report that their platform lacks a clear strategy. The association is strong, but it is not as simple as “build from scratch means you don’t have a plan.”
Most Teams Buy And Choose Deliberately
Across the features platform teams own, we found that using an underlying tool is the most common: 51.3% of respondents said this was their primary approach, ahead of building on an existing template (31.2%) and building from scratch (17.5%). High performers lean more heavily on tools (58.8%) than on building from a template (47.8%) or from scratch (33.3%). This could reflect a broader maturity pattern: as architectural choices in Platform Engineering settle, teams increasingly standardize on tools rather than maintain their own. David Tuite has described the alternative as the “build-versus-buy trap,” where teams stuck maintaining custom interfaces sink 6 to 18 months into upgrades and operational overhead instead of shipping value.
The exceptions are where it gets interesting. Local development environments, one-click projects, and ephemeral environments skew toward templates rather than tools, because they’re bound to a specific tech stack and golden paths that off-the-shelf tools rarely provide. Ephemeral environments are worth pausing on because they also mark where AI is landing well. Teams whose platforms offer them were far more likely to report that AI has positively affected the speed and stability of software delivery; the same was true of code coverage and cost control. Among teams reporting an extremely positive effect, more than three-quarters had ephemeral environments.
This association also likely reflects the platform rather than the feature. Teams with ephemeral environments tend to run on broad platforms with a range of automated delivery capabilities around them, and that breadth itself tracks with positive AI impact on delivery. Ephemeral environments, then, could be a sign of a platform mature enough to absorb AI-generated volume and change, without losing stability. This is consistent with DORA’s research finding that organizational gains from AI depend on platform quality: strong platforms amplify the effects, while weaker ones dampen them.
The features that break the pattern reflect fit rather than a reluctance to buy, and the reasoning behind these decisions supports this. When asked to explain their build-or-buy logic, the most common response was a cost-benefit analysis (29.6%), followed by a preference for open source (28.6%), a fit-and-requirements assessment (22.4%), a preference for commercial tools (b22.4%), and building for core differentiation (16.3%). As one respondent summarized it, “Build what makes us unique, buy or adopt what’s standard, and always consider long-term cost and lock-in.” This is the same central idea presented in domain-driven design, which distinguishes the core domain, where custom work creates competitive advantage, from supporting and generic domains, where it mostly adds complexity and maintenance for something that could have been bought.
The Build-from-Scratch Pattern
Given how deliberately most teams choose, the strategy finding is more interesting. When classified by dominant build method, teams building from scratch are about 3.5x more likely to report a lack of clear strategy as an obstacle (57.9%) than teams building from a template (15.6%) or using an underlying tool (16.7%).
AI clusters here, too, with predominantly build-from-scratch teams more likely to use AI moderately or extensively for legacy modernization and language migration. There is a clear pattern here: the teams building the most lean hardest on AI for maintenance. This isn’t because they use AI more generally: their reported adoption, impact, and expected effects match those of everyone else. The difference is specific to the work that follows custom-built features.
Building First, Deciding Later
One interpretation is that strategy comes first, and the build-or-buy decision comes later: a team without clear direction has no basis for deciding what to buy, so it builds by default. Another is that building is the strategy rather than a sign of a missing strategy. Building can help identify the problem and show progress before the team has settled on the platform’s purpose.
This is an interesting take, and the one the data can’t tell us which is right. Simon Wardley’s work on mapping describes a similar pattern: teams that can’t see what tools already exist tend to build their own solutions to problems that have already been solved better elsewhere.
With AI, the gap between having an idea and having a working tool has almost closed. An agent can now build a custom incident-management tool before anyone has asked whether one is needed. Building has become easier, but maintaining what gets built hasn’t. DORA’s research suggests why this matters: good platforms provide capabilities and set boundaries on their use, and in AI-assisted development, those boundaries may currently matter more. Established tools come with those boundaries built in; a platform built piece by piece has only the ones someone thought to add.
In either case, the relationship holds. Building from scratch isn’t the problem. Building from scratch by default, without a reason, is where the strategy gap appears.
A Better Question Than Build or Buy
This isn’t a case for buying everything, as we found that some features need to be built around their organization’s own context. It is a case of buying deliberately. Where a team builds from scratch, there should be a reason. When teams buy a tool, the reason is usually already evident: nearly every team buys for the well-defined parts of the platform, and as agents write more code, the value of tools that solve those problems well only grows.

articles.title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region.
GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles.
In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring.
Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6
The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference.
- GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week.
- GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume.
- GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work.
All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock. For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock.
Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region.
The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post.
| Global cross-Region inference profiles | Source Regions | Destination Regions | 
| global.openai.gpt-6-sol global.openai.gpt-6-luna | Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3 Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5 Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7 Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2 | Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed | 
| global.openai.gpt-6-astra | Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 | Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed | 
Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra. For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.
Getting started with OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client.
Prerequisites
- An IAM identity with permission to invoke the profile. The IAM policy in the Security and permissions section grants only what these examples need.
- Your source Region activated. Only the Region you call from needs activating. You do not activate destination Regions, which run on Amazon Bedrock managed capacity. Singapore (ap-southeast-1) is a Region that is enabled by default. Jakarta (ap-southeast-3), Malaysia (ap-southeast-5), Thailand (ap-southeast-7), and Taipei (ap-east-2) are opt-in Regions you must activate first. For more information, see Enable or disable AWS Regions in your account.
- A current AWS SDK or CLI. The OpenAI-compatible examples also require the OpenAI SDK and the Amazon Bedrock token generator. Install them with pip install boto3 openai aws-bedrock-token-generator.
The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1.
Invoke GPT-6 models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime
Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model in every case.
Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. Set BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID to global.openai.gpt-6-luna or global.openai.gpt-6-astra to switch models, or call converse_stream for streaming.
OpenAI Chat Completions API. Point the OpenAI SDK at the Regional endpoint and pass the same profile ID.
When migrating an existing OpenAI client:
- Set the model parameter on every request, including those referencing a previous response.
- Use supported tool types: function, mcp, custom, namespace, and tool_search.
- Configure the inference profile ID directly in your client rather than querying the models endpoint.
Set up the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex CLI
The ChatGPT desktop app and the Codex CLI share ~/.codex/config.toml, so one change covers both. Of the two built-in Amazon Bedrock providers, only amazon-bedrock-runtime accepts an inference profile.
SigV4 signing means there is no key to rotate. Add profile = "<your-profile>" for a non-default profile, and set region explicitly, because the client otherwise falls back to AWS_REGION. Substitute another profile ID for model to change models.
Codex reports a 272,000-token window for these profiles, which is its own bundled figure rather than a service limit. Raise it with model_context_window. This configuration needs Codex CLI 0.148 or later.
Figure 2 shows the result in the app.
Security and permissions
Amazon Bedrock offers a range of controls over inference. Two of them matter here. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies control which roles can invoke which profiles, and service control policies (SCPs) apply organization-wide controls, including Region scope. This section covers both, and where request data lands.
IAM permissions for global cross-Region inference
To call any of these models through a global cross-Region inference profile, your IAM policy needs four statements:
- Access to the inference profile and the project/default resource in your source Region.
- Access to the foundation model in your source Region, scoped to the inference profile.
- The Region-agnostic Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for the foundation model, arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol, with aws:RequestedRegion set to unspecified to permit cross-Region routing.
- bedrock:CallWithBearerToken for API-key authentication.
This IAM policy grants permission to invoke GPT-6 Sol through global cross-Region inference from ap-southeast-1. Replace with your AWS account ID and ap-southeast-1 with your source Region.
If you use streaming (converse_stream or stream=True), add bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream to the Action in the first three statements. Converse authorizes as bedrock:InvokeModel. If you only call Converse with SigV4 credentials, drop the fourth statement.
To switch models, replace openai.gpt-6-sol with openai.gpt-6-luna or openai.gpt-6-astra throughout. For the complete reference, see IAM policy requirements for global cross-Region inference.
Service control policy considerations for global cross-Region inference
A global cross-Region inference request carries no Region name. Amazon Bedrock sets aws:RequestedRegion to unspecified, so a Region allowlist in an SCP denies the call, and the error names only the policy type, not which policy. That is a common reason a first call fails in an enterprise account.
Rather than widening the allowlist, scope the exception. Amazon Bedrock populates the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key during authorization, so an SCP can allow these profiles while keeping Region controls for everything else. The following SCP does that.
The first statement enforces your Region allowlist for every service except Amazon Bedrock inference. The second denies that inference outside those Regions unless it routes through a global cross-Region inference profile. For geographic profiles, add their prefix (for example inference-profile/us.*) to the ArnNotLike list, because geographic requests carry a real Region name. Keep your source Region in the allowlist, and add the global services your organization uses to NotAction.
A blunter alternative is to add unspecified to your existing allowlist, which works but opens the same exception to every other service. For a ready-to-use policy file, see the aws-samples service-control-policy-examples repository.
Data retention and abuse detection
For automated offline abuse detection, classifier-flagged traffic is retained by AWS for up to 30 days and processed programmatically. Under cross-Region inference that retention happens in the destination Region, which for a global profile is any supported commercial AWS Region where the model is deployed. Eligible customers might request full zero data retention through their AWS account team. For more information, see Amazon Bedrock abuse detection and Data retention.
If your organization has data residency requirements, take this to your risk and compliance team early. See the AWS Financial Services Compliance Center country pages for these five countries. We recommend you obtain your own advice on compliance with the requirements relevant to your business.
Quota management
GPT-6 quotas on bedrock-runtime are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tracked against the source Region you call from. Input and cache-write tokens count 1:1, and each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota. For example, a request with 2,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens depletes 12,000 tokens from your quota.
Amazon Bedrock reserves the full max_tokens up front, so set it close to the completions you expect. One quota covers InvokeModel, Converse, Responses, and Chat Completions. Review and raise it on the Service Quotas console from your source Region. Before production, request increases early and alarm on EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage in the AWS/Bedrock namespace at 70–80 percent of your allocation. See How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas for current values.
Monitoring and logging
Your operational surface stays in your source Region. Amazon CloudWatch metrics, AWS CloudTrail events, model invocation logs, quota accounting, and billing all remain in the Region you called from. You pay that Region’s rates, not the processing Region’s.
CloudTrail records where each request was processed. AWS documents a global cross-Region inference profile’s destinations as its commercial Regions rather than enumerating them. GetInferenceProfile returns the Region-agnostic and source-Region model ARNs rather than a destination list. Your per-request record is additionalEventData.inferenceRegion in CloudTrail in your source Region. Inference on this endpoint is a management event, logged by default at no extra cost. CloudTrail Event History retains 90 days, so longer horizons need a trail or model invocation logging. Retrieve the CloudTrail events with this command.
Set the window around a call you just made, because CloudTrail delivery lags by a few minutes. If the most recent event was a failed call, it carries an errorCode and no inferenceRegion. Raise --max-results and pick an event without errorCode.
Metrics and coding-agent usage stay in CloudWatch. Where developers reach GPT-6 through a coding agent, CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights adds ready-made dashboards under GenAI Observability that break token use down by user, team, and cost center. The agents emit OpenTelemetry metrics natively. For Codex, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex.
Clean up
This post adds an IAM policy and optionally an SCP statement and a logging destination. Detach or delete the IAM policy you attached, and revert the SCP entry if you added one. Delete the model invocation logging destination in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs if you created one, to avoid storage charges. The global cross-Region inference profiles are system-defined, so there is nothing to delete.
Conclusion
This post showed how to invoke GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna from five Asia Pacific source Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore), through global cross-Region inference on bedrock-runtime. Pass a global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model parameter, and configure the IAM policy and SCP exception from this post. The same endpoint serves the OpenAI-compatible APIs, so an existing OpenAI integration moves across by changing a base URL and a key.
To get started, attach the IAM policy from this post, and send a first request through global.openai.gpt-6-sol. Size your tokens-per-minute quota at the 10x burndown rate, and confirm in CloudTrail that additionalEventData.inferenceRegion appears on your calls.
For more information, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference, and Amazon Bedrock pricing.

articles.title: Nothing OS 5.0 débarque sur le Phone (3) avec Android 17 et plus de 80 nouveautés — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les propriétaires d’un Nothing Phone (3) peuvent installer Nothing OS 5.0 depuis ce lundi 12 octobre. Nothing avait dévoilé cette nouvelle version de son interface le 25 août. Carl Pei, cofondateur et CEO de la marque, la présente comme sa plus importante mise à jour logicielle. Elle repose sur Android 17 et touche autant à l’apparence du téléphone qu’à ses outils d’intelligence artificielle.
Nothing annonce plus de 80 améliorations, réparties en quatre familles : design, personnalisation, performances et IA. Pour l’instant, seul le Phone (3) y a droit. Les autres smartphones Nothing et ceux de sa sous-marque CMF suivront progressivement dans les prochains mois.
Nothing a publié ce calendrier modèle par modèle. Les Phone (4a) et (4a) Pro, ainsi que les Phone (3a) et (3a) Pro, sont attendus début novembre. Suivront les Phone (2a) et (2a) Plus mi-novembre, puis le Phone (3a) Lite fin décembre. Le Phone (4b) et le CMF Phone 2 Pro fermeront la marche mi-janvier 2027. La mise à jour pèse environ 2,84 Go pour les téléphones qui n’étaient pas inscrits à la bêta, et 1,68 Go pour les autres.
Trois nouveautés absentes de la bêta
La version publique apporte des changements que les testeurs de la bêta n’avaient pas encore vus. Le plus visible concerne l’écran d’accueil, repensé avec des effets de transparence et des couleurs adaptatives.
L’écran de verrouillage gagne aussi un nouveau cadran, baptisé Micrographics, qui regroupe la date, l’heure, la météo et les prochains rendez-vous de l’agenda.
Enfin, Essential Space, l’un des outils d’IA maison de Nothing, reçoit des améliorations. Elles arrivent par Google Play, avec une mise à jour de l’application. Nothing prévoit la prise en charge du protocole MCP vers octobre, puis une refonte de l’écran de capture à partir de novembre.
Le reste, déjà testé en bêta
Les autres nouveautés étaient déjà accessibles aux testeurs de la bêta. Côté design, Nothing OS 5.0 adopte une nouvelle police de caractères, Geist, pour l’ensemble de ses textes.
Côté personnalisation, deux widgets arrivent, Collector et Away Time. Surtout, on peut désormais déplacer plusieurs widgets d’un coup, tout comme les icônes d’applications.
Côté IA, Essential Voice devient plus rapide et une fonction Smart Collections fait son apparition. Essential Apps Builder, l’outil de Nothing pour créer des applications, s’utilise maintenant directement sur le téléphone.
Android 17 apporte aussi ses propres changements. Le volet des notifications et celui des réglages rapides peuvent désormais être séparés. Un glissement depuis la gauche de l’écran ouvre les notifications, un glissement depuis la droite ouvre les réglages. L’affichage combiné reste proposé.
Quick Share, le partage de fichiers sans fil d’Android, devient multiplateforme. Les indicateurs de confidentialité montrent plus clairement quand une application utilise la caméra, le micro ou la localisation. L’écran des applications récentes change aussi de présentation.
Trois modèles manquent au calendrier, les Phone (1), Phone (2) et CMF Phone 1. Ils ne passeront pas à Nothing OS 5.0 ni à Android 17.

articles.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
articles.text:
If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.
Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.
Gurmeet Saran
Employer
Anthropic in San Francisco
Title
Member of technical staff
Member grade
IEEE senior member
Alma maters
University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India
“My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications.
Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.
“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”
Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta
Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.
“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.
“That felt magical to me.”
After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.
While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.
“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”
The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.
With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.
From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.
Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.
“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”
“This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.”
Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.
“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.
That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.
He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.
Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic
Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.
To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.
“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”
His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.
“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”
Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.
“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”
IEEE can play a role in shaping AI development
Saran joined IEEE in March 2025.
“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”
He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.
“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”
Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

articles.title: Marvell Structera X 3406 and 3506 CXL 3.2 Memory Expanders
articles.text:
CXL has seen a massive surge recently, and Marvell announced its second-generation Structera X CXL memory expanders, adding CXL 3.2 support, PCIe Gen6 connectivity, and increasing memory channels from four to six. For hyperscalers running DDR4 and lower-speed DDR5 reclamation projects, that means the DDR4 version can support up to 18 DDR4 RDIMMs.
Marvell Structera X 3406 and 3506 CXL 3.2 Memory Expanders
Patrick gave us the decoder for the models:
- CXL 3 support is indicated by the first digit 3, just as the 2 in last year’s 2404 and 2504 marked CXL 2.0.
- 5 or 4, is the DDR generation
- The trailing two digits are the memory channel count.
Structera X 3406 is therefore a CXL 3 DDR4 part with six channels, while the 3506 is the CXL 3 DDR5 part, also at six channels. This announcement covers only the Structera X memory expansion line, not the Structera A near-memory compute controller that Marvell showed us last year. Still, CXL is focused on optimizing either bandwidth per core (since CXL bandwidth is in addition to native DDR bandwidth) and also capacity expansion.
PCIe Gen6 infrastructure and CXL 3.2 means we get roughly twice the bandwidth over the link, so that is how Marvell is adding more bandwidth from more memory channels.
Both new controllers stay on Marvell’s 5nm process and have LZ4 compression. Compression means the installed memory is storing more than the physical DRAM capacity. In this generation, Marvell is ensuring that the LZ4 can keep up with the interface so it is not a bottleneck. Here is the comparison table with key specs:
Structera X 3506 pairs six DDR5 channels with LZ4 compression at 250GB/s, while the 3406 runs DDR4 with six channels at 1600MT/s and 3DPC. That lets the DDR4 part take 18 DIMMs for up to 9TB per controller, and the DDR5 3506 takes 12 DIMMs for up to 6TB. CXL 3.2 lets up to four hosts share pooled memory, with up to 256GB/s of host bandwidth, double the prior generation’s 128GB/s.
We have known that memory pages have varying levels of compressibility, and Marvell gave us some data on that.
Final Words
We covered the first-generation Structera X and Structera A when we visited Marvell’s labs last year, including how line-rate LZ4 compression makes attached memory roughly half as costly per gigabyte. That hands-on look explains why CXL expanders are attractive as AI demand tightens DRAM supply and pushes DDR5 prices up.
For hyperscalers, this seems like a better version of the 2000 series. Unlike many of Marvell’s competitors who are moving to four channels in their CXL 3.x generation, six channels put 50% more DRAM behind a single controller.

articles.title: Critical SonicWall Vulnerability Exploited Days After Disclosure
articles.text:
Threat actors started exploiting a recently patched critical vulnerability in SonicWall SMA1000 appliances within days after public disclosure.
Tracked as CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score of 10), the security defect is described as a pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) issue affecting the SMA1000 Work Place interface.
According to SonicWall, an unintended alternate access path could allow a remote attacker “to direct the appliance to issue requests on their behalf and reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations.”
The company disclosed CVE-2026-102255 on October 6, urging customers to update their 6210, 7210, and 8200v models to software versions 12.5.0-03082 and 12.4.3-03670.
On Friday, threat intelligence firms Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) and Defused warned of the first exploitation attempts targeting the security bug.
Defused said that the first exploitation attempts reached its SMA decoys on October 8, only two days after public disclosure.
“SonicWall SMA1000 exploitation attempts are now being observed by Previdian sensors, consistent with CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS 10.0). The vulnerability allows unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF),” Previdian said.
Successful exploitation of the flaw could allow attackers to take over vulnerable devices, cybersecurity firm Horizon3.ai warned.

articles.title: The Fitbit Edge is for folks who don’t want to go totally screenless
articles.text:
The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official.
The Fitbit Edge is for folks who don’t want to go totally screenless
A middle-of-the-road option that combines the Air’s simplicity with some of the Pixel Watch’s smarts.
The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6.
Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. It also sports a replaceable battery that gets about a week on a single charge, though that estimate drops to two days if you enable the always-on display. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. As for dust and water resistance, the Edge is rated IP68 and is safe for swimming up to 5ATM.
There are a few notable hardware omissions. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. Also, unlike the Charge 6, it lacks an NFC chip for contactless payments. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. That price does, however, include three months of Google Health Premium.
The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Beyond supporting racket sports, it pulls in location data and routines to make inferences about activities. For example, if you go to a tennis court, it’ll assume any activity logged there is tennis. If you regularly do yoga on Tuesday mornings, it’ll infer that’s what your activity is. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities.
The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. It’ll also support turn-by-turn directions.
Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. It’ll also get the same Google Health software updates for features like blood pressure trends and insulin resistance levels. As far as non-fitness tracking features go, it has a clock, timers, alarms, media controls, and push notifications. It also supports heart rate broadcasting to certain gym equipment.
Despite the screen, the overall look is more in line with the Air. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

articles.title: Notebooks devem ficar mais caros em 2027, aponta relatório • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Notebooks devem ficar mais caros em 2027, aponta relatório
TrendForce relaciona aumento de preços causado por encarecimento de componentes e menor demanda de computadores.
Um relatório da consultoria TrendForce aponta para um aumento nos preços dos notebooks em 2027, assim como uma menor demanda de mercado. O principal motivo seria o encarecimento dos componentes de hardware, o que levaria a uma queda de quase dois dígitos na porcentagem de vendas. A firma também condiciona a situação a como as fabricantes vão lidar com esses valores mais altos: se vão absorver ou repassar os custos para os clientes.
No documento, foi analisada a precificação de um modelo não revelado durante o terceiro trimestre financeiro de 2026, indicando 68% do valor de produção referente a CPU, DRAM e SSD. A expectativa é por um aumento desse percentual no próximo ano, forçando as fabricantes a decidirem entre a alta dos preços finais ao consumidor ou a piora das especificações.
Vale lembrar que a indústria de hardware vem sofrendo um forte impacto pela crise das memórias RAM. O cenário já afetou os princiopais produtos de empresas como Samsung, Sony e Apple, incluindo celulares, cartões SD e até videogames.
Uma das saídas apontadas pelo relatório é levar a fabricação de volta para a China, desde que as condições geopolíticas e tarifárias se mantenham estáveis. O país asiático produz hoje cerca de 79% dos modelos vendidos, contra 76% em 2025. Este indicador deve chegar a 80% no próximo ano. Os custos de fabricação por lá costumam ser menores, em parte por causa da logística mais bem integrada e a mão de obra barata.
Outra solução que envolve o país é a melhoria de suas memórias DRAM, o que também pode ser uma saída para a crise no setor. É importante lembrar que, desde o início de 2025, os Estados Unidos vêm adotando políticas protecionistas contra eletrônicos chineses, dificultando o acesso de empresas americanas a componentes produzidos no país asiático.
O principal “inimigo” do mercado de hardware é o avanço das inteligências artificiais, que vêm demandando cada vez mais memória RAM para funcionar. Acontece que os servidores de IA precisam de peças incompatíveis com eletrônicos pessoais, como notebooks, computadores de mesa e videogames, entre outros exemplos. As indústrias têm de decidir entre um ou outro.
A TrendForce reafirmou que a expectativa é pela manutenção do cenário em 2027, mas há uma boa notícia: a previsão de menor impacto na oferta de memórias NAND Flash ao longo do próximo ano. Isso deve significar valores mais estáveis principalmente em SSDs.

articles.title: 82% of approved electronics are tested in China, but the FCC wants that figure down to zero by 2028
articles.text:
What just happened? The FCC's crackdown on Chinese electronics testing labs continues to move forward, this time with a proposed deadline for cutting them out of the US approval process. The commission will vote on October 29 on rules that would force manufacturers to move testing out of mainland China by December 2028. With 82% of devices authorized last year tested in the Asian nation, it could be a relocation headache for the companies affected.
The restrictions would cover test labs and certification bodies in countries that deny reciprocal treatment to their US counterparts. Chairman Brendan Carr says fewer than 4% of electronic devices are tested in American labs.
If this all sounds familiar, there's a reason. In May 2025, the FCC initially targeted labs owned, controlled, or directed by blacklisted companies and foreign adversary governments. There was also a separate proposal to extend restrictions to every lab in China.
In April 2026, the FCC voted to advance broader restrictions and seek public comment. The latest action would turn that proposal into adopted rules, assuming commissioners approve the draft, with a transition ending December 1, 2028.
Compared with the original 2025 restrictions, the broader proposal focuses on where the testing happens. Under the draft, recognition would be limited to labs in the US or economies with reciprocal recognition agreements. That means a Western company operating a lab in mainland China would still be affected.
Previous reports described the proposal covering China and Hong Kong, but law firm Steptoe notes that the latest draft includes Hong Kong and Taiwan among eligible reciprocal economies. Mainland China remains excluded, of course.
The draft would prevent approved labs from carrying out substantive certification work in excluded countries, including measurements, technical analysis, and preparation of test reports. However, routine administrative work and research testing outside the certification process would remain exempt.
The FCC argues that concentrating so much testing in one country creates security and disruption risks. Its earlier ownership restrictions have already cost 29 labs their recognition, according to the agency, but most Chinese facilities remained eligible.
The proposed transition gives manufacturers roughly two years to find alternatives. Existing certifications would remain valid, so devices already approved wouldn't suddenly need another trip through a testing lab.
Getting future hardware cleared for sale could be an issue, though. Moving testing away from factories might add expense and delays, particularly for smaller companies. And while consumers would keep their existing devices, the cost of approving the next ones could eventually reach store shelves.

articles.title: Impressão sem complicação: veja uma seleção de impressoras em promoção na Amazon
articles.text:
Se você está precisando renovar a impressora de casa ou do escritório, este é um bom momento para pesquisar. Reunimos três opções de impressoras multifuncionais em oferta na Amazon — modelos que combinam praticidade, economia de tinta e conectividade para diferentes perfis de uso. Confira.

articles.title: How bionic eyes are becoming a reality
articles.text:
If you’ve delved into the worlds of Star Trek, The Terminator or William Gibson’s cyberpunk novel Neuromancer, you’ll know that enhanced, electronic vision is a staple of science fiction. Now, what was once futuristic fiction is becoming a reality.
Researchers have developed bionic eyes that can restore some lost vision. These devices’ capabilities are currently basic, but they have been steadily improving in recent years.
One day, they might even offer features that transcend the limits of natural human eyesight – for instance by manipulating images in a way the human eye cannot or by seeing beyond the spectrum of visible light.
Technology that boosts people’s physical and mental abilities is no longer the preserve of science fiction. In this series, we explore cutting-edge ways that human capabilities could be augmented both now and in the near future – and the ethics of these innovations.
To date, implants have focused on combatting problems with the retina, the light-sensing layer of cells inside the back of the eye. Akin to the film in the back of a camera, the retina allows us to see the outside world. When things go badly wrong with it, the result can be a total loss of vision.
Work to fix retinal blindness with implants began more than two decades ago. One of the first devices, developed by the German manufacturer Retina Implant AG, featured a light-sensing chip placed under a person’s damaged retina. This connected with their remaining healthy retinal cells, which then transmitted the chip’s vision signal from the eye to the occipital cortex, the brain region where vision is perceived.
Surgery to implant the chip took about eight hours. This included creating a recess in the skull behind the ear to implant a power receiver and then connecting this with a wire beneath the skin to the chip.
The device offered only rudimentary vision, with patients seeing flashes of light that corresponded roughly to the shape of the object they were looking at. Many implants also broke over time, possibly because of the frequent rapid movements of the eye or corrosion caused by its salty liquid interior. Retina Implant AG ceased operations in 2019, citing its lack of medical progress as one of the main reasons.
The other leading early device, Argus II, combined a glasses-mounted camera with a chip surgically inserted on top of the retina. The camera’s picture was converted into a signal and transmitted wirelessly to the chip (along with power), which then stimulated healthy cells in the damaged retina using an array of 60 electrodes.
Despite positive early results and FDA authorisation in 2013, ARGUS II also ultimately failed to deliver sufficiently convincing results. It was discontinued in 2019.
Newer approaches
Despite these setbacks, investigators have persisted in trying to create artificial vision.
A newer approach is to use an external camera that wirelessly transfers power and image data to a chip implanted in the occipital cortex. This built research that placed electrical probes directly into the occipital cortex to stimulate visual perception.
This approach can help both patients with diseases of the retina and those with conditions affecting the optic nerve, which connects the retina to the brain. But exactly how much resolution can be achieved with this technique isn’t clear, as the retina’s high resolution and complex signal processing is lost.
One company trying this technique, Belgium-based ReVision Implant, is launching its first human clinical test in October 2026.
Another option is to use spectacles that transmit both images and power to a surgically inserted subretinal chip via an infrared signal. A device using this technique, Prima, has been tested in a specific disease of the retina called dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of blindness.
In a small clinical trial, the device restored functional central vision to 81% of patients, allowing them to read letters, numbers and words. The device is now authorised in 30 European countries.
As AMD is far more common than the inherited retinal diseases treated by most earlier devices, this device is much more appealing to investors. However, there are ethical questions here. Unlike patients with inherited retinal diseases, most with AMD still have good peripheral vision, so have much to lose if things go wrong. The complex surgery to implant a subretinal chip is far from zero risk.
Super-human vision?
Because these technologies relay visual information electronically, extra functionality could potentially be built into them. With Prima, patients can already use optical zoom, while algorithms that could allow for image sharpening have been proposed.
In the future, it is possible that devices may emerge that use cameras capable of seeing beyond the visible light spectrum. This could potentially offer thermal imaging and night vision. One device offering near-infrared vision has already been tested in primates.
But while exciting, these will probably not offer enhanced vision until the currently rudimentary artificial vision is advanced to the point that these “optional extras” become more relevant.
For now, there are still many biomaterial and electrical challenges preventing retinal implants from offering full, long-term vision restoration. However, a potentially greater challenge comes from competing biological solutions, such as stem cells, which are in the early stages of human trials.
These have also had a few false dawns and there are big obstacles to overcome in terms of cell survival and integration. But if new human retinal cells can replace those lost to disease, they could one day overtake bionic eyes entirely as the solution for vision restoration.

articles.title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure.
This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX, vLLM-Omni – Part 1, and vLLM-Omni – Part 2.
In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint. You then extend the same runtime with SemIf, formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options.
Solution overview
Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options.
For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model, maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions, and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments.
The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter.
Understand the input and output schemas
The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content, plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream:
The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content.
SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options:
The response returns option_ids, probabilities, and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose.
SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev, a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B, a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs.
Choose the right decision workflows
Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence.
Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint. The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access.
Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use.
Tune for your latency and quality targets
The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint.
| Configuration | AWS DLC for llama.cpp | Valid responses | Accuracy | Client p50 | Client p95 | 
| Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M, ml.c6i.8xlarge, 32 threads | llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 | 231/231 | 179/231 (77.5%) | 1.715 seconds | 19.291 seconds | 
| Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M, ml.g6e.xlarge, full GPU offload | llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 | 231/231 | 180/231 (77.9%) | 0.352 seconds | 0.599 seconds | 
Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e, g6, g5, then g4dn. SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge, and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality.
Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B Q4_K_M model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees.
Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context.
Prerequisites
You need:
- An AWS account and an S3 bucket in your deployment AWS Region.
- Python 3.10 or later, Git, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
- A purpose-specific CodeBuild service role for the optional SemIf extension.
- An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that SageMaker AI can assume.
- Permissions for SageMaker AI, Amazon ECR, Amazon S3, CodeBuild, IAM pass-role actions, and Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
- Quota for a compatible x86 CPU or NVIDIA GPU SageMaker real-time endpoint.
The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The SemIf extension keeps CPU as the default for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and offers an optional CUDA image with ordered instance pools. Review SageMaker AI pricing before creating an endpoint.
Deploy a decision model and extend it with SemIf
Use the following procedure to deploy the standard text-generation endpoint, then build the optional SemIf extension for structured decisions on CPU or GPU.
- Clone the code sample and install its dependencies.
- Set the deployment values for your account.
- Package the pinned GGUF model and tokenizer with CodeBuild.
         
         Wait for the returned build ID to reach SUCCEEDED. The build records the source revisions and checksums in model-manifest.json and stops if the GGUF checksum differs from the validated value.
- Deploy the GGUF model with the AWS DLC for llama.cpp.
         Resolve a digest-pinned server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 image from the AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation, then create the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint:
Select a server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 or server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 image rather than the corresponding EC2 image. The SageMaker AI images implement the /ping and /invocations container contract and map invocation payloads to chat completions.
This walkthrough supplies the GGUF model through the SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon S3. As an alternative, you can configure SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_REPO and SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_FILE to download a GGUF file from Hugging Face when the endpoint has network egress.
You don’t need a Dockerfile or an ECR repository for this path. Wait for the endpoint to enter InService, then send an OpenAI-compatible chat request:
- Build the optional SemIf child image and resolve its immutable digest.
         For CPU: For GPU, build the CUDA child image instead: After the build succeeds, construct the immutable image URI: The deployment script rejects mutable image tags.
- Deploy the SemIf endpoint.
         The CPU configuration uses a fixed instance type: Wait for the returned endpoint name to enter InService. This path sets n_gpu_layers=0. The adapter serializes scoring around one stateful llama.cpp context, so scale out with endpoint instances after measuring your workload rather than assuming parallel scoring inside one container.
For the GPU image, provide ordered instance pools and request full model offload: Instance pools are ordered placement fallbacks, not inference load balancing. SageMaker selects one available type for the variant. Endpoint creation can take longer while SageMaker AI works through the pool. Check the startup logs for the selected GPU and a message confirming that all model layers were offloaded.
- Invoke the SemIf endpoint with the example decision.
         The request declares stable IDs for each allowed option: The response preserves the option order and includes conditional probabilities, raw logits, token and prompt metadata, and the pinned model identity: Apply application-level thresholds and fallbacks. Don’t use a model decision as a substitute for authorization.
Clean up
Delete the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model:
The script deletes only those explicitly named SageMaker AI resources. Delete the CodeBuild projects, ECR repository, model and source objects in Amazon S3, logs, and purpose-specific IAM roles when you no longer need them.
Conclusion
The AWS DLC for llama.cpp gives you a managed foundation for serving decision models on SageMaker AI across CPU and GPU instances. It can load GGUF models from SageMaker AI model artifacts or a configured Hugging Face repository, then serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint without requiring a custom container. When your application needs direct logits and model state operations, you can extend the DLC with a SemIf adapter. Choose CPU for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive, and choose GPU when prompt prefill and tail latency affect the application experience.
Review the code sample, AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation, and SageMaker AI custom inference container contract to adapt the deployment for your workload.

articles.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
articles.text:
At a glance
- StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers
- AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale
- StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student
- The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance
- Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor
In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration.
StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics.
Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage.
Measuring what a student simulator needs to do
A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable.
Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.
StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance.
These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance.
Training personalized simulators from sparse student records
StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.
Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.
StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student.
The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records.
StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.
Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors
The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.
The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition.
The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors.
Looking ahead
StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students.
The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes.
The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

articles.title: A Spanish museum built a Cray-1 replica powered by 30 old Mac minis
articles.text:
In a nutshell: A Spanish computing museum has built a working cluster of 30 Mac minis inside a full-size replica of the Cray-1 supercomputer. Most of the Macs are from 2012, but together they have reached a reported 1.3 teraflops in matrix-multiplication tests. Visitors can watch calculations run on a single core before seeing the workload distributed across the cluster.
The Museo de Historia de la Computación spent 18 months developing the exhibit. The replica preserves the appearance of the 1976 machine without trying to reproduce its internal hardware. Built to mark the 50th anniversaries of the Cray-1 and Apple's founding, the model is now on permanent display at the museum alongside two unused authentic Cray CX1 systems.
The cluster contains five quad-core Intel Core i7 machines and 25 dual-core Core i5 models. All but two units, which date to 2014, were made in 2012. That configuration provides 70 cores, although only 64 were active in the most recent tests after one node went offline.
The museum previously reported 1.5 teraflops with all 70 cores running. Both results came from a custom Python matrix-multiplication script, so the figures reflect performance on that test rather than across a range of applications.
A master Mac mini in the exhibit's control terminal coordinates the other machines. The team chose macOS Mojave 10.14 instead of Linux, using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) to handle communication between nodes.
This is a different approach from the original Cray-1's vector processing, which applied an instruction to multiple data elements. The replica distributes calculations among independent processors. The original machine had a theoretical peak performance of approximately 160 megaflops, far below the results reported for the Mac cluster.
It's worth remembering that one figure is a theoretical peak, while the others come from the museum's custom test. Nevertheless, the exhibit gives visitors a way to see the difference between a purpose-built supercomputer and a cluster assembled from consumer machines.
The team mounted the Macs vertically on aluminum trays inside a steel rack chassis. That arrangement allows warm air to rise through the tower and escape through grilles at the top, cooling the enclosure by natural convection without additional mechanical fans.
The museum says the cluster is quiet enough that visitors must stand close to hear it. Its two gigabit Ethernet switches, installed at the base, reportedly produce the most noticeable noise, at 30 – 33 decibels. The developers plan to replace them with silent models.
The control terminal borrows design elements from the DEC VT05 and Processor Technology Sol-20. An analog control panel adds to its 1970s appearance, while the Mac mini inside controls the cluster.
The developers originally intended to install CRT monitors. They switched to flat Samsung displays to avoid the connection problems involved in pairing older monitors with newer computers.
Further additions are planned. These include original lamps from an IBM System/3, 3.5-inch and 5.25-inch floppy drives mounted beneath the desk, and a 3D-printed keyboard shell based on the HP 250 design.
The team also wants to expand the computing hardware. Half of the replica's tower is still empty, and a proposed crowdfunding campaign would pay for 70 – 80 M4 Mac minis. The goal is to build a cluster powerful enough to make the TOP500 list.

articles.title: Why Koho won’t bet on prediction markets | BetaKit
articles.text:
This week, we’re talking with Canada’s newest fintech unicorn, Koho.
Earlier this year, Koho raised $130 million CAD as part of its quest to move from challenger bank to an actual bank.
“I think that we will look back on prediction markets the same way we look back on altcoins and … NFTs.”
The company is nearing the end of its 5-year journey to secure a Schedule 1 banking licence, which CEO Daniel Eberhard claims will help Koho offer more competitive lending and savings rates to everyday Canadians.
With the company having recently achieved one major milestone and on the precipice of another, it seemed like a good time to check in. And this convo is wide-ranging, covering the increasing amount of international competition flooding into the Canadian financial space, the lack of participation in new payments infrastructure from the Big Six banks, and all the new features Koho has launched or plans to launch in its ever-expanding portfolio—including maybe a Koho telco?
We also talked about one feature Koho does not plan to launch: prediction markets.
Subscribe: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Overcast, Pocket Casts, RSS
To Eberhard, prediction markets are techwashing what amounts to gambling, which could lead to a bunch of negative downstream social effects. It’s a principled stance you’d hope to see from someone about to run a bank, and it’s not the only candid moment Eberhard offers. I prompted him to reflect on lessons learned from this decade-plus journey, and Koho’s CEO and founder had a lot to share.
So what has Daniel Eberhard learned as Koho approaches the end of the beginning?
Let’s dig in.
PRESENTED BY
The BetaKit Podcast is presented by BetaKit Most Ambitious.
Amid global uncertainty, the path forward is clear: Canada’s moment to build is now.
Presented by Uber Canada, DMZ, and National Bank of Canada, BetaKit Most Ambitious is back, telling stories of nearly 100 Canadian innovators strengthening our nation’s autonomy, security, and prosperity.
