articles.title: Fervo’s Utah Geothermal Plant Starts Sending Clean Power To The Grid
articles.text:
This article was originally published by Canary Media.
The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah — marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide.
The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since then. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California.
Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity.
“Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” says Dawn Owens, Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets.
With the first unit online, Fervo says it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 January, 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW — which is supported by a new agreement with Google — is under construction and slated to come online in 2028.
Fervo’s Next-Generation Geothermal Journey
Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens says the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets.
“This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she says.
Fervo, which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments.
Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy
Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers — all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say.
“Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” says Mitchell Smith, who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added.
Enhanced Geothermal Energy Gets Cheaper
Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per kilowatt, the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per kilowatt in 2025.)
Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers. While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods — like in the evening, when solar output declines — to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “behind the meter” to directly power data centers, so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens says.
“We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she says. On Cape Station’s powering-up, she adds, “That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”

articles.title: ReplaySSM: Rethinking State Storage for Faster Hybrid-Model Decoding | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Hybrid models interleave state-space model (SSM) layers with a few attention layers. NVIDIA Nemotron 3, Qwen3.5 through Qwen3.8, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3-Flash are all built this way, with Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) as the SSM layer.
SSM layers are designed to make decoding fast: they use a fixed-size state in place of a key-value (KV) cache that grows with context length. At serving batch sizes, however, the SSM layers, not attention, can be the latency bottleneck up to 100K tokens of context. SSM layers also complicate two techniques that reliably speed up attention decoding: speculative decoding and quantization.
ReplaySSM makes SSM layers the fast part again. It represents the SSM state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs. This separates output computation from state updates and addresses three challenges in current SSM decoding: state traffic, rollback for speculative decoding, and error accumulation in a quantized state.
ReplaySSM is joint work between NVIDIA and the Dao AI Lab at Princeton. The paper, ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State, details all three benefits and presents the full evaluation. It is available on arXiv, with code on GitHub. It is integrated into NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer, and also runs in production in GLM-5.3-Flash and Kimi-K3.
Why SSM layers can become a decoding bottleneck
Take the Mamba-2 layer used in NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra as an example. It decodes one token with the following recurrence:
where \(S_t\) is the state, \(\alpha_t\) is a data-dependent decay, and \(v_t\), \(k_t\), and \(q_t\) are the token’s inputs. Each step loads \(S_{t-1}\) from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), applies the decay and a rank-1 update, computes the output with \(q_t\), and stores \(S_t\) back. GDN and KDA add a delta-rule correction, but their updates can be written in the same outer-product form, so what follows applies to them too.
During decoding, the state does two jobs. It is read to produce this token’s output, and it is updated to become the next token’s state. Conventional decoding does both at once: each step updates the state, reads the output from it, and stores it for the next step. All three challenges come from this fusion.
State memory traffic
An SSM decoding step loads and stores the full state while performing little arithmetic on it, so the kernel is bound by HBM bandwidth, not compute. At serving batch sizes, that makes the SSM layers, not attention, the largest component of the decode step up to 100K tokens on Nemotron-3-Super-NVFP4 at batch size 256 on one NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU (Figure 2, left).
Two factors drive this:
- Layer count: The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers.
- State size: One layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, while an FP8 KV entry is 0.5 KiB per token, so an SSM layer’s state is the size of an attention layer’s KV cache for 8K tokens.
Rollback for speculative decoding
Speculative decoding has a drafter propose T tokens, verifies them in one pass through the target model, and rolls back to the last accepted token. Attention naturally supports rollback by moving the KV cache pointer. But once an SSM has summarized the drafts into its state, the update has no easy inverse, so rollback becomes expensive. Serving engines such as vLLM work around this by storing a state snapshot after every draft token and picking the one that matches the accepted prefix. That is one read and T writes per step on a memory-bound path, and the snapshots cap how many requests fit in GPU memory. As a result, speculative decoding, a reliable speedup for Transformers, barely helps SSMs at serving batch sizes.
State quantization
The quantized state produces the output and is the input to the next update, so its rounding error re-enters the recurrence at every step. A KV cache has no such loop: a quantized entry is read many times but never written back into itself, which is why KV caches tolerate lower precision than SSM states. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4, for example, uses the NVIDIA NVFP4 4-bit floating-point format for its weights, with an FP8 KV cache and an FP32 SSM state.
How ReplaySSM represents the state
The SSM recurrence can be unrolled over a window of h tokens:
where \(S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}\) is the state before the window and \(\gamma\) is the cumulative decay. Conventional decoding follows the left side step by step. ReplaySSM uses the right side: it represents the state as a checkpoint plus a small buffer of recent input records (\(\alpha_j\), \(v_j\), \(k_j\)) for Mamba-2.
On most steps, which we call non-flush steps, it appends the current inputs to the buffer and computes the output from the checkpoint and the buffer without storing a state. When the buffer of L records fills, a flush step folds the buffered inputs into the checkpoint, writes the new checkpoint to HBM once, and clears the buffer. The outputs match conventional decoding up to floating-point differences. ReplaySSM’s approach can be summarized in three questions:
What does ReplaySSM do?
It caches recent SSM inputs and represents the state as a checkpoint plus those inputs.
What does this change?
It separates output computation from state updates: outputs are computed every step, while the checkpoint is updated once per window.
What does this achieve?
It reduces state memory traffic, simplifies speculative rollback, and supports low-precision state reads without propagating their rounding error through recurrent updates.
How we evaluated ReplaySSM
We evaluate four hybrid models from two families, Nemotron 3 with Mamba-2 layers and Qwen3.5 with GDN layers, from 4B dense models on one NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU to 120B-class mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on one NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU (Table 1). We implemented ReplaySSM in vLLM and compared it with vLLM’s own kernels at their best launch configuration.
Performance runs keep the SSM state in FP32, the default precision for these models, and use a window of L = 16, the best-performing window size for all four models. Speculative decoding tests use each model’s multi-token prediction (MTP) head to generate draft tokens.
| Model | SSM layer | Weights | GPU | SSM / attention layers | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3-Nano-4B | Mamba-2 | BF16 | 1×H100 | 21 / 4 | 
| Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B | Mamba-2 | NVFP4 | 1×B300 | 40 / 8 | 
| Qwen3.5-4B | GDN | BF16 | 1×H100 | 24 / 8 | 
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | GDN | NVFP4 | 1×B300 | 36 / 12 | 
Benefit 1: Reduce state memory traffic
Over a window of L tokens, conventional decoding reads the state L times and writes it L times. ReplaySSM still reads the checkpoint on every step, because the output needs it, but writes it only once, during the flush. A non-flush step has one job—computing the output—and writes only the new input record, a few vectors instead of a full matrix. This roughly halves the dominant state traffic.
At serving batch sizes, memory bandwidth limits the conventional kernel’s performance, so reducing state memory traffic speeds up decoding. At batch size 1, other sources of latency dominate, and ReplaySSM provides no speedup in these tests. At batch size 256, the kernel runs 1.46× to 1.80× faster, and the decode step runs 1.20× to 1.47× faster across the four models (Figure 3). The end-to-end gain grows with batch size because the SSM share of the step grows.
Benefit 2: Simplify rollback and speed up verification
In speculative decoding, ReplaySSM appends the inputs of all T draft tokens to the input buffer before verification and commits the accepted prefix afterward by advancing the buffer pointer. As with a KV cache, records beyond the pointer are ignored, and the next append overwrites them. There is no state snapshot to save for each draft token and no state to restore (Figure 2, middle). A flush folds only committed records into the checkpoint, so it never waits for the accepted length.
This separation offers another benefit. Conventional decoding must produce two things per token, the output and the updated state, because the next token consumes the state. A non-flush step in ReplaySSM produces only the output, and computing only the output opens up a different computation method. For one update from a zero state, \(o = (v k^\top)q = v(k^\top q)\). The expression on the left builds a \(d_v \times d_k\) state and reads it. The expression on the right forms a scalar and scales a vector without building the state. For T drafts against h committed records, the same idea gives the following expression:
with D holding the cumulative decays of the draft positions and W a causally masked matrix of decays. We call this output-only evaluation. The checkpoint is used once for all T queries, and everything else is two small matrix products over the cached keys, the cached values, and the draft queries. No intermediate state is formed, which saves on-chip memory and FLOPs, and Tensor Cores can speed up these computations. Also, \(K^\top Q\) is shared by all value heads in a group. This is the same chunkwise computation that prefill kernels already use, with the buffer and the drafts as the chunk. GDN can also use this form. Output-only evaluation applies to standard decoding too, but it matters most in verification, where T multiplies the arithmetic per step.
Figure 4 shows speculative serving throughput on GSM8K prompts with T = 4 on the two 120B-class models. At batch size 512, ReplaySSM delivers 1.85× and 2.10× the throughput of vLLM’s speculative decoding, with matched acceptance lengths.
The gain has two sources.
- Faster verification: vLLM’s kernel stores one snapshot per token, so its latency grows with T and at T = 8 is almost five times that of vLLM’s standard decoding step. ReplaySSM writes no state on most steps, so it verifies eight tokens in about the time of one standard step, flushes included (Figure 5).
- Higher concurrency: Draft state snapshots consume GPU memory and cap concurrency. Conventional speculation stops gaining beyond batch size 128, and on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4, it falls below standard decoding at batch size 512, while ReplaySSM keeps scaling with batch size.
Benefit 3: Limit error accumulation with separate precisions
A lower-precision state requires fewer bytes, which reduces latency when memory bandwidth limits kernel performance. On Mamba-2, the non-flush kernel runs 3.8× faster when reading NVFP4 state than when reading FP32 state.
ReplaySSM changes quantization in two ways. First, the checkpoint is written once per window instead of once per step, so a single low-precision checkpoint is rounded once every L steps. The Nemotron 3 Ultra report explores this periodic checkpointing approach. It reduces rounding frequency, but rounding error still enters later updates.
Second, non-flush steps read the state only to compute outputs, while flush steps update the checkpoint used in subsequent state updates. The two jobs can use different precisions. We keep a high-precision checkpoint for the recurrence and a low-precision copy for non-flush reads. A flush starts from the high-precision checkpoint, incorporates the buffered inputs, and casts the result independently into both formats. The low-precision copy is never read back into the recurrence, so its rounding error affects only the outputs of the current window and never propagates across the recurrence. Writing the additional low-precision copy during a flush reduces the amount of data read on every non-flush step. Acceptance, rollback, and buffer management are unchanged (Figure 2, right).
Figure 6 measures the output error as the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from FP32-state decoding under teacher forcing on PG-19 text, out to 128K generated tokens. A shared FP8 or NVFP4 checkpoint accumulates error with length. Keeping the recurrence in FP32 removes most of the growth: at 128K tokens on Qwen3.5-4B, NVFP4 reads with an FP32 recurrence cut the KL from 0.136 to 0.0038. What remains is the read error, which does not grow with length.
An FP16 recurrence with stochastic rounding (SR) tracks FP32 closely, so a half-precision recurrence checkpoint is enough. Better quantization of the read copy, such as separate scales along the state and channel dimensions, could cut the remaining read error further.
We also checked whether the KL gap shows up in downstream accuracy. Table 2 shows GPQA-Diamond, the benchmark with the longest generations of the three we ran. A shared NVFP4 checkpoint loses 3 to 31 percentage points of accuracy across the four models. NVFP4 reads with an FP16 or FP8 recurrence recover most of that and keep three out of four models within about 2 percentage points of FP32.
| GPQA-Diamond, change from FP32 (points) | FP32 accuracy | Shared NVFP4 checkpoint | NVFP4 read, FP16+SR recurrence | NVFP4 read, FP8+SR recurrence | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-3-Nano-4B | 56.7 | −31.3 | −6.7 | −5.6 | 
| Nemotron-3-Super-NVFP4 | 79.3 | −12.5 | −1.4 | −1.4 | 
| Qwen3.5-4B | 76.3 | −3.2 | +0.7 | +1.5 | 
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4 | 82.7 | −5.2 | −2.0 | −1.7 | 
Figure 7 shows how accuracy loss varies with generation length on GPQA-Diamond. Across the three benchmarks:
- GPQA-Diamond: On Nemotron-3-Super-NVFP4, the shared checkpoint tracks FP32 accuracy for shorter generations but diverges from it as generation length grows. The separate-precision configuration stays close to FP32 throughout.
- MMLU-Pro and Math-L5: Generations are generally shorter than those in GPQA-Diamond. Three out of four models lose at most 3 percentage points of accuracy with a shared NVFP4 checkpoint, while the separate checkpoint configurations stay within half a percentage point of FP32 on average.
The paper includes results for all three benchmarks and a long-input RULER test.
Get started with ReplaySSM
ReplaySSM is in production. GLM-5.3-Flash serves with ReplaySSM, and Z.ai’s infrastructure report describes adding it to the KDA decode kernel. Kimi-K3 caches the SSM inputs of draft tokens for verification in its KDA layers and cites ReplaySSM as a concurrent approach. ReplaySSM is also integrated into open-source inference frameworks such as TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, SGLang, and FlashInfer.
To learn more, check out these resources:
- Read the paper: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
- Try the code: github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM
- Serve hybrid models with ReplaySSM in TensorRT-LLM: PR 14203, PR 16464
- Serve hybrid models with ReplaySSM in vLLM: PR 48018, PR 52506, PR 52928
- Use the ReplaySSM kernels in FlashInfer: PR 3975, PR 4081
- Read the earlier post from the Dao AI Lab for a longer walkthrough of standard and speculative decoding

articles.title: Microsoft: Windows 11 23H2 reaches end of support in 30 days
articles.text:
Microsoft has reminded customers that systems running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions will stop receiving security updates next month.
The announcement follows the end of support for Windows 11 23H2 Home and Pro editions in November 2025.
Users are now advised to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 (also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update), which became generally available in September 2026 as an enablement package (eKB) and will reach end of support for consumers in October 2029.
"The November 2026 Windows security update will be the last update available for these editions. After this date, devices running these editions will no longer receive monthly security updates containing protections from the latest security threats," it said in a message center update. "We recommend updating eligible devices running Windows 11, version 23H2 to a supported version of Windows 11."
Windows 11 26H2 is now available in a phased rollout to eligible Windows 11 devices for those who have enabled the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" setting.
"If the update is ready for your device, it will download and install automatically, and a single restart will complete the process," Microsoft added.
You can also manually check if the update is available by clicking "Check for updates" in the Settings > Windows Update section. If the system is ready to update, you'll see the option to "Download and install Windows 11, version 26H2."
You can find more information about Windows 11 servicing dates on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool. Microsoft also provides a complete list of products that will reach end of support or be retired in 2026.
Earlier this year, Microsoft extended the free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for home users until October 2027.
Last month, it also announced that Windows Server 2022 reaches the end of mainstream support this Tuesday (but will switch to extended support until October 14, 2031) and that Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions will also stop receiving updates this week (with Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education editions remaining under mainstream support until October 2027).
More recently, on Thursday, it warned customers that devices running unsupported versions of Windows will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation.

articles.title: Très bonne nouvelle pour le prix du Jaecoo 5 électrique en France : comment sa production en Espagne va faire chuter les prix du SUV électrique chinois — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cela va faire un an qu’Omoda Jaecoo, la marque dédiée à l’export du groupe chinois Chery, est arrivée en France.
    Pour aller plus loin
« Nous ne sommes pas stupides » : le géant chinois Chery arrive aujourd’hui en France, voici ses voitures et sa stratégie pour réussir
            
Si la majorité de la gamme vendue en France est hybride, c’est pour une bonne raison : les voitures sont assemblées en Chine, excluant de fait les voitures électriques du bonus écologique (renommé coup de pouce CEE) et les rendant bien moins attractives pour notre marché.
Quelques semaines après l’arrivée du Jaecoo 5 EV en France, Chery a profité du Mondial de l’Auto pour annoncer une nouvelle dont beaucoup se doutaient : le début de production du SUV électrique dans l’usine Chery de Barcelone, en Espagne, garant a priori de l’éligibilité au coup de pouce CEE.
Des tarifs en baisse
Cette production européenne, avec des composants européens, permettrait donc au Jaecoo 5 EV d’atteindre l’éco-score minimal requis pour accéder aux incitations.
L’avantage est double. Pour les particuliers, cela permettra d’accéder au coup de pouce CEE, donc d’abaisser les prix.
En partant de la double hypothèse que la production européenne ne modifie pas les prix du SUV et que les montants n’évoluent pas d’ici là (des candidats à la présidentielle envisageaient d’aller jusqu’à la suppression totale du dispositif pour baisser les prix de l’essence), alors le Jaecoo 5 EV pourrait débuter à environ 28 900 euros pour tous et 26 490 euros pour les ménages les plus modestes.
Pour les professionnels et les flottes d’entreprise, le Jaecoo 5 pourrait donc être éligible aux règles sur les avantages en nature, de quoi s’offrir un nouveau canal de distribution.
Un rapport prix/prestation bien plus alléchant
Ne nous le cachons pas : côté technique, le Jaecoo 5 EV ne vend pas de rêve. Le SUV de 4,38 m de long s’offre une batterie LFP de 61 kWh, de quoi promettre jusqu’à 402 km d’autonomie selon le cycle WLTP. La recharge sur borne rapide demande 34 minutes pour passer de 10 à 80 %.
Oui mais voilà, ces chiffres assez moyens sont soudainement plus acceptables une fois que la prime CEE passe par là. En débutant sous les 30 000 euros avec un équipement pléthorique (toit vitré, sièges avant chauffants et ventilés, écrans connectés, pompe à chaleur, etc.) et un coffre généreux de 480 litres (+ 35 litres à l’avant), le Jaecoo 5 EV marque des points.
Face à lui, on pourra proposer la Renault 4 E-Tech (408 km WLTP) ou encore le Ford Puma Gen-E, proposés à tarifs équivalents mais aux équipements moindres. Bref, un repositionnement qui redonne un sacré coup de fouet à ce SUV chinois. Rendez-vous dans quelques semaines pour les chiffres définitifs.
Pour ne rater aucun bon plan, rejoignez notre nouveau channel WhatsApp Frandroid Bons Plans, garanti sans spam !

articles.title: “Les entreprises d’IA commencent à faire des téléphones” : Apple et Samsung sont prévenus
articles.text:
“Les entreprises d’IA commencent à faire des téléphones” : Apple et Samsung sont prévenus
Le patron de Qualcomm, le fabricant des puces qui font tourner une bonne partie des smartphones Android, vend la mèche : des géants de l’intelligence artificielle lui réclament, d’ici 2028, de quoi faire tenir dans un téléphone une IA trois fois plus grosse qu’aujourd’hui, allumée en permanence. Il refuse de dire qui, mais un nom revient avec insistance, celui d’OpenAI, le créateur de ChatGPT, qui préparerait en secret son propre smartphone.
Le 8 octobre, le journaliste américain Alex Heath a diffusé dans son podcast Sources un entretien avec Cristiano Amon, enregistré en public au Snapdragon Summit de Qualcomm, fin septembre à Hawaï. Le patron du concepteur des puces Snapdragon y lâche une confidence lourde de sens.
Certaines entreprises "à la pointe de l'IA" lui réclament de quoi loger au moins 100 milliards de paramètres dans un téléphone d'ici 2028, avec une intelligence artificielle active "à peu près tout le temps". Relancé, il enfonce le clou : "Les entreprises d'IA commencent à faire des téléphones." Leurs noms ? Amon les garde pour lui.
IA dans le smartphone : 100 milliards de paramètres, un saut vertigineux
Le Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, dévoilé le 22 septembre, sert d'étalon. Gravée en 2 nm, cette puce exécute localement des modèles de plus de 30 milliards de paramètres, dont environ 3 milliards seulement s'activent à chaque étape. La cible réclamée représente donc à peu près le triple.
Le calcul donne le vertige. Même compressé à 4 bits par paramètre, un tel modèle pèse une cinquantaine de gigaoctets, soit le double des 24 Go de mémoire vive que gèrent les nouvelles puces Snapdragon. Qualcomm compte sur le chargement depuis le stockage flash pour repousser ce plafond.
Pour Amon, l'effort se justifie. Le téléphone détient seul le contexte personnel (applications, capteurs, habitudes) dont un agent a besoin pour agir à la place de son propriétaire.
	
Les humains ne vont pas se rendre dans un data center, sonner à la porte et demander qu'on leur donne de l'IA.
Smartphone ChatGPT : OpenAI préparerait son propre téléphone
Fin avril, l'analyste Ming-Chi Kuo révélait qu'OpenAI préparait son propre smartphone taillé pour ChatGPT, d'abord attendu pour 2028. Huit jours plus tard, il assurait que le projet avait été accéléré, avec une production de masse visée dès le premier semestre 2027 et quelque 30 millions d'exemplaires d'ici fin 2028. Détail piquant, une puce MediaTek tiendrait la corde. OpenAI n'a rien confirmé.
	
Le smartphone est le seul appareil capable de saisir en temps réel toutes les données sur son propriétaire, l’information la plus importante pour le raisonnement des agents IA.
Dans la foulée, Amon confiait à Fortune travailler avec "à peu près tous" les grands noms de l'IA, OpenAI et Meta compris, sur des appareils confidentiels. Le précédent existe déjà en Chine : il cite le téléphone Doubao de ByteDance, la maison mère de TikTok, fabriqué par Nubia autour de l'assistant maison. "Et il y en a d'autres qui arrivent", prévient-il.
Pour Samsung et Apple, l’alerte est sérieuse. Les 30 millions d’exemplaires visés par OpenAI pèsent peu face aux 1,2 milliard de smartphones vendus chaque année, mais l’enjeu se situe ailleurs. Amon annonce une “bataille des agents”, ces assistants capables d’agir à notre place : celui qui contrôlera l’agent contrôlera l’usage du téléphone. Le patron de Qualcomm parie aussi sur un supercycle de renouvellement. Selon lui, les ventes de smartphones reculent de 20 % cette année, plombées par des prix de la mémoire multipliés par cinq ou six, et une demande en sommeil attend les premiers vrais smartphones IA.
